teile.einleitung: Cough syrup is a liquid medicine for coughs. It is thick and often tastes sweet, so it is easy to swallow. All the same, it is not a sweet but a medicine.
wichtigste: Cough syrup is meant to ease a cough.
It is liquid, thick and often sweet.
You measure it out exactly with a measuring spoon or cup.
Many children’s syrups contain an extract of ivy leaves.
Onion syrup and honey are old home remedies for coughs.
Too much cough syrup can do harm, because it is a medicine.
Babies under one year old must not be given honey.

abschnitte.text: **Cough syrup** is a medicine in liquid form. Syrup is thick and often sweet, so children, too, like to swallow it. There are syrups that **loosen the mucus** so that it is easier to cough up. Others are meant to calm the **urge to cough** so that you can sleep better. Which syrup is suitable is best told by a doctor or an expert at the chemist’s.

With many cough syrups, a **measuring spoon** or a **measuring cup** comes in the box. That way you take exactly the amount that is written in the **leaflet** or that the doctor recommends. An ordinary tablespoon is too inexact for this. Because syrup is sticky and germs stay on the spoon, you wash the measuring spoon after each use. Cough syrup should also be kept where small children cannot reach it.

Many cough syrups for children contain an **extract of ivy leaves**. It is meant to loosen the mucus. **Thyme** or ribwort plantain are also found in some syrups. Ivy itself, by the way, is poisonous if you eat the leaves or berries. In the syrup, only a purified extract is used, in a precisely measured amount.

In the past, too, many families made their cough syrup themselves. For **onion syrup** you chop onions small and add sugar or honey. After a few hours a sweet juice forms. **Honey** on its own is also a popular home remedy: it coats the throat like a film and soothes it. **Babies under one year old**, however, must not be given honey, because it can be dangerous for them.

gewusst: The word syrup comes from Arabic and originally meant roughly “drink”.
A cough with a cold often lasts two to three weeks, even if you otherwise already feel well again.

teile.einleitung: The hip joint joins the pelvis to the thigh. It is one of the largest and strongest joints in the body. Every person has two of them, and they carry the whole weight of the upper body when standing.
wichtigste: A person has two hip joints.
The head of the thigh bone sits in a hollow in the pelvis, the hip socket.
The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint.
Because the hip socket is deep, the joint is very stable but less mobile than the shoulder.
When standing, the hip joints carry the weight of the upper body.
In Switzerland, babies’ hip joints are often examined with ultrasound.
If a hip joint is badly worn, it can be replaced with an artificial one.

abschnitte.text: The hip joint is a **ball-and-socket joint**. The round **femoral head** at the upper end of the thigh bone sits in a hollow in the pelvis, the **hip socket**. Both joint surfaces are covered with smooth **cartilage** so that they slide well. A joint fluid acts like lubricating oil. Strong ligaments and muscles hold the joint together.

The hip socket is **very deep** and closes well around the femoral head. That is why the hip joint is very stable but less mobile than the shoulder joint, whose socket is shallow. You can swing your arm almost in a circle, but not your leg so far. In return, the **hip joints** hold the whole weight of the upper body when standing, and when running and jumping even several times that.

When you march and pull your knee up to your chest, you **bend** the hip joint. You can also stretch the leg backwards, spread it out to the side and turn it inwards or outwards. In **hula hooping**, you make the hoop turn around your waist by circling your hips. Dancing, cycling and climbing stairs all need the hip.

In some babies, the hip socket is too shallow. This is called **hip dysplasia**. That is why babies’ hip joints in Switzerland are often examined with **ultrasound**, usually in the first weeks of life. If a misalignment is recognised early, it can be treated well, for example with special spreader trousers.

In older people, the cartilage in the hip joint can wear away. This wear is called **osteoarthritis** and can cause severe pain. When medicines and exercise therapy no longer help, those affected often get an **artificial hip joint**, a hip replacement. The operation is now one of the most common procedures on joints.

gewusst: The ligament at the front of the hip joint is regarded as the strongest ligament in the human body.
When walking, several times your own body weight acts on a hip joint.

teile.einleitung: In the brain there are not only nerve cells. At least as important are the **glial cells**. They support, supply, protect and insulate the nerve cells so that these can work well.
wichtigste: Glial cells support the nerve cells in the nervous system.
The name comes from the Greek word “glia” for glue.
In the 19th century, Rudolf Virchow coined the term neuroglia, meaning “nerve glue”.
Oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheaths in the central nervous system.
Astrocytes help with the blood-brain barrier, and microglial cells take over the immune defence.
According to newer estimates, there are about as many glial cells in the brain as nerve cells.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, the German doctor **Rudolf Virchow** described cells between the nerve cells. He called them **neuroglia**, that is, “nerve glue”. The word **glia** comes from Greek and means **glue**. For a long time people thought that these cells only held the nerve cells together. Today we know that they have many important jobs.

Nerve cells carry electrical signals along long extensions. Many of these are surrounded by a fat-rich casing, the **myelin sheaths**. They work like the insulation of a cable and make conduction much faster. In the **central nervous system**, that is, in the brain and spinal cord, the **oligodendrocytes** make these casings. In the nerves outside it, the **Schwann cells** do this.

The **astrocytes** are named because they look star-shaped. They are very versatile. They supply the nerve cells with nutrients and **buffer potassium**, which is released when nerve cells fire. With their extensions, they surround the blood vessels and help with the **blood-brain barrier**. This barrier keeps many harmful substances in the blood away from the brain.

The **microglial cells** are the defence cells of the brain. They take over the **immune defence**, look for germs and clear away dead cells. The **ependymal cells** line the brain ventricles, which are fluid-filled cavities in the brain. They also line the central canal of the spinal cord.

For a long time it was said that there were ten times more glial cells than nerve cells in the brain. Newer counts, however, show: there are **about the same number**. Unlike most nerve cells, glial cells can still divide even in adults. If this division gets out of control, a tumour can form. A brain tumour that starts from glial cells is called a **glioma**.

gewusst: The figure “ten times more glial cells” stood in textbooks for decades, until people counted again.
Rudolf Virchow was not only a doctor and researcher but also a politician in Berlin.

teile.einleitung: Brain death means that the whole brain has failed irreversibly. In Switzerland a person is then regarded as dead, even if their heart is still beating with the help of machines. The diagnosis follows strict rules.
wichtigste: Brain death is the irreversible failure of all functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem.
The heart can keep on beating because it has a pacemaker of its own and artificial ventilation supplies oxygen.
The Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences issues the guidelines for determining death.
Two qualified doctors who do not belong to the transplant team determine brain death.
In the apnoea test, doctors check whether any breathing of the person’s own starts.
In a vegetative state the brainstem is still working, in brain death it is not.

abschnitte.text: In **brain death**, all functions of the **cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem** have failed completely and **irreversibly**. The brain can never recover from this. The cause is usually a severe brain injury or a brain haemorrhage. Because the brain controls the whole body, brain death is regarded in Switzerland and in many other countries as the **death of the person**.

In the **intensive care unit**, the heart of a brain-dead person can keep beating for a while. The heart has a **pacemaker of its own** and needs no signal from the brain for this. A machine takes over the breathing. The **artificial ventilation** supplies oxygen, and so the body still has a blood supply. For relatives this is often hard to understand, because the person is warm and seems to be asleep.

In Switzerland, the **Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences** (SAMS) issues guidelines for determining death. If an **organ donation** is being considered, **two suitably qualified doctors** must determine brain death. They must not belong to the transplant team. Among other things, the **brainstem reflexes** are tested, for example the **corneal reflex**: if you touch the cornea of the eye, a person normally blinks.

An important part is the **apnoea test**. Apnoea means a stop in breathing. Here the artificial ventilation is briefly changed so that more **carbon dioxide** builds up in the blood. Normally this at once triggers a strong urge to breathe. If no breathing of the person’s own starts, this shows that the brainstem has failed as well.

Brain death is not the same as a **vegetative state**. In a vegetative state, consciousness is severely disturbed, but the **brainstem is still working**, for example for breathing. These people are alive. Influential criteria for “irreversible coma”, which is now regarded as brain death, were laid down in **1968** by a committee of **Harvard Medical School** in the USA. Since then the rules have been developed further.

gewusst: Irreversible means “not able to be reversed”.
In Switzerland, the federal Transplantation Act sets out the conditions under which organs may be donated.

teile.einleitung: The Human Brain Project was a large European research project on the human brain. It ran from 2013 to 2023 and was led from the EPFL in Lausanne. Its aim was to understand and model the brain better with computers.
wichtigste: The project ran for ten years, from October 2013 to September 2023.
It was coordinated from the EPFL in Lausanne.
The initiator was the brain researcher Henry Markram.
The EU funded it as a so-called FET flagship.
A budget of around one billion euros was planned.
The research platform EBRAINS came out of the project.
In 2014, hundreds of researchers criticised the project in an open letter.

abschnitte.text: The human brain is made of billions of nerve cells that are connected to one another. Exactly how thinking, feeling and remembering arise from them is still far from understood. The neuroscientist **Henry Markram** proposed **simulating** the brain on a computer step by step, that is, modelling it. At the **EPFL** in Lausanne he was already leading the **Blue Brain Project**. From 2005, this had modelled parts of the cerebral cortex of rats on a supercomputer.

In 2013 the European Union chose two giant research projects as the first **FET flagships**. FET stands for “Future and Emerging Technologies”. One was the Graphene project, the other the **Human Brain Project**. For ten years, around **one billion euros** was planned, paid by the EU and the countries taking part. Later, over a hundred universities and institutes from all over Europe took part.

Not all researchers agreed with the project. In **2014**, hundreds of neuroscientists wrote an **open letter** to the EU Commission. They criticised the management and said the aims were too narrow or too ambitious. After this, the leadership of the project was reorganised. The project shifted more towards shared tools and data for brain research.

The most important legacy is **EBRAINS**, a digital research platform. It brings together brain atlases, data, simulation programs and computing tools and will continue to be run after the end of the project. In addition, **neuromorphic computers** were built, which work like nerve cells. They include **SpiNNaker** from Manchester, which is made of very many simple processor cores, and **BrainScaleS** from Heidelberg.

gewusst: Neuromorphic means “shaped like nerve cells”: such computers process signals in a similar way to a brain.
The Human Brain Project was one of the largest research projects ever led from a Swiss university.

teile.einleitung: **Taste buds** are tiny sense organs with which we taste. Most of them sit on the tongue, hidden in small bumps.
wichtigste: Most taste buds sit on the tongue.
They lie in small bumps, the papillae.
A human has a few thousand taste buds.
Their sensory cells are replaced roughly every one to two weeks.
Nerves connect them with the brain.
Some also sit on the palate and in the throat.

abschnitte.text: The surface of the tongue feels **rough**. This is because of many small bumps, the **papillae**. In many of them sit **taste buds**. Most taste buds lie on the tongue. Some, however, also sit on the **palate** and in the **throat**.

A human has **a few thousand** taste buds. Each consists of many **sensory cells** that together look like a little bud. At the top it has a tiny opening. Through it come the substances from food, dissolved in saliva. The sensory cells then recognise how something tastes.

abschnitte.titel: From the mouth to the brain
abschnitte.text: The sensory cells send their message along **nerves** to the **brain**. Only there does the feeling of **sweet**, **sour**, **salty**, **bitter** or **umami** arise. Umami is a savoury taste, as in meat broth or cheese. The **nose** also contributes to the full taste, which is why you taste less with a cold.

The sensory cells in the taste buds live only a short time, about **one to two weeks**. Then **new** ones grow. This is handy: if you burn your tongue on hot tea, the heat injures the sensory cells. You then taste less for a while. By the time new cells have grown, however, it is over again.

gewusst: The idea that you taste each flavour only in one particular place on the tongue is an old mistake.
Children often find bitter tastes stronger than adults do.

teile.einleitung: The family doctor model is a form of insurance within Swiss basic health insurance. Those who choose it always go first to their own family doctor when they have complaints. In return, they pay a lower premium.
wichtigste: In the family doctor model, you always go first to your chosen family doctor.
The family doctor acts as a guide, which is called gatekeeping.
Insured people get a discount on the premium for this.
In an emergency, you may go straight to another place.
Other models are the Telmed model and the HMO model.
In 2012, the voters rejected the managed care proposal.
In 2014, an article on basic medical care was added to the Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.titel: The family doctor as a guide
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, every person must have **basic insurance** with a health insurer. Besides the **standard model** with free choice of doctor, there are **alternative models**. With the **family doctor model**, you promise always to go first to your chosen family doctor. They decide whether and where you are sent on. This guiding role is called **gatekeeping**. This is meant to avoid unnecessary double examinations.

Because coordinated treatments are usually cheaper, insurers give a **discount on the premium**. In return, you have to stick to the rules. If you go straight to a specialist without a **referral**, the insurer can refuse to pay the costs. Someone who breaks the rules repeatedly can be put back into the more expensive standard model. In a **medical emergency**, however, you may go to another place at once and usually inform them afterwards.

There are other models as well. With the **Telmed model**, before a visit to the doctor you first call a telephone advice line. A medical professional works out whether and where treatment is needed. With the **HMO model**, you first go to a health centre with doctors employed there. HMO stands for **Health Maintenance Organization**.

In June 2012, the voters clearly rejected the **managed care proposal**. It wanted to promote care networks in which doctors work closely together. In 2014, the people and the cantons accepted the **federal decree on basic medical care**. Since then, the **Federal Constitution** says that the Confederation and the cantons promote good basic care with family medicine. The advantages and disadvantages of the models are still being discussed.

gewusst: Many insured people in Switzerland have by now chosen an alternative model instead of the standard model.
The word “gatekeeping” comes from English and means roughly “minding the gate”.

teile.einleitung: The palm is the inside of our hand. With it we grasp, hold, clap and catch. Its skin is special: thick, without hairs and with many sweat glands.
wichtigste: The inside of the hand is called the palm.
Hairs never grow on the palm.
The big folds are called palm lines.
The skin is thicker than on the back of the hand.
In the palm there are very many sweat glands.
In people with dark skin, the palm is usually lighter.
If you shape the hand into a bowl, you get a cupped hand.

abschnitte.text: The inside of the hand is called the **palm**. The outside is called the back of the hand. With the palm, we hold and grasp things. You catch a **ball** best with the palm: it is soft and large, the ball lands in it, and the fingers close around it. When **clapping**, we strike the two palms together.

The skin of the palm is **thicker** and firmer than that on the back of the hand. This way, it can stand a lot of rubbing and gripping. It has no hair roots, so **hairs never** grow there. It also has less colouring matter. That is why in many people with dark skin the palm is **lighter** than the back of the hand.

In every palm there are big folds, the **palm lines**. They help the skin to fold when gripping. Besides these there are many fine grooves, the **skin ridges**. They give the hand a good hold, so things slip away less easily. On the fingertips, they form the **fingerprints**, which are different in every person.

In the palm there are **very many sweat glands**. When you are very excited or nervous, they often sweat. Then the hands become damp. This happens, for example, before an exam or a performance. A little moisture, by the way, also helps with gripping.

If you shape the palm into a small **bowl**, you get the **cupped hand**. In it you can, for example, scoop water from a fountain and drink. Berries or small stones can also be collected this way. The German saying “to hold something in the hollow of the hand”, meaning to have it under control, comes from this shape.

gewusst: The palms also have skin ridges, which form a pattern of their own in every person.
Palms and soles of the feet are the only larger areas of skin completely without hair.

teile.einleitung: Anyone who breaks a bone often gets a **plaster cast**. It keeps the arm or leg still so that the bone can grow back together in peace. Today many casts are made of lightweight plastic.
wichtigste: A cast keeps the broken bone still so that it heals well.
Plaster bandages are made wet and then wrapped around the arm or leg.
Soft padding goes under the cast to protect the skin.
Many modern casts are made of plastic instead of plaster.
A real plaster cast usually must not get wet.
Plaster is originally a mineral.

abschnitte.text: With a **broken bone**, the pieces grow back together by themselves. For that, however, they have to stay **still** in the right place. A **plaster cast** holds the arm or leg firmly so that the bone does not move. Depending on the break, you wear the cast for a few weeks. Often you get it around the leg or the arm. Sometimes the doctor has to set the bone first.

**Plaster**, or gypsum, is a **mineral** that occurs in nature, including in Switzerland. Chemically it is calcium sulphate with bound water. If you heat gypsum, it loses part of the water and becomes a fine powder. If you mix this powder with water again, it becomes hard after a short time. This property is used for casts, but also on building sites and for figures.

First a thin tube of fabric is pulled over the skin. Over it comes soft **padding**, which protects the skin and prevents pressure sores. Then the **plaster bandages are made wet** and wrapped around the arm or leg. The bandages can be shaped well. After a few minutes they become firm, but a cast is only fully hard after about a day.

Today many casts are made of **plastic**. They are **lighter** and more stable than real plaster and become hard faster. Some can even cope with a little water. A cast made of **real plaster**, by contrast, usually **must not get wet**, or it goes soft. That is why you protect it with a plastic bag in the shower. Even so, many people simply call plastic casts “plaster”.

Someone who wears a cast for a long time often feels **itching** under the cast. You should not stick objects inside, however, because you can injure the skin. To take it off, the doctor uses a special **cast saw**. Its blade only moves back and forth very quickly. It cuts the hard plaster but does not hurt the soft skin. Afterwards the arm is often a little thinner, because the muscles have worked little.

gewusst: Many children let their friends sign or draw on their cast.
With plaster you can also make impressions, for example of animal tracks in the woods.

teile.einleitung: The wrist joins the hand to the forearm. It makes the hand mobile, so that we can wave, write and throw. It consists of several small bones.
wichtigste: The wrist joins the hand and the forearm.
In the wrist lie eight carpal bones in two rows.
The forearm reaches from the wrist to the elbow.
In a fall onto the outstretched hand, the wrist is often injured.
On the wrist you wear a wristwatch.
A sprained wrist is wrapped with an elastic bandage.

abschnitte.text: The **wrist** lies where the hand begins. It joins the hand to the **forearm**. The forearm reaches from the wrist to the elbow. In it lie two bones, the **ulna** and the **radius**. In the wrist itself lie **eight small carpal bones**. They are arranged in two rows and firmly joined by ligaments.

The wrist makes the hand mobile. You can tilt it up and down and move it to the side. When **waving**, the hand tilts to and fro, a movement that the wrist makes possible. In writing, painting, throwing or playing ball games, too, it is constantly in use. Turning the hand, on the other hand, happens mainly in the forearm.

On the wrist, you usually wear a **wristwatch**. This way you can read the time quickly. At the **outdoor pool**, many people wear the key to their locker on an elastic band around the wrist. This way you have it with you when swimming and do not lose it. On the inside of the wrist, you can also feel the **pulse** well.

When someone falls, they often catch themselves with **outstretched hands**. This puts a lot of strain on the wrist. It can be **sprained** or even break. A break of the radius near the wrist is one of the most common broken bones of all. A sprained wrist is often wrapped with an **elastic bandage**. It supports the joint and helps it to swell less. With strong pain, a doctor should examine it.

gewusst: A hand with its wrist has 27 bones together.
In inline skating and snowboarding, special wrist guards protect against breaks.

teile.einleitung: Not every food rich in carbohydrates makes blood sugar rise equally fast. The **glycaemic index**, **GI** for short, shows this difference as a number. It helps us to understand how foods affect the body.
wichtigste: The GI states how strongly a food raises blood sugar compared with glucose.
Glucose serves as the reference with the value 100.
A GI of 70 or more is usually regarded as high.
The glycaemic load is calculated like this: GI times grams of carbohydrate divided by 100.
Fructose has an especially low GI.
Fibre generally lowers the blood sugar effect of a meal.

abschnitte.text: The **glycaemic index** compares foods with each other. You measure how strongly blood sugar rises after eating and compare this with pure **glucose**. Glucose has the value **100** as the **reference**. A food with a GI of 50 therefore makes blood sugar rise about half as strongly. The usual grouping is this: from **70** a GI counts as **high**, below 55 as low, and in between as medium.

The GI says nothing about the **amount**. That is why there is the **glycaemic load**. You calculate: **GI times grams of carbohydrate divided by 100**. Example: a portion with 30 g of carbohydrate and a GI of 70 has a glycaemic load of 70 times 30 divided by 100, so **21**. This shows that a small portion of a food with a high GI has less effect than a large one.

The GI depends not only on the food but also on the **preparation**. **Pasta** cooked **al dente** has a **lower GI** than pasta cooked soft. The starch is then harder to get at and is digested more slowly. Ripe bananas also have a higher GI than unripe ones. And mashed potato affects blood sugar more strongly than whole boiled potatoes.

In a meal, the ingredients influence each other. **Fibre**, as found in wholemeal bread, pulses and vegetables, generally lowers the effect on blood sugar. Fat and protein also slow down digestion. Among the sugars, **fructose**, or fruit sugar, has an especially **low GI**, because it is first converted in the liver.

When blood sugar rises strongly, the **pancreas** releases a lot of **insulin**. The hormone moves the sugar into the cells. This is especially the case after meals with a high GI. For people with **diabetes**, the GI can therefore be a help in choosing foods. For everyone else, a varied diet with plenty of vegetables and wholegrain is more important than individual numbers.

gewusst: The glycaemic index was developed in the early 1980s by researchers in Canada.
Because every body reacts a little differently, the GI values of the same food can differ slightly in tables.

teile.einleitung: The family doctor is the first point of contact for most health problems. They treat many complaints themselves and send you on to specialists only if needed. For children, the paediatrician often takes on this role.
wichtigste: The family doctor is the first point of contact for health problems.
They take care of basic medical care.
With a referral, they send patients to specialist doctors.
Someone who always goes to the same doctor is well known to them.
For children, the paediatrician is often the family doctor.
Check-ups help to recognise illnesses early.
In the health insurer's family doctor model, you go first to your chosen family doctor.

abschnitte.text: With a cough, tummy ache, an injury or a vaccination, you usually go first to the **family doctor**. They take care of **basic medical care**. Many complaints they treat themselves. With the **stethoscope**, they listen to the heart and lungs and recognise, for example, pneumonia.

If a closer examination is needed, the family doctor writes a **referral**. With it, they send the patient to a **specialist**, for example for skin, eyes or heart. The referral says what is to be investigated. The family doctor keeps an overview and afterwards gets a report back.

Someone who has gone to the same family doctor for a long time is well known to them. They know about earlier **illnesses**, **allergies** and **medicines**. This helps to do the right thing faster. In Switzerland, children and young people are often looked after by a **paediatrician**. For people who can no longer come to the practice, the doctor makes a **home visit**.

In a **check-up**, you are examined even if you feel healthy. This way, illnesses can be discovered early and treated better. In children, the doctor checks, for example, height, weight, sight and hearing. They also check whether all the recommended **vaccinations** have been done.

In Switzerland, you can choose the **family doctor model** with your health insurer. Then, except in an emergency, you always go first to your chosen family doctor. In return, the **premium** is usually cheaper. Since 2014, the Federal Constitution says that the Confederation and the cantons are to promote good basic medical care with family medicine.

gewusst: The stethoscope was invented in 1816 by the French doctor René Laennec; at first it was a simple tube of paper.
In the past, family doctors in the countryside made many home visits, sometimes by horse and carriage.

teile.einleitung: The greenstick fracture is a typical broken bone in children. The bone does not break right through but buckles like a young, green branch.
wichtigste: Greenstick fractures occur mainly in children.
The bone breaks only on one side and buckles.
The periosteum usually stays uninjured.
Children's bones contain a lot of elastic collagen.
The forearm is especially often affected.
An X-ray reliably shows the break.
Usually a cast for a few weeks is enough.

abschnitte.text: If you bend a fresh, **green twig**, it does not break cleanly through. It splinters on one side, and the other side still holds together. This is exactly what this kind of break looks like. That is why it is called a **greenstick fracture**. “Fracture” is the technical word for a broken bone.

**Children's bones** are more flexible than the bones of adults. In proportion to the minerals, they contain more **collagen**, an elastic protein substance. They therefore bend more before they break. In addition, children have a strong **periosteum**, the skin around the bone. In a greenstick fracture it stays intact like a sleeve and holds the broken pieces together.

The greenstick fracture occurs most often in the **forearm**. When a child falls, for example while playing or riding a bike, it props itself up with an outstretched hand. The **ulna** and **radius** then bend strongly and buckle. Another typical children's break is the **torus fracture**. In it, the bone is compressed and bulges out like a ridge.

From the outside, a greenstick fracture is often hard to recognise. The arm hurts and swells. It can be established reliably with an **X-ray**. On it you can see whether and how the bone is broken or bent. If the bone is hardly displaced, a **cast** for a few weeks is usually enough. Strongly bent bones are first straightened by the doctor.

gewusst: Children's bones usually heal faster than the bones of adults.
In adults, greenstick fractures hardly occur, because their bones are more brittle.

teile.einleitung: Haemophilia, in German also called the “bleeder's disease”, is an inherited illness in which the blood clots too slowly. Even small injuries can therefore bleed for a long time. Today it can be treated well.
wichtigste: In haemophilia, a clotting factor is missing or works too weakly.
In haemophilia A, factor VIII is missing; in haemophilia B, factor IX.
Around 80 to 85 per cent of those affected have haemophilia A.
The gene lies on the X chromosome, so mainly boys and men are affected.
Typical are bleeds into the joints.
Today the missing factor is injected into a vein.
World Haemophilia Day is on 17 April.

abschnitte.text: When we cut ourselves, a plug forms after a short time, and the bleeding stops. The platelets and many **clotting factors** in the blood take care of this. They work together like a chain and carry numbers in Roman numerals. In **haemophilia**, one link of this chain is missing or works too weakly. In **haemophilia A** it is **factor VIII**, in **haemophilia B** **factor IX**. Haemophilia A is much more common, at around 80 to 85 per cent of cases.

Haemophilia is **inherited**. The changed gene lies on the **X chromosome**. Men have only one X chromosome. If the gene on it is changed, there is no second X that could make up for the fault. That is why **boys and men** fall ill much more often. Women can carry the trait and pass it on without being seriously ill themselves.

Haemophilia became famous through the British **Queen Victoria**. She was a carrier of the trait. Through her descendants, the illness reached the royal houses of **Spain**, **Russia** and **Prussia**. A well-known sufferer was **Alexei**, the son of the last Russian tsar, **Nicholas II**, and a great-grandson of Victoria. In those days his illness was hard to treat and caused the tsar's family great worry.

In severe haemophilia, there are often **internal bleeds**, especially into the **knee, elbow and ankle joints**. Without treatment, the joints can be permanently damaged. Today many of those affected inject the **missing clotting factor** into a vein regularly or when needed. This way, they can lead an almost normal life and also do sport. Every year on **17 April** is **World Haemophilia Day**, the birthday of Frank Schnabel, the founder of the World Federation of Hemophilia.

gewusst: Many of those affected learn as children to inject the medicine into their own vein.
Haemophilia comes from Greek and literally means something like “love of blood”.

teile.einleitung: A corn is a small, hard thickening of the skin, mostly on the toes. It is caused by constant pressure, for example in shoes that are too tight, and can hurt quite a lot when walking. In German it is called a Hühnerauge, “chicken’s eye”.
wichtigste: A corn is caused by pressure and rubbing, for example in tight shoes.
It forms most often on the toes.
In the middle sits a hard core of horny skin that presses down into the tissue.
The German name Hühnerauge comes from its look: a pale rim and a dark core.
The technical term is clavus.
A podiatrist removes corns professionally.
Suitable, comfortable shoes are the best protection against new corns.

abschnitte.text: A **corn** forms when a spot on the skin is exposed to **pressure and rubbing** for a long time. This often happens in **tight shoes** or with misaligned toes. The skin protects itself by making more **hard skin** at this spot. Corns form most often on the **toes**, on the top or between two toes.

In the middle of a corn, a **hard core** of horny skin forms. It grows inwards into the skin like a wedge. When you walk, this core presses on nerves deeper down, which is why a corn hurts. The technical term is **clavus**, which is Latin and means nail. An old German name is **Leichdorn**.

The German name Hühnerauge, “chicken’s eye”, comes from its **appearance**. It has a pale rim and, in the middle, a darker, glassy core. That is why it reminds people of the eye of a chicken. Very similar is the **callus**: it, too, is thickened hard skin caused by pressure. But a callus is flat and has no hard core, so it usually does not hurt.

You should not cut corns out yourself with a knife or scissors, because you can hurt yourself. A **podiatrist**, an expert in foot care, removes them properly. In the chemist’s you can also find plasters that soften the hard skin. The most important thing is to remove the pressure: **suitable, comfortable shoes** help best to stop the corn coming back.

gewusst: Pressure spots on the soles of the feet can also turn into corns.
People with diabetes should always have corns treated by experts, because small wounds on the foot heal badly in them.

teile.einleitung: The hip bone is a large, flat bone and, together with the sacrum, forms the pelvis. Every person has two hip bones, one on the left and one on the right. They carry the weight of the upper body and give support to many muscles.
wichtigste: Each hip bone develops from three bones that fuse in the teenage years.
The three parts are called the ilium, the ischium and the pubis.
The ilium is the biggest part.
Two hip bones and the sacrum form the pelvic ring.
You can feel the iliac crest at the side of the waist.
When you sit, you rest on the ischium.
The pelvis passes the weight of the trunk on to the legs.

abschnitte.text: In children, each hip bone still consists of **three bones**: the **ilium**, the **ischium** and the **pubis**. They are joined by cartilage. In the teenage years this cartilage turns to bone, and the three parts **fuse** into a single bone. The place where they meet lies in the **hip socket**. That is where the head of the thigh bone sits.

The **ilium** is the biggest of the three parts. It is broad like a shovel. You can feel its upper edge, the **iliac crest**, at the side of the waist when you put your hands on your hips. At the front, at the side of the lower belly, you can feel the **front iliac spines**, two hard bony points. When you sit, you rest on the **sitting bones**, which belong to the ischium.

The two hip bones and the **sacrum** together form the **pelvic ring**. At the back, the hip bones are joined to the sacrum by the sacroiliac joints. At the front they meet in the **pubic symphysis**, a firm joint made of cartilage. This ring is very stable and protects organs such as the bladder and the intestine.

The pelvis is the link between the spine and the legs. It **passes the weight of the trunk** on to the legs, when standing, walking and jumping. Many strong muscles attach to the hip bone, for example the buttock muscles and the stomach muscles. Without a stable pelvis we could not walk upright.

abschnitte.titel: Bone marrow at the iliac crest
abschnitte.text: Inside the hip bone lies **red bone marrow**, where blood cells are made. When doctors need to examine the bone marrow, they often take a small sample from the **iliac crest**. The spot is easy to reach and lies close under the skin. The examination helps, for example, to recognise blood diseases.

gewusst: The Latin name of the hip bone is Os coxae.
The ilium is called that in German (Darmbein, “gut bone”) because parts of the intestine lie in its shovel-shaped hollow.

teile.einleitung: Heat can be pleasant, like warm sunshine or a warm bath. But too much heat can burn the skin and harm the body. Our body has clever tricks to protect itself and cool down.
wichtigste: In great heat, the body sweats to cool down.
A reflex is a lightning-fast movement without thinking.
You pick up a hot pan with an oven glove.
A glowing sign on the hob shows that it is still hot.
Too much sun without protection gives you sunburn.
A burn can cause a blister.
Dogs pant to cool down in the heat.

abschnitte.text: If you touch something hot by mistake, you pull your hand back in a flash. This happens before you even think. A movement like this is called a **reflex**. The nerves send the signal straight through the spinal cord to the muscles. Only afterwards do you really feel that it was hot. The reflex protects you from worse injuries.

There is a lot of heat in the kitchen. You always pick up a hot pan **with an oven glove**. Even a switched-off **hob** can stay hot for a long time. Many cookers show this with a **glowing sign**, often a small “H”, for hot. As long as it glows, you must not touch the hob. For a baby’s bath water, parents often test the warmth with their **elbow**, because the skin there is sensitive.

In great heat the body **sweats**. The sweat evaporates on the skin, and in doing so it cools it down. That is why it is important to drink plenty of water on hot days. Animals have other tricks. A **dog** has hardly any sweat glands. It **pants** with an open mouth so that moisture evaporates from its tongue.

Anyone who stays in the sun unprotected for too long gets **sunburn**. The skin turns red and hot and hurts. Shade, clothes, a hat and sun cream give protection. The ground gets hot, too. In summer, **tarmac** can get so hot that you **burn the soles of your feet** if you are barefoot.

In a burn, the skin is injured. It turns red, and a **blister** can form. You should not prick the blister. You cool a small burn straight away with lukewarm running water. For large burns, or with small children, you get help at once, in Switzerland by calling the emergency number **144**.

gewusst: On a hot day, a person can lose several litres of sweat.
The pull-back reflex takes only a fraction of a second.

teile.einleitung: **Glucocorticoids** are hormones from the adrenal gland. The most important is **cortisol**. It helps the body to cope with strain and is used as a medicine against inflammation.
wichtigste: The most important glucocorticoid made by the human body is cortisol.
Cortisol is made mainly in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex.
Glucocorticoids are made from cholesterol.
Cortisol raises the blood sugar level.
In the early morning, the cortisol level is highest.
Synthetic glucocorticoids such as prednisone slow inflammation.
A long-lasting excess leads to Cushing's syndrome.

abschnitte.text: On top of each kidney sits a small **adrenal gland**. Its outer layer is called the **adrenal cortex**. It has three zones. In the middle one, the **zona fasciculata**, **cortisol** is mainly made. The starting substance is **cholesterol**. Glucocorticoids therefore belong to the **steroid hormones**. The making of it is controlled by the brain: the pituitary gland releases the hormone ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal cortex.

The name gives away an important effect: **gluco** stands for sugar. Cortisol **raises the blood sugar level**. It stimulates the liver to make new sugar and for this also breaks down protein. This way the body has enough energy in difficult situations. Cortisol is therefore often called a **stress hormone**, alongside adrenaline.

Cortisol follows a **daily rhythm**. In the **early morning**, the level in a healthy person is highest. This helps with waking up and starting the day. Towards evening and during the night, it falls sharply. That is why experts always measure cortisol at a particular time of day, so that the values can be compared.

abschnitte.titel: How it works in the cell
abschnitte.text: Cortisol dissolves in fat and passes easily through the cell membrane. Its **receptor** is therefore **inside the cell**, in the **cytoplasm**. When cortisol binds to it, the complex travels into the cell nucleus. There it switches certain genes on or off. That is why cortisol often does not work at once but only after a few hours.

Artificially made glucocorticoids such as **prednisone** are important medicines. They are used mainly to **slow inflammation** and to damp down an overactive immune defence, for example in asthma, allergies or rheumatism. They are often simply called “cortisone”. With longer use in high doses, side effects can occur. A long-lasting excess of glucocorticoids leads to **Cushing's syndrome**, with, among other things, a round face and weight gain.

gewusst: For the discovery of the adrenal cortex hormones, the Swiss chemist Tadeus Reichstein, among others, received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1950.
After long use, you must not simply stop cortisone medicines suddenly, because the dose is lowered slowly.

teile.einleitung: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. Most often it is caused by viruses, of which there are several types. A vaccination protects against some of them.
wichtigste: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver.
The most common cause is viruses, especially types A, B, C, D and E.
You usually catch hepatitis A from dirty water or food.
Hepatitis B and C are passed on mainly through blood.
There is a vaccination against hepatitis A and B.
In adults, hepatitis C especially often becomes chronic.
World Hepatitis Day is on 28 July.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek: **“hepar”** means liver, and the ending **“-itis”** stands for inflammation. **Hepatitis** is therefore an inflammation of the **liver**. The liver is an important organ that breaks down toxins and makes many substances for the body. When it is inflamed, you often feel tired, and sometimes the skin and eyes turn yellow. This is called **jaundice**.

Most often **hepatitis viruses** cause the inflammation. The main types are **A, B, C, D and E**. **Hepatitis A** leaves the body in the stool and is passed on through contaminated water or food. Thorough **hand washing** protects. **Hepatitis B and C** pass from one person to another mainly through **blood**, for example through shared syringes. That is why hospitals work with sterile single-use needles.

Hepatitis A almost always heals completely. Hepatitis B, too, only rarely becomes **chronic**, that is, long-lasting, in adults. With **hepatitis C**, on the other hand, the infection stays for years in most adults. The **hepatitis D virus** is incomplete. It can only multiply if the hepatitis B virus is present as well. Anyone who is vaccinated against hepatitis B is therefore also protected from hepatitis D.

There are effective **vaccinations** against **hepatitis A and B**. There is so far no vaccination against hepatitis C, but there are good medicines. The American **Baruch Blumberg** found the so-called **Australia antigen** in the 1960s, which turned out to be part of the hepatitis B virus. This made blood tests possible, and later a vaccination. For this he received the Nobel Prize in 1976. Every year on **28 July**, **World Hepatitis Day** draws attention to the disease.

gewusst: 28 July was chosen as World Hepatitis Day because it was Baruch Blumberg’s birthday.
After an injury, the liver can regrow to a large extent.

teile.einleitung: The hand is one of the most versatile tools of the human body. With it you can grasp, hold, write, feel and even speak, for example in sign language. It consists of many small bones, muscles and tendons that work together perfectly.
wichtigste: The hand helps you to grasp and hold with your fingers.
Each hand has five fingers: thumb, index finger, middle finger, ring finger and little finger.
A hand consists of 27 bones.
The thumb can be brought opposite the other fingers.
Most of the muscles that move the fingers lie in the forearm.
In the fingertips there are especially many touch receptors.
Every person has a unique fingerprint.

abschnitte.text: A hand has 27 bones. Eight small **carpal bones** form the wrist. Joined to them are five **metacarpal bones**, which lie in the palm. The fingers consist of the finger bones, with the thumb having two and the other fingers three each. Both hands together have over a quarter of all the bones of the body.

The fingers themselves have no large muscles. The strong muscles that bend and stretch the fingers sit in the forearm. Long **tendons** run into the fingers like the strings of a puppet. When you move your fingers, you can feel at your forearm how the muscles move. Small muscles in the palm take care of fine movements.

Thanks to its saddle joint, the thumb can be brought opposite the other fingers. This gives the **pincer grip**, with which you can pick up a pea or a thread. With the power grip, you hold, for example, a hammer or a climbing pole. Apes also have an opposable thumb. In humans, however, it is especially mobile and strong.

The skin of the fingertips contains very many **touch receptors**. That is why you can feel fine differences with your fingers, for example whether a fabric is rough or smooth. Blind people read **Braille** with their fingers, a writing made of raised dots. The lines on the fingertips, the papillary ridges, help with gripping. Their pattern forms the fingerprint, which is different in every person.

With our hands, we write, paint, cook and make music. Most people are right-handed; about one in ten is **left-handed**. In sign language, including Swiss German Sign Language, people speak with hands, face and body. Gestures such as waving or thumbs up are understood almost everywhere. Hands should be washed regularly, because they touch many things all day.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm strand that joins a muscle to a bone.
The part of the hand with eight small bones at the wrist.
A small sense organ in the skin that feels touch.
A dot writing that blind people read with their fingers.

gewusst: Fingernails grow about three to four millimetres a month.
Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
In the brain, an especially large area is responsible for the hands.

teile.einleitung: The carotid artery is a large blood vessel in the neck. It brings oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the head and above all to the brain. There is one on each side of the neck.
wichtigste: The technical term for the carotid artery is arteria carotis.
Humans have two common carotid arteries, left and right.
Each divides into an internal and an external carotid artery.
The internal one supplies mainly the brain.
The external one supplies the face, scalp and neck.
At the fork, sensory cells measure the blood pressure.
With ultrasound, the carotid artery is checked for narrowing.

abschnitte.text: The **carotid artery** is called **arteria carotis** in Latin, carotid for short. There is a left and a right **common carotid artery**. Each supplies its side of the head and neck with blood. The left one branches off directly from the **aortic arch**, the large main artery at the heart. The right one arises from a common vessel trunk with the right arm artery.

At about the level of the **larynx**, the common carotid artery forks. This gives the **internal** and the **external carotid artery**. The internal one runs through the base of the skull into the inside of the skull. There it supplies large parts of the **brain** and the eye. The external one stays outside the skull. Its branches supply, among other things, the **face**, tongue, scalp and neck.

At the fork lies a slightly widened spot, the **carotid sinus**. There sit sensory cells that measure the **blood pressure**. They constantly report to the brain how high the pressure is. The brain can then adjust heartbeat and vessels and so regulate the blood pressure. Next to the larynx, you can also feel the **pulse** well at the carotid artery.

Over the years, arteries can narrow, for example through deposits. If the carotid artery is strongly narrowed, the brain gets too little blood, and the risk of a **stroke** rises. With an **ultrasound machine**, you can look at the carotid artery from the outside and measure the blood flow. The examination is painless and needs no operation.

gewusst: In emergencies, professionals often feel for the pulse at the carotid artery, because it is easy to feel there.
The brain gets a large part of its blood through the two internal carotid arteries.

teile.einleitung: Every day we lose hairs, and new ones grow. People speak of hair loss when clearly more hairs are lost than normal. The causes are very varied.
wichtigste: Losing 50 to 100 hairs a day is normal.
At the end of the resting phase, the telogen phase, a hair falls out.
In alopecia areata, the immune system attacks the hair roots.
Iron deficiency is a common cause of increased hair loss.
The thyroid gland can also trigger hair loss.
After a high fever, hair often falls out only 2 to 3 months later.
With heavy hair loss, you should have the cause checked by a doctor.

abschnitte.text: Every hair grows for a time, then rests and finally falls out. The resting phase is called the **telogen phase**. In it, the hair no longer grows and sits only loosely in the hair follicle. After that it falls out, and a new hair pushes up. Losing about **50 to 100 hairs** a day is therefore quite normal.

In **alopecia areata**, the body's own **immune system** wrongly turns against the hair roots. The immune system normally protects us from germs. Here, however, it attacks the body's own hair roots. Round, bald patches result. Often the hair grows back there after some time.

Hair roots need a lot of **iron**, because their cells divide quickly. In **iron deficiency**, more hairs therefore often fall out. The **thyroid gland** also plays a part. Its hormones control metabolism, including in the hair roots. If it works too strongly or too weakly, the hair can become thinner. Besides this, there is also hereditary hair loss, which is common in some families.

After a **high fever**, a serious illness or strong **stress**, hairs often fall out only after a delay. The strain sends many hairs into the resting phase at the same time. This lasts a few months. That is why the hair falls out only about **2 to 3 months** later. Usually it grows back afterwards.

In many cancer treatments with **chemotherapy**, the hair falls out. The medicines are aimed at cells that divide quickly, such as cancer cells. The cells of the hair roots also divide quickly and are hit. After the treatment, the hair usually grows back. If you lose a noticeably large number of hairs over a longer time, you should have the cause **checked by a doctor**.

gewusst: After chemotherapy, hair sometimes grows back a little differently than before, for example curlier.
Hair loss after a fever often shows only when you have almost forgotten about the illness.

teile.einleitung: You cannot move all muscles on purpose. **Smooth muscle** works inside the body entirely by itself, for example in the gut and in the blood vessels. It is slow but very enduring.
wichtigste: Smooth muscle works involuntarily, that is, without conscious will.
It is found, for example, in the wall of the gut and of the blood vessels.
Its cells are spindle-shaped and have no cross-striping.
It pushes the food pulp through the gut by peristalsis.
It works more slowly than skeletal muscle but is very enduring.
It is controlled by the autonomic nervous system.

abschnitte.text: You can raise your arm whenever you want. That is done by **skeletal muscle**. **Smooth muscle**, by contrast, works **involuntarily**, without conscious will. It is controlled by the **autonomic nervous system**, which also helps to regulate breathing, digestion and heartbeat. Hormones and substances from the surroundings also influence it. This way it takes care of many jobs that we never think about.

The cells of smooth muscle are **spindle-shaped**: thick in the middle and pointed at both ends. Each cell has a cell nucleus. Under the microscope, skeletal muscle shows fine stripes, the **cross-striping**. This is missing in smooth muscle, which is why it looks “smooth”. The proteins that produce muscle force are not arranged so regularly here.

In the wall of the gullet, stomach and **gut** lies smooth muscle. It contracts in waves and so pushes the food pulp along. This movement is called **peristalsis**. It works even when you stand on your head. That is why you can also eat and drink lying down without the food flowing back.

In the wall of the **blood vessels**, too, there is smooth muscle. It regulates the **width of the vessels**: when it contracts, the vessel becomes narrower, and when it relaxes, it becomes wider. This is how the body controls blood pressure and distributes blood to where it is needed. Smooth muscles are also found in the bladder, in the bronchi of the lungs and in the eye, where they make the pupil narrower or wider.

Smooth muscle contracts more **slowly** than skeletal muscle. In return it is **very enduring** and needs little energy. It can hold tension for a long time without tiring. This is important, because blood vessels and gut have to work day and night. The heart muscle, by the way, is a separate, third kind of muscle.

gewusst: Hairs stand up in the cold because tiny smooth muscles at the hair roots contract: this is how goosebumps arise.
Thanks to peristalsis, a mouthful takes only a few seconds to travel through the gullet into the stomach.

teile.einleitung: Healthy eating means eating a varied diet and in suitable amounts. This way your body gets everything it needs to grow, think and play. The food pyramid shows you how to eat in a balanced way.
wichtigste: The food pyramid shows how to eat in a balanced way.
Five portions of vegetables and fruit a day are recommended.
Water or unsweetened tea are the best thirst quenchers.
Milk and cheese provide calcium for strong bones and teeth.
Oranges contain plenty of vitamin C.
An apple is an especially healthy mid-morning snack.
Sweets and salty snacks are allowed, but only in small amounts.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss **food pyramid** is published by the Swiss Society for Nutrition together with the Confederation. At the bottom stand the things of which you need the most, and right at the top those that you should eat only rarely. The base is made up of drinks, above all water. Above come vegetables and fruit, then cereal products and potatoes. Further up stand dairy products, meat, fish, eggs and tofu, then oils and nuts, and at the top sweet and salty things.

For vegetables and fruit, the rule is **“five a day”**, that is, five portions daily. A portion is roughly a handful, for example an apple, a carrot or a bowl of berries. It is best to eat more vegetables than fruit and to choose many colours. Vegetables and fruit provide **vitamins**, minerals and fibre. Oranges, kiwis and peppers, for example, contain a lot of vitamin C, which supports the body's defences.

**Carbohydrates** from bread, pasta, rice and potatoes give energy, and wholegrain products keep you full especially long. The body needs **protein** from milk, eggs, meat, fish, pulses or tofu to build muscles. Milk, yoghurt and cheese provide **calcium**, which makes bones and teeth strong. Fats from rapeseed oil, olive oil and nuts are important in small amounts. Variety is the best way to get everything that is needed.

Children should drink about one to one and a half litres a day, more in heat and when doing sport. The best are tap water and unsweetened tea. In Switzerland, tap water has a very good quality almost everywhere. Sugary drinks such as lemonade and iced tea contain a lot of sugar. One can can contain several sugar cubes.

A good **mid-morning snack** is, for example, an apple, a few carrot sticks or a wholemeal sandwich. A breakfast gives energy for the school morning. Eating together at the table and without a screen helps you to eat slowly and to notice when you are full. Regular meals prevent sudden hunger. And exercise belongs to a healthy life just as much as food does.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substances that the body needs in small amounts to stay healthy.
A mineral that makes bones and teeth strong.
Nutrients that mainly give the body energy.
Indigestible parts of plants that are good for digestion.

gewusst: Potatoes also contain vitamin C.
Peppers contain more vitamin C than oranges.
More than half of a child's body is made of water.

teile.einleitung: The meninges are protective coverings that surround the brain and the spinal cord. Between them flows a clear fluid that cushions the delicate brain like a water pillow. Together with the skull bone, they form very good protection.
wichtigste: The meninges wrap around the brain and spinal cord and protect them.
There are three meninges: the dura mater, the arachnoid mater and the pia mater.
The cerebrospinal fluid flows between the meninges.
This fluid cushions knocks like a water pillow.
An inflammation of the meninges is called meningitis.
There are vaccinations against some of the germs that cause meningitis.
The technical word for meninx is meninx, in the plural meninges.

abschnitte.text: On the very outside, directly under the skull bone, lies the **dura mater**, the tough outer layer. It is thick and tough like leather. Underneath follows the delicate **arachnoid mater**, which gets its name from its fine, net-like fibres. On the very inside lies the **pia mater**, which lies closely on the brain and follows every fold. It contains many small blood vessels.

Between the arachnoid mater and the pia mater lies a gap containing the **cerebrospinal fluid**, also called CSF. It is made in hollow spaces in the brain, the ventricles. An adult has about 150 millilitres of it, roughly a cup. The fluid is renewed several times a day. It cushions knocks and lets the brain almost float, so that it is not squashed by its own weight.

The meninges continue down into the spine and also wrap around the **spinal cord**. There they are called the spinal meninges. For examinations, a doctor can take some fluid with a fine needle in the lower back, which is called a **lumbar puncture**. At this spot the spinal cord itself no longer reaches, so the procedure is safe there. The fluid shows, for example, whether there is an inflammation.

When the meninges become inflamed, this is called **meningitis**. It can be caused by viruses or bacteria. Typical signs are severe headache, fever, a stiff neck and sensitivity to light. Bacterial meningitis is an emergency and must be treated at once. In the Swiss vaccination schedule there are vaccinations against important germs such as pneumococci, meningococci and Haemophilus influenzae type b.

In many parts of Switzerland, ticks can pass on the virus that causes **tick-borne encephalitis**, or TBE for short. This disease can inflame the meninges and the brain. The Federal Office of Public Health recommends the tick vaccination for people who live in or stay in almost all of Switzerland, except in the cantons of Geneva and Ticino. After a walk in the woods, you should check your body for ticks. Long trousers and socks pulled over the trouser legs help as well.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tough outer covering directly under the skull bone.
A clear fluid around the brain and spinal cord that cushions knocks.
Inflammation of the meninges.
Inflammation of the meninges and brain passed on by ticks.

gewusst: The brain weighs around 1.3 kilograms, but floating in the cerebrospinal fluid it feels like only about 50 grams.
The dura mater is called that in Latin, and it means “tough mother”.
The brain itself feels no pain; headaches arise, among other places, in the meninges and blood vessels.

teile.einleitung: Pulses are the seeds of plants that grow their fruits in a pod. They include lentils, peas, beans and chickpeas. They are healthy, fill you up well and provide a lot of protein.
wichtigste: Lentils, peas, beans, chickpeas and soya beans are pulses.
They grow in a pod on the plant.
Pulses contain especially large amounts of protein.
In Switzerland it is recommended to eat pulses at least once a week.
Dried beans must be cooked, and raw they are harmful.
Hummus is made from chickpeas, tofu from soya beans.

abschnitte.text: Pulses are the **seeds** of plants from the **legume family**. These plants grow their seeds in a **pod**, which you can see clearly on the pea. Well-known pulses are **lentils**, **peas**, **beans**, **chickpeas** and **soya beans**. Many people already know the small, round, green pea from childhood. The peanut, by the way, is also a pulse.

Pulses contain especially large amounts of **protein**. That is why they matter for people who eat little or no meat. They also provide a lot of **fibre**, which fills you up well and supports digestion, as well as minerals such as iron. In Switzerland it is recommended to eat pulses **at least once a week**, for example in place of meat.

abschnitte.titel: Dishes from all over the world
abschnitte.text: Pulses are found in many well-known dishes. **Hummus** is a paste made of **chickpeas** that comes from the Middle East. A **chilli con carne** needs red **kidney beans**. **Tofu** is made from **soya beans**: soya milk is made and allowed to curdle, rather like in making cheese. Lentil soup and pea soup are also popular dishes.

Dried beans must be **cooked well** before eating. Raw, they contain substances that harm the body and can cause stomach ache or vomiting. Cooking destroys these substances. Many dried pulses are soaked in water for a few hours beforehand so that they cook faster. Lentils usually do not need soaking.

Legumes have small nodules with **bacteria** on their roots. These bacteria take **nitrogen** from the air and make it usable for the plant. In this way the plants fertilise themselves, so to speak, and improve the soil. That is why farmers like to grow them in rotation with other crops.

gewusst: The United Nations declared 2016 the International Year of Pulses.
Lentils are among the oldest crops of humankind.

teile.einleitung: With a skin test, doctors check whether someone reacts allergically to certain substances. Tiny amounts of these substances are put on or into the skin. The reaction of the skin shows whether there is an allergy.
wichtigste: The prick test is the most common skin test for allergies such as hay fever.
It is usually done on the inside of the forearm.
It is read after about 15 to 20 minutes.
A wheal with redness shows a positive reaction.
Histamine and saline solution serve as comparisons.
Allergy medicines against histamine have to be stopped beforehand.
Contact allergies are checked with the patch test.

abschnitte.text: The most common skin test is the **prick test**. It shows allergies such as **hay fever** or an allergy to animal hair. Usually it is done on the **inside of the forearm**, sometimes on the back. First, drops with different **allergens** are put on the skin. Then the skin is lightly pricked through the drops with a fine lancet. This hardly hurts.

abschnitte.titel: Reading after a quarter of an hour
abschnitte.text: Allergies of the **immediate type** show quickly. After about **15 to 20 minutes**, the specialist looks at the test spots. In an allergy, a raised, itchy **wheal** with a red halo forms. Its size is measured: the bigger it is, the more strongly the body reacts to this substance.

So that the test can be judged correctly, there are two comparisons. **Histamine** causes a wheal on every skin. If it fails to appear, the test is not meaningful. A harmless **saline solution**, on the other hand, should cause no reaction. It shows whether the skin already reacts to the mere pricking. Allergy medicines against histamine suppress the skin reaction, so you have to stop them a few days beforehand.

**Contact allergies**, for example to nickel, are checked with the **patch test**. In it, plasters with test substances are stuck on the back. It is read only after two to three days, because contact allergies appear with a delay. If a skin test is not possible, for example with a strong rash, a **blood test** can help. It measures special **antibodies** against individual allergens.

gewusst: In the prick test, many different allergens can be tested side by side on one arm at the same time.
Histamine is the substance that the body itself releases in an allergy and that causes itching and swelling.

teile.einleitung: The sense of balance makes sure that you can stand upright, ride a bike and hop on one leg without falling over. Its most important organ sits well hidden in the inner ear. Together with the eyes and the muscles, it constantly senses where up and down are.
wichtigste: The organ for balance is called the balance organ or vestibular organ.
It lies in the inner ear, right next to the cochlea.
Three semicircular canals report turning movements of the head.
Two small sacs report how the head is tilted and whether you are accelerating.
The brain combines these signals with information from the eyes and the muscles.
When the signals do not match, you can feel dizzy or sick.
Balance can be trained, for example by balancing.

abschnitte.text: The **balance organ**, also called the **vestibular organ**, lies deep in the temporal bone of the skull. It is filled with fluid and only a few millimetres in size. There is one in each ear. It shares the space with the cochlea, which is responsible for hearing. That is why hearing and balance belong to the same sense organ, the ear.

Three half-circle-shaped **semicircular canals** stand almost at right angles to each other, like the three sides of a corner of a room. This way every direction of turning of the head can be recognised. When you turn your head, the fluid in the canals lags behind for a moment because of its inertia. This bends fine **sensory hairs**. They send a signal to the brain.

Beside the canals lie two sacs with tiny crystals of lime, the **otoliths** or ear stones. They lie on a layer of jelly above sensory hairs. When you tilt your head or set off in a lift, the little stones shift because of gravity and acceleration. This way the brain knows where down is even in the dark. You also feel it when a train pulls away.

Several senses work together for balance. The eyes show what the surroundings look like. Sensory cells in muscles and joints report the position of the arms and legs. The **cerebellum** calculates everything in a flash and controls the muscles so that you do not fall over. Try standing on one leg with your eyes closed, which is much harder.

If you spin in a circle for a long time and then stop, the fluid in the canals keeps moving. That is why the world seems to keep turning. In **travel sickness** in a car, on a ship or in a Swiss Post bus on mountain passes, the eyes and the inner ear report different things. The brain is confused, and you feel sick. It helps to look out of the window into the distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical word for the balance organ in the inner ear.
Three curved tubes filled with fluid that detect turning.
Tiny lime crystals in the inner ear that sense tilting and acceleration.
The part of the brain that controls movements and balance.

gewusst: Figure skaters and ballet dancers train so as not to feel dizzy in pirouettes.
Astronauts often feel sick at the start in weightlessness, because the ear stones no longer pull downwards.
The balance organ is fully formed even before birth.

teile.einleitung: The urinary bladder is a stretchy hollow organ in the lower abdomen. It collects the urine that the kidneys make all the time. Thanks to it, we do not have to go to the toilet constantly.
wichtigste: The bladder stores the urine.
It lies in the small pelvis behind the pubic bone.
Its wall is stretchy and folded on the inside.
When it is well filled, we feel the urge to urinate.
A sphincter muscle keeps the exit closed.
When passing water, the bladder muscle presses the urine into the urethra.
A bladder infection is usually caused by bacteria.

abschnitte.text: The **kidneys** filter the blood and make urine all the time as they do so. Through two thin tubes, the **ureters**, it flows into the **urinary bladder**. There it is collected. The bladder lies well protected in the **small pelvis**, behind the pubic bone. When it is full, the urine leaves the body through the **urethra**.

The bladder wall consists largely of muscles and is lined on the inside with a folded **mucous membrane**. When it fills, the folds smooth out, and the bladder gets bigger like a balloon. This way it can hold a few hundred millilitres of urine. When empty, it is small and folded together.

In the bladder wall sit **stretch sensors**. When the bladder is well filled, they report this to the brain, and we feel the **urge to urinate**. A **sphincter muscle** keeps the exit closed until we are on the toilet. Then it relaxes, and the **bladder muscle** in the wall contracts. This presses the urine out. Small children only learn to control this with time.

In a **bladder infection**, bacteria have usually got into the bladder. Typical are burning when passing water and frequent urges to go. Drinking a lot helps to flush the bacteria out. If someone cannot hold back the urine, this is called **incontinence**. It occurs more often in older people and can often be improved with **pelvic floor training**.

gewusst: The kidneys of an adult make about one and a half litres of urine a day.
The urine stays in the bladder because the ureters run at a slant through the bladder wall and so act like a valve.

teile.einleitung: Immunoglobulin E, IgE for short, is a class of antibodies. Originally it helps the body against parasites such as worms. It is best known, though, because it plays a main part in allergies such as hay fever.
wichtigste: IgE is one of five classes of antibodies.
It mediates the classic immediate-type allergy.
Originally it is aimed mainly at parasitic worms.
Of all antibodies, IgE is present in the smallest amount in the blood.
On mast cells, IgE binds to the receptor FcεRI.
It was discovered in the mid 1960s by the married couple Kimishige and Teruko Ishizaka.
The medicine omalizumab catches free IgE.

abschnitte.text: **Antibodies** or **immunoglobulins** are proteins of the immune system that recognise foreign substances. In humans there are five classes: IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG and IgM. Each antibody is made of heavy and light chains. Typical of immunoglobulin E is the **epsilon chain**, a particular heavy chain. In blood serum, IgE is present in the **lowest concentration** of all the antibody classes.

Originally IgE is aimed mainly at **parasitic worms**. These are far too big to be eaten by individual defence cells. IgE marks them, and other cells then attack them. Whether B cells make IgE is controlled mainly by the messenger substance **interleukin-4**. This messenger substance is made by certain **T helper cells**.

In an **allergy**, the immune system reacts to harmless substances such as pollen, house dust or animal hair. The body then makes IgE against these substances. The IgE binds to the high-affinity receptor **FcεRI** on **mast cells**. If the substance meets these cells again, they release **histamine** within minutes. This triggers sneezing, itching or swelling. That is why it is called the classic **immediate-type** allergy.

Immunoglobulin E was discovered in the **mid 1960s**. The Japanese married couple of researchers **Kimishige and Teruko Ishizaka** were studying in the USA which substance in the blood causes allergies. At about the same time, researchers in Sweden also found an unusual antibody, which turned out to be the same one.

If an allergy is suspected, you can measure in the blood whether IgE against certain substances is present. For severe allergic **asthma** there is a special medicine: **omalizumab**. It is an antibody made in the laboratory, a so-called **monoclonal antibody**. It catches free IgE in the blood so that it can no longer attach to mast cells.

gewusst: Although only very little IgE is found in the blood, it can set off violent reactions.
The E in the name stands for erythema, a word for reddening of the skin.

teile.einleitung: The Heimlich manoeuvre is a first-aid hold for when someone is choking. It helps when something like a piece of food is stuck in the windpipe. A strong push on the upper belly forces air out of the lungs and pushes the object out.
wichtigste: The manoeuvre is named after the American doctor Henry Heimlich.
Henry Heimlich introduced it in 1974.
The helper stands behind the person and puts their arms around them.
The fist goes on the upper belly, between the belly button and the tip of the breastbone.
The pressure on the diaphragm forces air out of the lungs.
Up to 5 back blows and 5 upper-belly thrusts are given in turn.
The manoeuvre must not be used on babies.

abschnitte.titel: When something is stuck in the throat
abschnitte.text: Sometimes a piece of food goes into the **windpipe** instead of the gullet when eating. Usually you cough it back up. But if the person can no longer cough, speak or breathe, it is life-threatening. Then you must help at once and call the emergency number **144**. First you give up to five strong **blows between the shoulder blades**. If that does not help, the **Heimlich manoeuvre** follows.

The helper stands **behind the person** and puts both arms around them. One hand makes a **fist**. It goes on the **upper belly**, between the belly button and the tip of the breastbone. The other hand grips the fist. Then you pull sharply **inwards and upwards**. According to the guidelines, up to 5 back blows and up to 5 upper-belly thrusts are given in turn. In between, you check whether the object has come loose.

The sharp thrust pushes the **diaphragm** upwards. This is the big breathing muscle beneath the lungs. As a result, the air in the lungs is squeezed together strongly. It shoots upwards and pushes the object out, like a cork from a bottle. Because the hold is forceful, the person should always be examined by a doctor afterwards.

abschnitte.titel: When you do not use it
abschnitte.text: On **babies** you must not use the Heimlich manoeuvre, because their abdominal organs are too easily injured. For them you give **chest compressions** with two fingers. With very overweight people, too, you cannot reliably put your arms around the upper belly. Then you press on the lower **chest** instead. In Switzerland you can take a first-aid course with the Samaritans, for example.

gewusst: Henry Heimlich published the method in 1974 in an American medical journal, and after that it spread very quickly.
Heimlich is said to have used the hold on a real person for the first time himself only at the great age of over 90.

teile.einleitung: The skin is the largest organ of a person and wraps the whole body like a living coat. It protects against germs, sun and injuries, keeps the body temperature in balance and lets you feel touch. In an adult it is almost two square metres in size.
wichtigste: The skin is the largest organ of a person.
It protects the body from germs, drying out and UV rays.
The skin regulates body temperature to a large degree, above all by sweating.
We sweat when we are hot, to cool the body.
The skin consists of three layers: epidermis, dermis and subcutis.
Sun cream protects the skin from sunburn in summer.
The fingerprint is unique to every person.

abschnitte.text: On the very outside lies the **epidermis**. Its topmost cells are dead and flake off constantly, and new ones grow underneath. Below lies the **dermis** with blood vessels, nerves, hair roots, sweat glands and oil glands. At the bottom follows the **subcutis** with fatty tissue, which warms and pads. The skin is of different thickness in different places, very thin at the eyelids and thickest on the soles of the feet.

The skin is a barrier against bacteria, viruses and fungi. A thin acid mantle on the surface makes it harder for germs to multiply. The skin also stops the body from drying out. The pigment **melanin** protects against harmful UV rays of the sun. That is why the skin turns brown in summer.

When you are hot, the **sweat glands** make sweat. As it evaporates on the skin, it draws warmth from the body and cools it. At the same time, the blood vessels in the skin widen, which is why your face goes red. In the cold, the vessels contract so that less warmth is lost. In cold or fear, small muscles make the little hairs stand up, which is called **goosebumps**.

In the skin lie millions of sensory cells. They report touch, pressure, warmth, cold and pain to the brain. There are especially many on the fingertips and the lips. The lines on the fingertips form the **fingerprint**, which is different in every person. The police therefore use it to recognise people.

Too much sun leads to **sunburn**, which damages the skin and raises the risk of skin cancer. Switzerland is among the countries with especially many cases of black skin cancer. In the mountains, UV radiation is stronger, and snow throws it back as well. Protect yourself with sun cream, a hat, a T-shirt and sunglasses, and stay in the shade over midday. Small wounds should be cleaned and covered, and then the skin usually heals by itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outermost layer of skin, which constantly renews itself.
A pigment that colours skin and hair and protects against UV rays.
