A small gland in the skin that makes sweat for cooling.
The invisible part of sunlight that causes sunburn.

gewusst: The skin of an adult weighs several kilograms.
A large part of house dust consists of flaked-off bits of skin.
Humans have several million sweat glands.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes you can feel your heart pounding very clearly. This happens, for example, after running or when you get a fright. Most of the time this is completely normal and shows that your body is working well.
wichtigste: You usually feel the pounding in your chest.
After a fast run, the heart pounds especially hard.
During sport, the muscles need more oxygen.
The heart also beats faster when you get a fright or before a performance.
The substance adrenaline makes the heart beat faster when you get a fright.
Breathing calmly and deeply helps against a pounding heart caused by excitement.

abschnitte.text: When you run fast, your **muscles** work very hard. They need a lot of **oxygen**. The blood brings it. So the heart beats faster and harder to pump more blood. Then you feel it pounding **in your chest**. Sometimes you feel the pulse at your neck as well.

Your heart can also suddenly pound without any sport, for example when you **get a fright**. Then the body releases a substance, **adrenaline**. It gets the body ready to react quickly. The heart beats faster, and you are wide awake. This used to be important for running away from danger.

Perhaps you know this: before a **performance** at school, an exam or a match, you feel nervous. Then, too, your **heart beats faster**. This is completely normal and also happens to adults. It helps to **breathe calmly and deeply**. Breathe in slowly through your nose and breathe out for a long time. This calms the heart.

When you **rest** after sport, the pounding slowly **becomes calmer**. The muscles need less oxygen, and the heart does not have to work so hard. After a few minutes it beats at its normal rhythm again. Anyone who does sport often has a strong heart that recovers faster.

gewusst: If you lay your hand flat on the left side of your chest, you can often feel your heart pounding.
A child’s heart beats faster at rest than an adult’s heart.

teile.einleitung: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped section of the fine kidney tubules. It helps the kidney to save water and to concentrate the urine. To do this it uses a clever countercurrent principle.
wichtigste: The loop of Henle concentrates the urine using the countercurrent principle.
It lies mainly in the renal medulla.
In the descending limb, water leaves into the renal medulla.
The ascending limb is practically impermeable to water.
The Na-K-2Cl cotransporter pumps salt into the tissue there.
Loop diuretics block this salt transport.
It is named after the anatomist Jakob Henle.

abschnitte.text: Each kidney is made up of around a million tiny filtering units, the **nephrons**. After the filter, the fluid flows through fine tubules. Part of them dips down like a **hairpin** from the renal cortex into the **renal medulla** and back up again. This is the **loop of Henle**. It has a **descending limb** and an **ascending limb**. The loops of the nephrons close to the medulla reach especially deep.

The two limbs lie close together and the fluid flows through them in **opposite directions**. This is called the **countercurrent principle**. The **ascending limb** pumps salt into the tissue but lets no water through. As a result the renal medulla becomes very rich in salt. The **descending limb** lets water through easily. Because the medulla is salty, water flows out by **osmosis**, and the urine becomes more concentrated.

In the thick ascending limb the **Na-K-2Cl cotransporter**, or **NKCC2** for short, is at work. It takes up one sodium, one potassium and two chloride ions at the same time. It is the motor for the salt content of the renal medulla. Because salt, but no water, is removed here, the fluid afterwards is **hypotonic**, that is, more dilute than the blood plasma. That is why this part is also called the **diluting segment**. **Loop diuretics** such as furosemide block the transporter, and then the amount of urine rises sharply.

Blood plasma has a concentration of around **290 mosmol/l**. Thanks to the countercurrent system, humans can concentrate their urine to about **1200 mosmol/l**, that is, to around four times as much. The loop is named after the German anatomist **Friedrich Gustav Jakob Henle**, who described it in the 19th century. Among other places, he taught at the **University of Zurich**.

gewusst: Desert animals such as the kangaroo rat have especially long loops of Henle and can therefore produce very concentrated urine.
Without the loops of Henle, a person would have to drink much more every day, because they would lose much more water.

teile.einleitung: Hydroxyapatite is a mineral made of calcium and phosphate. It makes our bones and teeth hard and strong. Tooth enamel is made almost entirely of it.
wichtigste: The formula of hydroxyapatite is often written as Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2.
The main components are calcium and phosphorus, as phosphate groups.
The ratio of calcium to phosphorus is about 1.67.
By weight, bone is about 60 to 70 per cent mineral.
Tooth enamel is about 95 per cent hydroxyapatite.
Fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant to acid.
Artificial hydroxyapatite is used to coat bone implants.

abschnitte.text: **Hydroxyapatite** is a **calcium phosphate**. It contains calcium ions, phosphate groups and hydroxide groups. Its formula is often written as **Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2**. In it there are 10 calcium atoms to 6 phosphorus atoms. This gives a ratio of about **1.67**. In mineralogy, hydroxyapatite belongs to the **apatite group** and so to the class of the **phosphates**. It also occurs in nature in rocks.

By weight, bone is about **60 to 70 per cent** mineral, mainly hydroxyapatite. The rest is an organic base substance, mainly the protein **collagen**, and water. The mineral makes the bone hard, and the collagen makes it a little flexible. Together, the bone is strong and does not break so easily. That is why the skeleton is also the body’s biggest **store of calcium and phosphate**.

Even more hydroxyapatite is in **tooth enamel**: about **95 per cent**. This makes it the hardest tissue in the human body. Bone and the **dentine** under the enamel contain clearly more organic material. Acids, for example from sugary drinks or from bacteria, can attack and dissolve the enamel, however. This is how **tooth decay** can arise.

**Fluoride** can replace the hydroxide group in tooth enamel. This produces **fluorapatite**, which dissolves less easily in acid. That is why many toothpastes contain fluoride, and in Switzerland there is also fluoridated table salt. In medicine, artificially made hydroxyapatite is used as a **coating for implants**. Because it resembles bone mineral, bone grows onto it well, for example with hip replacements or dental implants.

gewusst: The name apatite comes from the Greek word for “to deceive”, because the mineral was easily mistaken for others.
Shark teeth, too, are made largely of apatite.

teile.einleitung: Hand, foot and mouth disease is a contagious viral illness that mainly small children get. Typical are blisters in the mouth and spots on the hands and feet. Usually it is harmless.
wichtigste: The illness is caused by viruses, so-called enteroviruses.
Children under ten are the most often affected.
It often begins with fever and a sore throat.
Small painful blisters form in the mouth.
There are also spots and blisters on the hands and feet.
Usually it heals by itself after seven to ten days.
Thorough hand washing protects against infection.

abschnitte.text: **Hand, foot and mouth disease** is caused by certain **viruses**, so-called **enteroviruses**. It passes from person to person. **Small children** catch it most often, mainly under ten, often in day care and kindergarten. Adults are usually already protected, because they had the illness earlier.

First you often have a slight **fever**, a **sore throat** and little appetite. One or two days later the typical signs come. In the **mouth**, small **blisters** form, which can hurt. On the **hands** and **feet**, red spots and blisters appear. The illness is named after these three parts of the body.

The blisters in the mouth hurt when chewing and swallowing. That is why sick children often eat badly. **Cool, soft foods** such as yoghurt or porridge are more pleasant than hard or sour ones. It is especially important to **drink a lot**. Usually the illness is **harmless** and heals by itself after seven to ten days. Severe cases are rare.

The viruses are in the **saliva**, in the blisters and in the stool. Through the hands they easily reach other people. That is why **thorough hand washing** protects well, especially after going to the toilet and after changing nappies. You should also keep toys and surfaces clean.

The name is reminiscent of the **foot-and-mouth disease** of animals. These are two different illnesses, however. They are caused by different viruses. Foot-and-mouth disease affects animals such as cattle and pigs. Hand, foot and mouth disease, on the other hand, passes from person to person.

gewusst: You can get hand, foot and mouth disease several times, because there are different viruses that cause it.
Despite the similar name, you cannot catch hand, foot and mouth disease from cows.

teile.einleitung: In altitude training, athletes train in the mountains, where the air is thinner. The body adapts to the lack of oxygen and makes more red blood cells. Back down in the valley, people can then often perform better in endurance sports.
wichtigste: At altitude you take in less oxygen with each breath.
The body therefore makes more red blood cells.
The hormone EPO stimulates this production, and injecting it artificially is banned.
St Moritz, at over 1800 metres, is a well-known place for altitude training.
“Live high, train low” means sleeping high up and training low down.
An altitude training camp usually lasts at least two to three weeks.

abschnitte.text: In the mountains the **air pressure** is lower than in the valley. With each breath, **less oxygen** therefore reaches the lungs. In the first days you get **out of breath** more quickly during sport and tire more quickly with the same effort. After a few days the body gets used to it. It is exactly this adaptation that **endurance athletes** such as runners, cross-country skiers or cyclists use in **altitude training**.

When the body notices a lack of oxygen, the **kidney** makes more of the hormone **erythropoietin**, or **EPO** for short. This stimulates the making of **red blood cells** in the bone marrow. They carry the oxygen in the blood. With more red blood cells, the blood can bring more oxygen to the **muscles**. Because this takes time, an altitude training camp usually lasts **two to four weeks**, or at least about two to three. EPO injected artificially is banned in sport as **doping**.

At great heights you cannot train as hard as in the valley because of the lack of oxygen. That is why there is the principle “**Live high, train low**”: you sleep high up and train lower down. You live at altitude so that the blood adapts. But you train lower down, where you can run faster and harder. Some athletes also sleep in special tents or rooms where the air contains less oxygen.

With its Alps, Switzerland offers good conditions. **St Moritz** in the **Upper Engadine** in the canton of the Grisons is well known, lying at over **1800 metres** above sea level. Many runners and cross-country skiers from all over the world train there. It is important not to climb too high too fast. Otherwise **altitude sickness** can occur, with headache and nausea, because the body cannot adapt in time.

gewusst: Many runners from Kenya and Ethiopia grow up in highlands above 2000 metres.
The effect of altitude training wears off again a few weeks after returning to the valley.

teile.einleitung: The venae cavae are the biggest veins in the body. They collect the used blood from the whole body and bring it back to the heart. There is an upper and a lower vena cava.
wichtigste: Two venae cavae open into the heart.
They open into the right atrium.
The venae cavae carry blood low in oxygen.
The superior vena cava collects blood from the head, neck and arms.
The inferior vena cava brings blood from the legs and abdomen.
The inferior vena cava is the biggest vein in the body.
Vena cava is Latin and means “hollow vein”.

abschnitte.text: Arteries carry the blood away from the heart, and **veins** bring it back to the heart. The biggest veins are called the **venae cavae**, singular **vena cava**, Latin for “hollow vein”. There are **two** of them. Both open into the **right atrium** of the heart. From there the blood flows into the right ventricle and on to the lungs.

The **superior vena cava** collects the blood from the upper part of the body. It brings the blood from the **head, neck and arms** to the heart. It is relatively short and lies in the chest to the right of the aorta. Its blood flows from above into the right atrium.

The **inferior vena cava** is the **biggest vein** in the human body. It collects the blood from the **legs** and the **abdomen**, for example from the kidneys and the liver. It runs upwards to the right of the spine, passes through the diaphragm and opens from below into the right atrium.

The venae cavae carry **blood low in oxygen**. The organs and muscles have used up the oxygen on the way and given off carbon dioxide in exchange. In pictures, this kind of blood is often drawn blue. In reality, however, it is dark red. Only in the lungs does it get fresh oxygen again.

In the **aorta** the blood pressure is high, because the heart pushes the blood out with force. In the venae cavae near the heart, on the other hand, the blood pressure is **very low**. So that the blood from the legs still gets upwards, **vein valves** in the leg veins and the movement of the leg muscles help. That is why it is good to get up now and then when you have been sitting for a long time.

gewusst: The pressure near the venae cavae is called central venous pressure, and it is often measured in intensive care units.

teile.einleitung: In sudden hearing loss, you suddenly hear much worse in one ear, or hardly anything at all. Often no clear reason can be found for it. It is important to see a doctor quickly.
wichtigste: Sudden hearing loss is a sudden loss of hearing, usually in one ear.
The inner ear is affected.
Many describe the feeling as if they had cotton wool in the ear.
A ringing in the ear often goes with it.
Cortisone is often used as a medicine.
A mild sudden hearing loss often heals by itself.
It occurs most often around the age of 50.

abschnitte.text: In **sudden hearing loss**, you suddenly lose part of your hearing, usually in **one ear** only. The **inner ear** is affected, where sound is turned into nerve signals. The hearing loss can be slight or very severe. It usually comes without pain and without warning, sometimes even in sleep.

Many of those affected say it feels **as if they had cotton wool in the ear**. Often a **noise in the ear** goes with it, a whistling, rushing or humming that is called **tinnitus**. Some also feel pressure in the ear or slight dizziness. Sounds in the affected ear can sound distorted or dull.

In sudden hearing loss, usually **no clear cause** can be found. That is why it differs from an **acoustic trauma**, which is caused by a very loud bang. Experts suspect, for example, problems with the blood supply to the inner ear, inflammation or stress as possible triggers. But this is not proven. Sudden hearing loss occurs most often in adults around the age of **50**, but it can also affect younger people.

Anyone who suddenly hears almost nothing in one ear should **see a doctor quickly**, for example an ear, nose and throat practice. There the hearing is tested carefully with a hearing test. Other causes such as a plug of earwax are ruled out. Often **cortisone** is given, a medicine that reduces inflammation and swelling.

A mild sudden hearing loss often has a good outcome: the hearing **recovers by itself in many cases**, usually within days or weeks. With a severe sudden hearing loss, part of the loss can stay. Then hearing aids sometimes help. Rest and less noise are good for the ear during this time.

gewusst: Sudden hearing loss usually does not hurt, which is why some people do not take it seriously enough.
A plug of earwax can also cause sudden poor hearing, but that is not sudden hearing loss.

teile.einleitung: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation helps people whose heart is no longer pumping. With chest compressions and rescue breaths, blood with oxygen is moved around the body until help arrives. Anyone can learn it, for example in a first-aid course.
wichtigste: In a cardiac arrest you start chest compressions straight away.
You press on the breastbone in the middle of the chest.
You press about 100 to 120 times a minute.
In adults, 30 compressions and 2 rescue breaths take turns.
After each press, the chest is released completely.
A defibrillator can end ventricular fibrillation with an electric shock.

abschnitte.text: When the heart stops, the **brain** no longer gets oxygen. After just a few minutes it is damaged. That is why it is so important to start **chest compressions** at once. In Switzerland you call the emergency number **144** first. The person on the phone also helps you with what you need to do.

The person lies on their back on a **hard, flat surface**, best of all on the floor. On a soft bed, the pressure would be lost. You kneel beside them and place your hands one on top of the other in the **middle of the chest**, on the **breastbone**. Your arms are **straight** and vertical above the chest. In adults you press down about 5 to 6 centimetres.

You press about **100 to 120 times a minute**, which is almost twice a second. After each press you let the chest come all the way back up. Only then can the heart fill with blood again. In adults, **30 compressions** and **2 rescue breaths** take turns. Anyone who cannot or does not want to give rescue breaths simply keeps pressing without a break.

Often the reason for a cardiac arrest is **ventricular fibrillation**. Here the heart muscle twitches in a disordered way and pumps no blood. A **defibrillator** gives an electric shock so that the heart can beat in an orderly way again. Public devices are called **AEDs**. They explain every step in a spoken voice and only give a shock if it is needed.

Resuscitation is important for children too. You press the chest in by about **a third of its depth**. With small children you use only one hand, and with babies two fingers. Because in children the cause is often a lack of oxygen, rescue breaths play a big part.

gewusst: Many helpers find the right rhythm by thinking of a well-known song with about 100 beats a minute.
You cannot do anything wrong with chest compressions: doing nothing is the only mistake.

teile.einleitung: The brainstem is the lowest part of the brain. It joins the brain to the spinal cord. Here, vital processes such as breathing and heartbeat are controlled without our having to think about them.
wichtigste: The brainstem controls breathing and heartbeat.
It is made up of the midbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata.
The medulla oblongata passes directly into the spinal cord.
Through the pons, the cerebrum is connected to the cerebellum.
Coughing, sneezing and swallowing are controlled in the medulla oblongata.
Most of the twelve pairs of cranial nerves leave the brainstem.
The reticular formation is important for wakefulness and sleep.

abschnitte.text: The **brainstem** lies at the very bottom of the brain, beneath the cerebrum and in front of the cerebellum. It looks like a short, thick stalk. At the bottom it passes into the **spinal cord**. All signals between the brain and the body run through the brainstem, for example when you move your hand or feel something.

The brainstem is made up of three parts. At the top is the **midbrain**. Underneath follows the **pons**, a bulging part. Through the pons, the cerebrum is connected to the **cerebellum**. At the very bottom is the **medulla oblongata**. It passes directly into the spinal cord.

The brainstem controls processes that must always be running, even in sleep. These include **breathing** and the **heartbeat** as well as blood pressure. In the **medulla oblongata**, **protective reflexes** are also controlled, for example **coughing**, **sneezing** and **swallowing**. These reflexes protect us, for instance when something goes down the wrong way.

Besides the nerves of the spinal cord, there are **twelve pairs of cranial nerves**. They supply mainly the head and neck, for example the eyes, face, tongue and ears. **Most** of them leave **from the brainstem**. One important cranial nerve, the vagus, reaches as far as the heart, lungs and abdomen.

A fine network of nerves runs through the whole brainstem. It is called the **reticular formation**, which means “net-like structure”. This network is important for **wakefulness and sleep**. It helps to make sure that we wake up when the alarm clock rings and stay alert.

gewusst: In the history of evolution, the brainstem is one of the oldest parts of the brain.
If the brainstem fails completely, a person can no longer breathe on their own.

teile.einleitung: The neck joins the head to the trunk. Air, food, blood and nerves run through it. In addition, the larynx sits in the neck, and with it we speak and sing.
wichtigste: The neck joins the head and the trunk.
The back of the neck is called the nape.
The vocal cords sit in the larynx.
The windpipe and the gullet run through the neck.
With a cold, you often have a sore throat.
Around the neck there are scarves, necklaces and collars.
The German saying “Hals über Kopf” means very hurried and rash.

abschnitte.text: The **neck** joins the head to the trunk. In the neck lies the **cervical spine** with seven vertebrae. It carries the head and makes it mobile. At the back of the neck lies the **nape**. There sit strong muscles that hold the head. Through the neck run the **windpipe** to the lung and the **gullet** to the stomach.

In the neck sits the **larynx**. In it lie the **vocal cords**. When air flows past them, they vibrate and make sounds. This is how we can speak and sing. In many people, you can see the larynx at the front of the neck as a small bump. When swallowing, it moves up and down.

With a **cold**, the inside of the throat can be inflamed. Then swallowing hurts, and you have a **sore throat**. Often warm tea helps. In winter, you wear a **scarf** against the cold. You wind it once or twice around the neck, and so it stays warm.

There are many things around the neck. The **collar** is the upper edge of a shirt and lies around the neck. A **necklace** is a piece of jewellery that you put around the neck, often with a small pendant. Ties and neckerchiefs are also worn at the neck.

The German word for neck, “Hals”, appears in many sayings. Someone who does something **“Hals über Kopf”** (literally “neck over head”) acts in great haste and hardly thinks. Someone who **“makes a long neck”** stretches head and neck upwards to see something over other people. And someone who “cannot get their neck full” always wants even more.

gewusst: A giraffe has as many vertebrae in its neck as a human, namely seven.
Air and food run very close beside each other through the throat, and a small lid makes sure when swallowing that the food does not get into the windpipe.

teile.einleitung: The pituitary gland, also called the hypophysis, is a tiny hormone gland on the underside of the brain. Although it is only about as big as a pea, it controls many other glands. That is why it is often called the boss of the hormone glands.
wichtigste: The pituitary gland hangs from a small stalk under the brain.
It is about as big as a pea and weighs less than a gram.
It lies protected in a hollow in the bone, the sella turcica.
It consists of an anterior lobe and a posterior lobe.
ACTH stimulates the adrenal cortex, TSH the thyroid gland.
Insulin does not come from the pituitary gland but from the pancreas.
A tumour on the pituitary gland can cause problems with vision.

abschnitte.text: The **pituitary gland** lies on the underside of the brain, roughly behind the bridge of the nose. It hangs from a small **stalk** and looks like an appendage, which is why in German it is called the **Hirnanhangdrüse**, “brain appendage gland”. It is only about one centimetre across, about the size of a **pea**, and weighs less than a gram. It lies protected in a hollow in the bone at the base of the skull. Because this hollow in the **sphenoid bone** reminds people of a riding saddle, it is called the **sella turcica**, or Turkish saddle.

The pituitary gland has two main parts. The **anterior lobe** makes many hormones itself. The **posterior lobe** makes no hormones of its own. It stores hormones that are made in the **hypothalamus** and releases them into the blood when needed. The hypothalamus lies directly above and gives the pituitary gland its orders. In this way the brain and the endocrine system work closely together.

**Hormones** are messenger substances that travel through the body in the blood. Many hormones of the pituitary gland tell other glands to get to work. **ACTH**, the adrenocorticotropic hormone, makes the **adrenal cortex** produce its hormones. **TSH** stimulates the **thyroid gland**. Another hormone is the **growth hormone**, which is important for the growth of bones and body. **Insulin** is not one of them, it comes from the pancreas.

Directly above the pituitary gland, the **optic nerves** of the two eyes cross. If a tumour grows on the pituitary gland, it can press on these nerves. Then parts of the **field of vision** can be lost, and you may see less well at the sides, for example. Such tumours are mostly harmless and can often be treated. Doctors examine the pituitary gland with **magnetic resonance imaging**, a kind of X-ray picture without X-rays.

gewusst: The name hypophysis comes from Greek and means roughly “that which has grown underneath”.
Although it is so small, the pituitary gland influences growth, metabolism and how we deal with stress.

teile.einleitung: Hairs grow almost everywhere on our skin. They protect, warm a little and help with touch. On the head, a person has about 100,000 of them.
wichtigste: About 100,000 hairs grow on the head.
Over the whole body, there are several million hairs.
Hairs consist mainly of keratin, a horn-like substance.
Each day about 50 to 100 head hairs fall out.
A head hair grows for several years.
A hair is about 0.05 to 0.1 millimetres thick.
In old age, hairs turn grey because they get less pigment.

abschnitte.text: On a person's head grow about **100,000 hairs**. In blond people there are often a few more, because their hairs are thinner. Almost everywhere on the body, fine little hairs also grow. Together there are **several million**. Only a few places are completely without hair, for example the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet and the lips.

Hair consists mainly of **keratin**, a **horn-like substance**. Our fingernails are made of the same substance. A single head hair is only about **0.05 to 0.1 millimetres** thick. The hair above the skin consists of horny, dead cells. That is why cutting hair does not hurt.

The hair grows in the **hair root** under the skin. A head hair usually grows for **several years**, about one centimetre a month. Then it falls out, and a new one grows. Every day you lose about **50 to 100 hairs**. That is quite normal. By the way, having your hair cut often does not make it grow faster. That is a mistake, because growth happens in the root.

Hair gets its colour from a **pigment** that is made in the hair root. In old age, the root makes less and less of it. Without pigment, the hair looks **grey** or white. When someone gets grey hair varies greatly and also depends on the family.

Some people let their hair grow for decades. In 2004, the hair of **Xie Qiuping** from China was measured. It was over **5.6 metres** long, which was a **world record**. For such long hair to be possible, the growing time has to be especially long and you must never cut it.

gewusst: The record-breaking hair of Xie Qiuping was longer than three adults standing on top of each other.
Hair and fingernails are made of the same horn-like substance, keratin.

teile.einleitung: Helicobacter pylori is a bacterium that can live in the stomach even though there is a great deal of acid there. It can cause inflammation of the stomach and stomach ulcers. Its discoverers received the Nobel Prize for it in 2005.
wichtigste: Helicobacter pylori is a Gram-negative, spiral-shaped bacterium with flagella.
With the enzyme urease it protects itself from stomach acid.
It causes inflammation of the stomach lining and ulcers.
Barry Marshall and Robin Warren received the Nobel Prize in 2005.
A urea breath test detects the infection in the air you breathe out.
The World Health Organization has classed it as carcinogenic since 1994.
It is treated with an acid blocker and antibiotics.

abschnitte.text: For a long time people thought that no bacterium could survive in the acidic **stomach**. **Helicobacter pylori** manages it all the same. It is **spiral-shaped** and moves through the stomach mucus with **flagella**. In the **Gram stain**, a laboratory method, it appears **Gram-negative**. With the enzyme **urease** it splits urea into **ammonia** and carbon dioxide. The ammonia neutralises the acid around the bacterium.

The two Australians **Barry Marshall** and **Robin Warren** showed in the 1980s that the bacterium causes **inflammation of the stomach lining** and **stomach ulcers**. At first many experts did not believe them. In 1984 Marshall therefore drank a bacterial culture himself and came down with **gastritis**. This **self-experiment** helped to convince the scientific world. In 2005 both received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

Many people carry the bacterium without noticing. But long-lasting **chronic inflammation** can have consequences. Since 1994 the **International Agency for Research on Cancer** has classed the bacterium as a **group 1 carcinogen**, that is, as definitely cancer-causing. A chronic infection raises the risk of **stomach cancer**. The **MALT lymphoma** of the stomach is also closely linked with it. Early MALT lymphomas often shrink once the bacterium has been removed.

In the **urea breath test** you drink marked urea. If the bacterium is present, it splits the urea, and marked carbon dioxide appears in the air you breathe out. The classic **eradication therapy**, that is, getting rid of the bacterium, combines an **acid blocker** with **two antibiotics**, usually for 7 to 14 days. Because some bacteria have become **resistant** to antibiotics, quadruple therapies are often used today.

gewusst: About half of all the people in the world carry Helicobacter pylori in their stomach.
Barry Marshall proved his idea with a self-experiment, because he could not test the bacterium on animals.

teile.einleitung: Histamine is a messenger substance that our body makes itself. It plays a big part in allergies, but has many other jobs too. Histamine also occurs in some foods.
wichtigste: The body makes histamine from the amino acid histidine.
In an allergy, mast cells release especially large amounts of histamine.
In the skin, histamine causes itching, redness and swelling.
Antihistamines block the effect of histamine.
In the brain, histamine keeps you awake, which is why older allergy medicines make you tired.
Matured cheese, sauerkraut and badly chilled tuna contain a lot of histamine.
The enzyme diamine oxidase breaks down histamine from food in the gut.

abschnitte.text: **Histamine** is a **messenger substance** that passes on signals between cells. The body makes it from the **amino acid histidine**. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Histamine acts in many places: in the body’s defences, in the stomach in making stomach acid, and in the brain.

In an allergy, the body’s defences react too strongly to something harmless, for example pollen. Then certain defence cells, the **mast cells**, release especially large amounts of histamine. In the **skin**, this leads to **itching, redness and swelling**. In the nose it causes a runny nose, and the eyes water. With a mosquito bite, too, histamine is involved in the itching.

Medicines that block the effect of histamine are called **antihistamines**. They help, for example, with hay fever. In the **brain**, histamine makes sure we stay **awake**. Older allergy medicines easily reach the brain and block the histamine there. That is why they often make you **tired**. Newer medicines have this side effect much less.

Histamine is also formed in food when bacteria are at work there. Foods that contain a lot of histamine include **long-matured cheese**, raw sausage and fermented vegetables such as **sauerkraut**. Badly chilled fish is especially dangerous. In **tuna**, a great deal of histamine can form if it is stored wrongly. This can lead to poisoning with redness, headache and nausea.

Normally the body breaks down histamine from food quickly. In the **gut**, this is done mainly by the enzyme **diamine oxidase**, or DAO for short. Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical processes. Some people do not tolerate foods rich in histamine well. Whether and how often such an intolerance occurs is still being discussed in medicine.

gewusst: Histamine was discovered at the start of the 20th century, long before its part in allergies was known.
Once it has formed, histamine is hardly destroyed by boiling or frying.

teile.einleitung: Panting is quick, shallow breathing with an open mouth. Dogs pant mainly to cool down, because they can hardly sweat. Other mammals, such as cats, sometimes pant too.
wichtigste: A dog pants on hot days to cool down.
Dogs have only a few sweat glands, mainly on their paws.
When panting, the dog sticks its tongue far out.
Evaporating moisture cools the body.
A panting dog breathes quickly and shallowly.
On hot days a dog needs water and shade.
You must never leave a dog in a closed car.

abschnitte.text: People sweat when they are hot. The sweat evaporates on the skin and cools it. **Dogs** can hardly do this. They have only a few **sweat glands**, mainly on the **paw pads**. That is not enough to cool down. So dogs **pant**. This is how they get rid of heat when it is hot or when they have been running a lot.

When panting, the dog breathes **quickly and shallowly**. The tongue hangs far out of the mouth. A lot of air flows over the moist **tongue** and through the airways. As it does, moisture **evaporates**. Evaporating needs heat, and this heat is taken from the body. Our sweat cools our skin in exactly the same way.

It is not only dogs that pant. Other **mammals** do it too, for example **cats** after wild play or great effort. In cats, however, it is rarer. If a cat pants often or for no reason, you should ask a vet. Fish, snails and worms cannot pant.

When panting, a dog loses **water**. On hot days it therefore always needs fresh water and a shady spot. It is better to go for walks in the morning or in the evening. You must never leave a dog in a **closed car**. A car heats up very quickly in the sun. The dog cannot cool down enough there, even by panting, and that is life-threatening.

gewusst: A panting dog can take several hundred breaths a minute.
Dogs with a very short nose, such as pugs, find it harder to cool down by panting.

teile.einleitung: When the body breaks down proteins, poisonous ammonia is made. The urea cycle turns it into harmless urea in the liver. The kidneys then remove this with the urine.
wichtigste: In humans, the urea cycle takes place mainly in the liver.
It turns poisonous ammonia into urea.
The first steps take place in the mitochondria, the rest in the cytoplasm.
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 sets the speed and needs N-acetylglutamate.
Arginase splits arginine into urea and ornithine.
3 ATP are used up per urea molecule.
Hans Krebs and Kurt Henseleit described the cycle in 1932.

abschnitte.text: Proteins are made of **amino acids**, which contain nitrogen. When they are broken down, **ammonia** is made. Ammonia is poisonous even in small amounts, above all for the brain. The **urea cycle** turns it into **urea**, which dissolves well in water and is harmless. Only the liver cells have all the enzymes needed. The kidneys then remove the urea with the urine.

The first two steps take place in the **mitochondrial matrix**. There the enzyme **carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1** joins ammonia and carbon dioxide into **carbamoyl phosphate**. Two ATP are used up in doing so. This step sets the speed of the whole cycle. The enzyme works only if **N-acetylglutamate** is present, which is made from glutamate and acetyl-CoA.

**Ornithine transcarbamylase** passes the carbamoyl group on to **ornithine**, giving **citrulline**. In the cytoplasm, the second nitrogen atom is added with **aspartate**. In this, one ATP is split into AMP, which is equal to two high-energy bonds. At the end, **arginase** splits the **arginine** that has formed into urea and ornithine. Ornithine returns to the mitochondrion and closes the circle.

The doctor and biochemist **Hans Krebs** and his student **Kurt Henseleit** described the urea cycle in 1932 in **Freiburg im Breisgau**. It was the first metabolic cycle to be discovered. Hans Krebs later also became known for the citric acid cycle, which likewise bears his name. For this he received the Nobel Prize in 1953.

gewusst: The urea cycle was the first cycle in metabolism ever to be described.
Urea was made in the laboratory as early as 1828 by Friedrich Wöhler, as the first substance from the body that could be built artificially.

teile.einleitung: The ureter is a thin muscular tube that carries urine from the kidney to the urinary bladder. Every person normally has two of them. With wave-like movements, it pushes the urine downwards, even when lying down.
wichtigste: The ureter joins the kidney to the urinary bladder.
Normally a person has two ureters, one for each kidney.
In an adult it is about 25 to 30 cm long and about 4 to 7 mm thick.
Wave-like muscle movements, called peristalsis, push the urine on.
The slanting opening into the bladder acts like a valve.
The ureter has three natural narrow points where stones can get stuck.

abschnitte.text: The two **kidneys** make urine all the time. It collects in the **renal pelvis** and then flows into the **ureter**. This runs down along the back wall of the abdomen as far as the small pelvis. There it opens into the **urinary bladder**. Because each kidney has its own ureter, two ureters open into the one bladder. In German, this tube is called the “Harnleiter”.

The urine does not simply flow downwards because of gravity. The wall of the ureter contains muscles that contract in waves. This movement is called **peristalsis**. It works in a similar way to the gut. That is why the urine reaches the bladder even when you are lying down or standing on your head.

The ureter passes **at a slant** through the bladder wall. When the bladder fills, it presses this spot shut. So the opening acts like a **valve**. That is why the urine normally cannot flow back from the bladder to the kidney. This protects the kidneys from bacteria in the bladder.

The ureter is naturally narrower in three places: at the upper end near the renal pelvis, where it crosses large blood vessels in the pelvis, and where it enters the bladder. If small **stones** form in the kidney, they often get stuck at these narrow points. This can cause very strong, cramp-like pain called **renal colic**. Many small stones pass by themselves with plenty to drink.

gewusst: The waves of muscle in the ureter run several times a minute, without us noticing anything of it.
A ureter is only a few millimetres thick but almost as long as a school ruler.

teile.einleitung: The heart has two ventricles, a right one and a left one. They are the powerful pumps that push the blood out of the heart. In German they are called Herzkammern.
wichtigste: The heart has two atria at the top and two ventricles at the bottom.
The right ventricle receives blood with little oxygen and pumps it to the lungs.
The left ventricle pumps blood with plenty of oxygen into the body.
The left ventricle has the thicker muscle wall.
The septum separates the right and left halves of the heart.
Heart valves stop the blood from flowing back.
At rest, a ventricle pushes out about 70 millilitres of blood with each beat.

abschnitte.text: The heart is a hollow muscle with four chambers. At the top are the two **atria**, at the bottom the two **ventricles**. The **septum** separates the right and left halves of the heart so that the blood does not mix. The whole heart sits in a bag of connective tissue, the **pericardium**.

Each ventricle works in two steps. First it relaxes and **fills with blood** from the atrium. Then the muscle contracts strongly and pumps the blood out. In an adult at rest this is about **70 millilitres** with each heartbeat. That is about as much as a small glass.

**Blood with little oxygen** comes into the right ventricle from the body. The right ventricle pumps this blood **to the lungs**. There it takes up fresh oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. Because the lungs are very close, the right ventricle does not need much strength.

The left ventricle receives the blood with plenty of oxygen from the lungs. It pumps it through the large artery of the body, the **aorta**, into the whole body, as far as the toes and the head. It needs a great deal of strength for this. That is why the **left ventricle** has a much **thicker muscle wall**.

So that the blood always flows in the right direction, there are **heart valves**. They act like valves. There is a valve between the atrium and the ventricle and at the exit of each ventricle. It opens in only one direction and stops the blood from **flowing back** out of the ventricles.

gewusst: The wall of the left ventricle is about three times as thick as that of the right.
Both ventricles pump about the same amount of blood with each beat, even though they differ in strength.

teile.einleitung: The hen’s egg is a valuable food and is found in many dishes, from the breakfast egg to cake. It provides a lot of protein and important vitamins. To keep it healthy, you have to store it properly and cook it well.
wichtigste: The yellow part of the egg is called the yolk.
Most of the vitamins are in the yolk.
An egg provides plenty of protein for the muscles.
A hen lays at most one egg a day.
You should boil or fry eggs well so that germs are killed.
A hard-boiled egg takes about 10 minutes.
You test whether an egg is fresh in a glass of water.

abschnitte.text: A hen’s egg consists of the **shell**, the **egg white** and the **yolk**. The egg white is mostly water and protein. In the yolk are **most of the vitamins**, for example vitamin A, vitamin D and vitamin B12, as well as fat and minerals.

An egg gives the body a lot of **protein**. The body needs protein to build muscle and renew cells. The body can make very good use of the protein from the egg. That is why eggs are also popular with athletes. As with all foods, eggs belong in a varied diet.

A hen lays **at most one egg a day**, because it takes about a day for an egg to be fully formed. The colour of the shell, white or brown, depends on the breed of hen and says nothing about quality. In Switzerland, keeping laying hens in narrow cages has been banned since the early 1990s. The packaging says how the hens were kept, for example barn, free range or organic.

Raw eggs can contain germs such as **salmonella**, which cause stomach ache and diarrhoea. That is why you should **boil or fry eggs well** before eating, so that the germs are killed. A **hard-boiled egg** takes about **10 minutes**, a soft one only about 4 to 5 minutes. After cracking raw eggs, it is best to wash your hands. Eggs are stored in the fridge.

You test whether a raw egg is still fresh by putting it in a glass of **water**. A fresh egg sinks and stays lying on the bottom. An older egg stands upright, and a very old egg floats at the top. This is because of the **air pocket** in the egg: over time water evaporates through the shell, and the air pocket gets bigger.

gewusst: An eggshell has thousands of tiny pores through which air gets in.
A boiled egg spins like a top, but a raw egg spins much worse because its inside is liquid.

teile.einleitung: House dust mites are tiny animals that live in almost every home. You cannot see them with the naked eye. For most people they are harmless, but some react allergically to them.
wichtigste: House dust mites belong to the arachnids and have eight legs.
They are only about a third of a millimetre in size.
They feed mainly on flakes of skin.
Especially many live in mattresses and bedding.
They like a warm and damp indoor climate.
In an allergy, it is mainly their droppings that cause the complaints.
Mite-proof covers and good airing help.

abschnitte.text: Like spiders, house dust mites have **eight legs**. That is why they belong to the **arachnids** and not to the insects, which have six legs. They are usually only about a third of a millimetre in size. So you can see them only under a **microscope** or a strong magnifying glass. They do not bite and do not pass on diseases.

Every day, people lose tiny **flakes of skin**. The mites feed on these. In **bed**, they find everything they need: warmth, damp from sweating and plenty of flakes of skin. That is why especially many live in **mattresses**, pillows and duvets. They take water directly from the air. In dry air and cold, they do badly.

The **allergens**, that is, the substances that cause an allergy, are found mainly in the mites' **droppings**. The tiny dropping pellets break up into fine dust, which you breathe in. Typical are a blocked nose, sneezing and watery eyes. Because you breathe in allergens for hours in bed, the complaints are usually worst **at night and in the morning**. Some of those affected also get asthma.

Special **mite-proof covers**, also called **encasings**, hold the allergens back in the mattress and pillow. Bed linen should be washed hot. Regular **airing** lowers the humidity in the bedroom. A vacuum cleaner with a **HEPA filter** also holds back the finest particles, whereas ordinary machines partly blow mite droppings back into the air. A doctor can also recommend medicines or a treatment against the allergy.

gewusst: Fewer house dust mites live in the mountains, because the air there is drier.
House dust mites never drink: they take up moisture directly from the air.

teile.einleitung: So that the brain and muscles always have enough energy, blood sugar has to stay within a certain range. The hormone **glucagon** helps with this. It raises blood sugar when it is too low.
wichtigste: Glucagon is made in the alpha cells of the pancreas.
It has been known since 1923.
Insulin and glucagon act as opposites on blood sugar.
The name comes from “glucose agonist”, that is, a sugar driver.
Glucagon is built from amino acids.
In severe low blood sugar, a companion can give glucagon as an injection or nasal spray.

abschnitte.text: Glucagon is made in the **pancreas**, in the **alpha cells**. These lie in small groups of cells, the islets of Langerhans. The hormone has been known **since 1923**. The name comes from **“glucose agonist”**, roughly “sugar driver”. Glucagon is a **peptide hormone**: it is built from **amino acids**, in humans from 29 of them.

**Insulin** and **glucagon** act as **opposites**. After eating, blood sugar rises, and then insulin makes sure that the cells take up and store sugar. When blood sugar falls, for example between meals, glucagon is released. It gets mainly the **liver** to release stored sugar from **glycogen**. This keeps blood sugar in balance.

With very long **fasting**, the glycogen store is eventually empty. Then glucagon helps in another way: the liver makes **new sugar from other substances**, for example from building blocks of proteins. This is called **gluconeogenesis**. In **endurance sport**, too, the glucagon level often rises. The muscles then use a lot of sugar, and glucagon makes sure that fresh supplies get into the blood.

People with **diabetes** who inject insulin can get **low blood sugar**. If it is severe, the person can become unconscious and unable to eat. Then a companion can give **glucagon as an injection or nasal spray**. It raises blood sugar within minutes. After that you call for medical help, in Switzerland for example on the emergency number 144.

gewusst: Glucagon was discovered because early insulin preparations first made blood sugar rise briefly: they still contained traces of glucagon.
The glucagon nasal spray works through the lining of the nose and does not have to be breathed in.

teile.einleitung: Hypothermia is a cooling of the whole body. It is the word used when the core body temperature falls below 35 degrees Celsius. In the mountains, in snow or in cold water, this can happen quickly.
wichtigste: Normally the core temperature is around 37 degrees, and below 35 degrees a person is hypothermic.
In the first stage, the person is awake and shivers strongly.
Below about 32 degrees, the shivering usually stops, a warning sign.
A person with severe hypothermia is moved gently and kept horizontal.
Small children cool down faster than adults.
Alcohol increases the risk because it lets heat flow away through the skin.
In hospital, severely hypothermic people are often rewarmed with a heart-lung machine.

abschnitte.text: The body keeps its temperature on the inside, the **core temperature**, at about **37 degrees**. If it loses more heat than it can make, it cools down. If the core temperature falls below **35 degrees**, this is called **hypothermia**. It can happen in an avalanche accident, in a fall into cold water or on a mountain tour when the weather turns. Wind and wet clothes also make the body lose heat quickly.

In emergency medicine, the **Swiss staging** is often used, because you can recognise it from the person’s condition without a thermometer. In **stage I**, the person is awake and has strong **shivering**. The shivering produces heat and is a protection. In **stage II**, the person becomes drowsy, and the shivering usually stops, at about **32 degrees**. By then the energy reserves are used up. In **stage III**, the person is unconscious, and in **stage IV** the circulation has stopped.

A person with severe hypothermia is moved as **gently and horizontally** as possible. Their heart is very easily irritated, and jerky movements or cold blood from the arms and legs can trigger **ventricular fibrillation**, a dangerous heart rhythm. You protect the person from further cold and call **144**. In a cardiac arrest, the saying applies: “**Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead**”. This is because cold greatly lowers the brain’s need for oxygen, so you keep resuscitating. In hospital, the blood is often warmed outside the body with a **heart-lung machine** or **ECMO**.

**Small children** cool down faster than adults. Their body has a large **surface** in proportion to its volume, and heat is lost through the surface. Older people are also at risk. **Alcohol** increases the risk: it widens the blood vessels of the skin, so you feel warm but lose more heat. It also clouds the judgement of the danger. Good clothing in several layers, a hat and dry socks give protection.

gewusst: There are cases in which deeply hypothermic people made a full recovery after a long cardiac arrest.
The head does not lose more heat than other parts of the body, but it is often the only one that is not covered.

teile.einleitung: HDL is a tiny transport particle in the blood that carries cholesterol. Because it brings cholesterol from the blood vessels back to the liver, HDL cholesterol is often called the “good” cholesterol.
wichtigste: HDL stands for high density lipoprotein.
HDL contains a lot of protein and little fat.
It carries excess cholesterol back to the liver.
That is why HDL cholesterol is seen as “good” cholesterol.
Its most important protein component is apolipoprotein A-I.
Endurance sport raises HDL, while smoking lowers it.
Very low HDL levels increase the risk of heart and circulatory disease.

abschnitte.text: Fats and **cholesterol** do not dissolve in water, and so they do not dissolve in blood either. That is why they are carried in small particles called **lipoproteins**. These are made of fats and proteins. **HDL** stands for high density lipoprotein. Other classes are LDL, VLDL and the chylomicrons.

Protein is heavier than fat. The more protein a lipoprotein contains, the greater its **density**. HDL contains the most protein in proportion, so it has the highest density of all lipoproteins. The **chylomicrons** contain the most fat and have the lowest density. The framework of the HDL particles is made of **apolipoprotein A-I**.

abschnitte.titel: The journey back to the liver
abschnitte.text: The main job of HDL is to pick up excess cholesterol from tissues and blood vessel walls and take it to the **liver**. This is called **reverse cholesterol transport**. An enzyme called **lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase**, or LCAT for short, helps with this. It attaches a fatty acid to the cholesterol. The resulting cholesterol ester repels water more strongly and moves into the inside of the HDL particle.

Because HDL carries cholesterol away from the vessel wall, higher levels are linked with less **arteriosclerosis**. Arteriosclerosis is a hardening and narrowing of the arteries. That is why HDL cholesterol is often called the “good” cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol the “bad” one. Very low HDL levels count as a **risk factor** for heart and circulatory diseases.

The HDL level depends partly on the genes you inherit and partly on your lifestyle. Regular **endurance sport** such as running, swimming or cycling demonstrably raises HDL. **Smoking** and lack of exercise lower it. HDL cholesterol is measured with a blood sample, often together with LDL and other blood fats.

gewusst: There is really only one kind of cholesterol: “good” and “bad” describe which transporter it is travelling with.
HDL particles are among the smallest lipoproteins in the blood.

teile.einleitung: In hand disinfection, you rub onto your hands a product that makes germs harmless. In hospitals it is one of the most important measures against infections. It is also handy when out and about, if there is no water.
wichtigste: To disinfect means to make germs harmless.
Most products contain alcohols such as ethanol or propanol.
You rub the product in for about 20 to 30 seconds, until the hands are dry.
You put it on dry hands, because water dilutes the alcohol.
If there is visible dirt, it is better to wash the hands with soap.
The thumb and fingertips are often forgotten.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis introduced hand disinfection with chlorinated lime in Vienna.

abschnitte.text: To **disinfect** means to reduce germs so much that they can no longer infect. Most **hand disinfectants** contain **alcohols** such as **ethanol** or **propanol**. These destroy the outer layer of many bacteria and viruses. They work badly against **bacterial spores**. These are very resistant resting forms of some bacteria. With such germs, you also have to wash your hands.

You put the product on **dry hands**, because water would dilute the alcohol. Then you rub it in for about **20 to 30 seconds**, until the hands are dry again. This is what the World Health Organization recommends. People often forget the **thumb**, the **fingertips** and the spaces between the fingers. So you rub these spots in on purpose. Many products contain **moisturising additives** so that the skin does not dry out despite the alcohol.

A disinfectant does **not remove dirt**. If the hands are visibly dirty, you therefore wash them with **water and soap**. In everyday life, thorough hand washing is usually enough. The disinfectant is handy when there is no wash basin nearby while out and about. In **hospitals** and doctors' surgeries, nurses and doctors disinfect their hands before and after every contact with patients.

In **1847**, the doctor **Ignaz Semmelweis** worked in a Viennese hospital. He noticed that strikingly many patients died of infections there. He suspected that doctors passed on the illness with their hands. So he had doctors and students clean their hands with a **chlorinated lime solution**. After that, clearly fewer patients died. At the time, many colleagues did not believe him; today he is regarded as one of the fathers of **hand hygiene**.

gewusst: In many Swiss hospitals, disinfectant dispensers hang at every patient's bed and in front of every room door.
Semmelweis did not yet know about bacteria. They were recognised as germs that cause disease only a few years later.

teile.einleitung: Hyposensitisation is a treatment for allergies. In it the body is given exactly the substance it is allergic to, in slowly rising amounts. In this way the immune system is meant to get used to it and react less strongly.
wichtigste: Experts also call it specific immunotherapy.
The allergen is injected or given as drops or a tablet under the tongue.
The treatment usually lasts about three to five years.
First the dose is increased, then the maintenance phase follows.
After an injection you stay in the practice for about 30 minutes.
In an allergy to bee and wasp venom it can be life-saving.
Leonard Noon reported the first trials in 1911.

abschnitte.text: In an **allergy**, the immune system reacts to a substance that is really harmless as if it were dangerous. Such a substance is called an **allergen**, for example pollen from grasses or birches, house dust mites or insect venom. Many people in Switzerland have **hay fever** in spring and summer. They sneeze, have a blocked nose and itchy eyes. In **hyposensitisation**, doctors try to weaken this exaggerated reaction.

Experts also call the treatment **specific immunotherapy**. The body gets the allergen in small, slowly **rising doses**. In the **build-up phase**, the amount is raised up to the highest dose. After that comes the **maintenance phase** with a constant dose at longer intervals. So that the immune system changes permanently, the treatment usually lasts about **three to five years**.

Often the allergen is **injected** under the skin. After each injection you stay in the practice for about **30 minutes**. This is because, rarely, a severe allergic reaction can occur, an **anaphylaxis**, and this usually appears early. That way it can be treated at once. In **sublingual immunotherapy**, on the other hand, you take the allergen as drops or a tablet **under the tongue**. Sublingual means exactly that: “under the tongue”.

During the treatment, the body makes more antibodies of the **IgG4** type. They catch the allergen before it can set off the allergic reaction, and are called blocking antibodies. The treatment is especially effective in an **allergy to bee and wasp venom**: it protects most of those treated from severe reactions when they are stung again. The founder of the method is the British doctor **Leonard Noon**. He injected people with hay fever with grass pollen extract and reported on it in **1911**.

gewusst: In hay fever, hyposensitisation can also prevent asthma from developing later as well.
In Switzerland there is a pollen measuring service that reports every day during the season how much pollen is in the air.

teile.einleitung: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a long-lasting inflammation of the thyroid gland. In it, the body's own immune system attacks the thyroid. In time it makes too few hormones, which can be made up for well with tablets.
wichtigste: Hakaru Hashimoto described the illness in 1912.
It is an autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks the thyroid gland.
Typical are antibodies against the enzyme thyroid peroxidase.
In the tissue, masses of lymphocytes are found.
In the long term, it usually leads to an underactive thyroid.
It is treated with levothyroxine; the missing hormone is replaced as a tablet.
In Switzerland, it is the most common cause of an underactive thyroid.

abschnitte.text: The **thyroid gland** lies at the front of the neck and has the shape of a butterfly. It makes hormones that control the **metabolism**, that is, how fast the body turns over energy. For these hormones it needs **iodine**. The enzyme **thyroid peroxidase** builds the iodine into the hormones.

abschnitte.titel: The immune system makes a mistake
abschnitte.text: In **Hashimoto's thyroiditis**, the immune system takes the body's own thyroid for foreign. This is called an **autoimmune disease**. The tissue is densely filled with **lymphocytes**, a kind of white blood cell. That is why the illness is also called chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis. In the blood of most of those affected, **anti-TPO antibodies** against thyroid peroxidase are found. The Japanese doctor **Hakaru Hashimoto** described it in 1912 in a German medical journal.

Bit by bit, thyroid tissue is destroyed, and an **underactive thyroid** results. The metabolism then runs more slowly. Typical are feeling very cold, tiredness and weight gain. The **pituitary gland** notices the shortage and releases more **TSH** to drive the thyroid. A raised TSH value in the blood is therefore an early sign.

The underactive thyroid is treated with **levothyroxine**. This tablet replaces the hormone T4, usually for life. Properly set, those affected can live well. In Switzerland, table salt is **iodised**, so iodine deficiency hardly plays a part any more. The most common cause of an underactive thyroid here is therefore Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Women fall ill clearly more often than men.

gewusst: Switzerland has iodised table salt since the 1920s, to prevent goitre.
Hakaru Hashimoto published his description in German in 1912, because German was then an important language of medicine.

teile.einleitung: HbA1c is a blood value that shows how high the blood sugar has been on average over the last weeks. It is especially important for people with diabetes. It is sometimes also called the “blood sugar memory”.
wichtigste: HbA1c is haemoglobin to which glucose is bound.
The value shows the average blood sugar of the last 8 to 12 weeks.
From 6.5 per cent, diabetes counts as diagnosed.
The glucose binds to the haemoglobin without an enzyme.
You do not have to be fasting for the measurement.
With red blood cells that live for a shorter time, the value can be too low.
HbA1c is well suited to monitoring diabetes over time.

abschnitte.titel: Sugar on the red blood pigment
abschnitte.text: In the red blood cells sits the red blood pigment **haemoglobin**. It carries oxygen. In the blood there is always sugar too, the **glucose**. Part of it attaches to the haemoglobin without the help of an enzyme. This is called **glycation**. This is how **HbA1c**, the **glycated haemoglobin**, comes about. The value says what percentage of the haemoglobin is joined to glucose. The higher the blood sugar, the more HbA1c is made.

Red blood cells live around **120 days**. That is why HbA1c shows the average blood sugar of the last **8 to 12 weeks**. A single meal hardly changes it. That is why you do not have to be **fasting** for the measurement. Internationally, it is exactly fixed where the glucose sits: on the end amino acid **valine** of the beta chains of the haemoglobin.

By the criteria of the **WHO** and the professional societies, an HbA1c from **6.5 per cent** counts as a sign of **diabetes mellitus**. In people with diabetes, the doctor measures the value regularly, often every few months. This way she sees whether the treatment is working well. Short-term **low blood sugar**, however, is not picked up by HbA1c. For that, you measure the blood sugar directly.

HbA1c is not always reliable. In **haemolytic anaemia**, red blood cells are broken down sooner. They have less time to take up glucose. That is why the value then comes out **falsely low** and underestimates the blood sugar. In such cases, the doctor uses other measurements.

gewusst: In Switzerland, HbA1c is often given in per cent, in some laboratories also in millimoles per mole.
An HbA1c of 6.5 per cent means that about one in fifteen haemoglobin particles carries sugar.

teile.einleitung: Cough etiquette means simple rules about how to protect others when you cough and sneeze. This is because tiny droplets with germs fly through the air. Anyone who knows the rules helps to make fewer people ill.
wichtigste: When you cough and sneeze, tiny droplets fly out of the mouth and nose.
These droplets can contain germs, for example cold viruses.
You turn away and cough or sneeze into the crook of your arm.
You easily pass germs on with your hands.
A hygiene mask holds back many droplets.
If you have a fever and a cough, it is better to stay at home.

abschnitte.text: When you sneeze or cough, many small **droplets** spray out of the mouth and nose. Most of them are so tiny that you cannot see them at all. They can hold **germs**, such as the viruses of a **cold**. If another person breathes in the droplets, they can catch the illness. The droplets fly only a short way, so **distance** helps.

abschnitte.titel: Into the crook of your arm
abschnitte.text: The most important rule is: **turn away and cough** or sneeze **into the crook of your arm**. That way the droplets land on your sleeve and not in the air in front of other people. You should not sneeze into your hands. This is because with your hands you touch **door handles**, tables and other people, and so the germs travel on. If you use a **tissue**, you throw it away afterwards and wash your hands.

Some people wear a **hygiene mask** over the mouth and nose. It holds back many droplets and so protects others. This makes sense, for example, in hospitals or with a bad cold. If you have a **fever** and a cough, it is better to stay at home. That way you recover faster and do not infect other children at school.

When someone sneezes, people in German-speaking Switzerland often say “**Gesundheit**”, which means “health”. With it you wish the person not to fall ill. In French-speaking Switzerland people say “Santé” or “À tes souhaits”, and in Ticino “Salute”. “**En Guete**”, on the other hand, is what you say before a meal. A friendly wish and good cough etiquette go well together.

gewusst: A strong sneeze can throw droplets several metres.
The word etiquette comes from French and means roughly good manners.

teile.einleitung: The pectoralis major, the large chest muscle, is a strong, flat muscle at the front of the rib cage. It moves the arm, for example when hugging, clapping or throwing.
wichtigste: The large chest muscle is called musculus pectoralis major in Latin.
It is fan-shaped and covers a large part of the chest.
It starts at the collarbone, the breastbone and the rib cartilages.
Its tendon attaches to the upper arm bone.
It pulls the arm towards the body and turns it inwards.
Below it lies the small chest muscle.
Bench presses and press-ups train it especially.

abschnitte.text: The pectoralis major is shaped like a **fan**. It spreads widely over the chest and narrows towards the shoulder. The Latin name is **musculus pectoralis major**: “pectus” means chest, and “major” means larger. In trained people, you can see its shape clearly under the skin. It also forms the front wall of the armpit.

A muscle has an **origin**, where it begins, and an **insertion**, where it ends. The pectoralis major starts, among other places, at the **collarbone**, the **breastbone** and the cartilages of the upper ribs. Its fibres run together into a strong tendon. This passes under the deltoid muscle and attaches at the front of the **upper arm bone**. When the muscle contracts, it therefore pulls on the upper arm.

The pectoralis major pulls the arm towards the trunk. Experts call this **adduction**. It also turns the arm inwards. If the arm is stretched out to the side, the muscle brings it forward towards the middle of the body, as when clapping in front of the chest or hugging. In throwing, swimming and climbing, too, it works hard.

Normally we breathe mainly with the **diaphragm**. After great exertion, many people rest their hands on their knees or on a table. Then the arm is held fixed, and the chest muscle can pull the other way on the rib cage. This lifts the ribs and helps with breathing in. That is why it is called an **accessory breathing muscle**.

In the **bench press**, you push a barbell away from the chest. This works mainly the pectoralis major and the triceps at the back of the upper arm. **Press-ups** also strengthen it. Directly beneath the large one lies the smaller, triangular **pectoralis minor**. It does not attach to the upper arm but to the shoulder blade.

gewusst: The pectoralis major also works when you push yourself out of the swimming pool or pull yourself up on a bar.
When you rest your hands on your knees after a sprint, the chest muscle helps you to breathe faster.

teile.einleitung: A pacemaker is a small device that helps the heart to beat in the right rhythm. It is placed under the skin and gives out fine electrical impulses when needed. Today many people around the world live with a pacemaker.
wichtigste: A pacemaker is used mainly when the heartbeat is too slow.
The first fully implanted pacemaker was put in in 1958.
Modern pacemakers usually have a lithium battery.
The electrodes usually reach the heart through a vein under the collarbone.
A capsule pacemaker sits directly in the right ventricle without any wires.
An ICD can also end ventricular fibrillation with a shock.

abschnitte.text: The heart has a pacemaker of its own. Sometimes it does not work properly, or the signals are not passed on well in the heart. Then the heart beats **too slowly**. Those affected feel tired, become dizzy or briefly lose consciousness. A **pacemaker** constantly measures the heartbeat. If it is too slow, the device gives a small electrical impulse.

The first pacemaker to be fully implanted in a person was used in Stockholm in **1958**. The surgeon **Åke Senning** put it in, and the engineer Rune Elmqvist had built it. Senning later worked for many years in **Zurich**. The first devices lasted only a short time. Today pacemakers usually have a **lithium battery** that lasts many years.

A classic pacemaker consists of a small housing and thin wires, the **electrodes**. The housing is placed under the skin below the collarbone. The electrodes are pushed through a **vein under the collarbone** as far as the heart. A newer **capsule pacemaker** is only as big as a fat tablet. It sits **without wires** directly in the right ventricle.

Doctors describe pacemakers with a code of letters, for example **VVI**. The **first letter** shows the **place of stimulation**, that is, where the impulse is given. V stands for ventricle, the lower chamber of the heart. The second letter shows where the device measures, and the third how it reacts to this.

A **biventricular pacemaker**, or **CRT** for short, stimulates both ventricles. It makes sure that in heart failure they beat at the same time again. An **implantable defibrillator**, or **ICD** for short, can do even more. It works like a pacemaker and can also end dangerous **ventricular fibrillation** with an electric shock.

gewusst: The first patient, Arne Larsson, received over 20 pacemakers during his life and lived to the age of 86.
Today pacemakers can be checked and adjusted from the outside with a device, without an operation.

teile.einleitung: Coughing is a protective movement of the body. With a strong burst of air, crumbs, mucus and irritants are pushed out of the airways. You often cough when you have a cold.
wichtigste: Coughing clears the airways.
Coughing is a reflex and happens completely by itself.
With a cold, you often cough.
Smoke can also set off a cough.
When you cough, tiny droplets with germs fly through the air.
Drinking plenty often helps when your throat is scratchy.
If you have coughed into your hands, you wash them afterwards.

abschnitte.text: If something wrong gets into the airways, for example a crumb or dust, it has to come out again. To do this you first breathe in, then the vocal cords close briefly. The muscles press, and suddenly the air is **pushed out** with great force. In this way crumbs, **mucus** and irritants are carried out of the throat and lungs. Coughing therefore keeps the airways clean and clear.

Coughing is a **reflex**. That is a movement that the body does completely by itself, without your having to think. **Sneezing** and **blinking** are reflexes too. You can also cough on purpose, but mostly it simply happens. The reflex is set off by fine nerves in the airways that notice an irritation.

Most often you cough with a **cold**. Then the airways are irritated by viruses and make more mucus. **Smoke**, dust or cold air also irritate the airways, and the body tries to push the irritants out. For a scratchy throat it often helps to **drink plenty**, for example warm tea. If a cough lasts a very long time or you find it hard to get your breath, you should see a doctor.

When you cough, tiny **droplets** with germs fly through the air. Anyone nearby can catch something from them. That is why you keep your **distance** when you cough and turn away from others. It is best to cough into the **crook of your arm**. If you have coughed into your hands after all, you wash them with **water and soap**, because otherwise you pass the germs on via door handles.

gewusst: When you cough, air can shoot out of the mouth very fast, much faster than a cyclist rides.
Animals such as dogs and cats can cough too.

teile.einleitung: Hormones are messenger substances that send signals to organs through the blood. Even tiny amounts are enough to affect growth, sleep, mood or blood sugar. They work like letters that are read only by the right recipients.
wichtigste: Hormones are messenger substances that send signals to organs through the blood.
They are made in hormone glands and in some organs.
Insulin lowers the blood sugar level.
Melatonin from the pineal gland controls the sleep-wake rhythm.
Adrenaline from the adrenal medulla raises pulse and blood pressure within seconds when you are under stress.
Erythropoietin from the kidney stimulates the making of red blood cells.
Luteinising hormone (LH) from the pituitary gland triggers ovulation.
Oxytocin helps contractions along during birth.

abschnitte.text: The word hormone comes from the Greek word for “to drive on”. The term was coined in 1905 by the British physiologist Ernest Starling. Hormones are made in glands and released into the blood. With the bloodstream they reach the whole body. They can only act on cells that have the matching **receptor**, like a key that fits only one particular lock.

**Insulin** is made in the pancreas. After a meal it makes sure that sugar gets from the blood into the cells. In this way the blood sugar level falls. Its opposite number is glucagon, which raises the blood sugar. People with type 1 diabetes no longer make insulin of their own and have to inject it or take it in through a pump.

**Adrenaline** is made in the adrenal medulla, which sits on top of the kidneys. When you are frightened, afraid or excited, it is released within seconds. Pulse and blood pressure rise, breathing becomes faster and the muscles get more energy. In the past this helped our ancestors to flee from danger or to fight. Today you feel it, for example, before an exam or on a roller coaster.

**Melatonin** is made in the pineal gland in the brain, mainly in darkness. It makes you tired and controls the sleep-wake rhythm. Bright screen light in the evening can slow down the making of melatonin. The **growth hormone** from the pituitary gland is released mainly during sleep. So children really do grow partly in their sleep.

**Erythropoietin**, or EPO for short, from the kidney stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells. In sport it is known as a banned doping substance. Luteinising hormone from the pituitary gland triggers ovulation in women. **Oxytocin** helps contractions along during birth and helps the flow of milk when breastfeeding. In puberty, sex hormones such as oestrogen and testosterone make sure that the body develops into an adult one.

begriffe.erklaerung: A messenger substance that sends signals to organs through the blood.
A receiving point on a cell to which only a matching substance can dock.
A hormone of the pancreas that lowers blood sugar.
A stress hormone that puts the body on alert in a flash.

gewusst: Insulin was discovered in Canada in 1921 and 1922, and since then it has saved the lives of millions of people with diabetes.
Oxytocin is also released when cuddling, and is therefore often called the cuddle hormone.
Plants, too, make hormones, which control, for example, the ripening of fruit.

teile.einleitung: Skin cancer prevention means not letting skin cancer develop in the first place or finding it very early. This includes sun protection and regular checking of the skin. If found early, skin cancer can usually be treated well.
wichtigste: Protection with clothing, a hat and shade is part of primary prevention.
Early detection is part of secondary prevention.
If your own shadow is shorter than you are, you should look for shade.
A mole that looks different from all the others is suspicious.
Dermatologists examine moles with the dermatoscope.
Cancer is confirmed for certain only by an examination of fine tissue.
A mirror or a second person helps with self-checking.

abschnitte.text: The most important cause of skin cancer is **UV radiation** from the sun. Measures that stop an illness from arising at all are called **primary prevention**. For skin cancer, that means: clothing, a hat, sunglasses, sun cream and shade. A simple rule helps: if your own **shadow is shorter** than you are, the sun is high and the radiation is strong. Then you should look for shade. Sun protection is especially important in children.

**Early detection** is part of **secondary prevention**. It is meant to find an illness that has already arisen as early as possible, while it can still be treated well. For this, you look at your own skin regularly. You can hardly see your back, neck and scalp yourself, so a **mirror** or a second person helps. The **ugly duckling sign** is helpful: a mole that looks different from all the others should be looked at more closely.

Dermatologists examine moles with the **dermatoscope**. It magnifies and lights up the skin, so that structures become visible that you cannot see with the naked eye. In **teledermatology**, photos are sent electronically to specialists, who judge from a distance whether an examination in person is needed. A suspicious spot is removed and examined under the microscope in **histology**. Only this result gives the certain diagnosis.

Switzerland is among the countries in Europe where **melanomas**, that is, black skin cancer, occur especially often.
