One reason is that many people have light skin and like being outdoors, in the mountains too. At altitude, UV radiation is stronger. The **Swiss Cancer League** therefore informs people every year about sun protection and skin checks.

gewusst: The ugly duckling sign is named after the fairy tale of the ugly duckling, which looks different from its brothers and sisters.
Even with a cloudy sky, a large part of the UV radiation gets through to the ground.

teile.einleitung: Sooner or later, almost everybody gets **grey hair**. This is a perfectly normal part of growing older. But why do hairs lose their colour, and is it true that you can go grey overnight?
wichtigste: The technical term for going grey is canities.
Many people get their first grey hairs from about 30 to 40 years of age.
A hair without pigment looks white, because tiny air bubbles scatter the light.
“Grey” hair is mostly a mixture of coloured and white hairs.
A hair that has already grown cannot turn grey overnight.
Pheomelanin makes red hair.

abschnitte.text: The colour of hair comes from pigments, the **melanins**. They are made in the hair root by special cells and built into the growing hair. There are two main kinds: **eumelanin** colours brown to black. **Pheomelanin** makes **red** and reddish tones. The mixture decides whether someone has blond, brown, black or red hair.

With age, the pigment cells in the hair root make less and less melanin until they stop altogether. The hair that grows afterwards is then **colourless**. The technical term for going grey is **canities**. A hair without pigment looks **white** because **tiny air bubbles** in the hair scatter the light, rather as in snow. Many people get their first grey hairs from **about 30 to 40 years of age**. When it starts depends strongly on the genes.

A single hair is actually not grey. It is either coloured or white. What we see as **grey hair** is mostly a **mixture of coloured and white hairs**. The more white hairs are added, the lighter the hairstyle looks. In the end, some people have completely white hair.

There are stories of people who went grey overnight after a fright. This is not possible. A dark hair that has already grown is dead material and cannot suddenly lose its colour. **Only hair that grows afterwards is colourless**. That is why a few weeks after dyeing, **grey roots** show again: the new hair keeps growing without pigment.

Some people say that if you pull out a grey hair, two grow back. That is not true. From every **hair follicle**, that is, every hair root, **only one hair** grows. If you pull it out, another grows in the same place, and it is grey again. Frequent plucking, however, can damage the hair root, so it is better to leave it alone.

gewusst: Red hair is the rarest natural hair colour in the world.
Red hair often does not go grey but fades over time to a pale blond or white.

teile.einleitung: In a **cataract**, the lens in the eye becomes cloudy. You then see as if through a fog or veil. It is the most common eye disease in old age and can today be treated very well with an operation. In German it is called the “grey star”.
wichtigste: A cataract is a clouding of the lens of the eye.
The medical term is cataract, in German “grauer Star”.
By far the most common form is the age-related cataract.
Typical are veiled vision and strong glare.
UV radiation is regarded as a risk factor.
In treatment, the cloudy lens is replaced by an artificial lens.

abschnitte.text: In the eye, behind the pupil, sits the **lens**. It is normally clear and focuses the light so that a sharp image forms on the retina. In a **cataract**, the lens becomes **cloudy**. The medical term for it is **cataract**. The German name “grey star” probably comes from the fact that those affected often stare fixedly into space and the pupil can look greyish.

A cataract usually develops slowly over years. Typical is **veiled vision**: everything seems to be behind frosted glass. Many of those affected notice **strong glare**, for example from headlights when driving at night. Colours look paler, and contrasts become weaker. A new pair of glasses then often helps only briefly.

By far the most common form is the **age-related cataract**. Over the years, the proteins in the lens change and it becomes cloudy. Besides that there are risk factors: **UV radiation** from the sun, smoking, diabetes, injuries to the eye or certain medicines such as cortisone taken over a long time. Rarely, children are born with a cataract. Sunglasses with UV protection therefore make sense not only in the mountains.

There are no medicines against cataract. In an operation, the **cloudy lens** is **replaced by an artificial lens**. Usually a tiny cut is made at the edge of the cornea. Then the lens is broken up with **ultrasound** and sucked out. This technique is called **phacoemulsification**. The fine capsule in which the lens sat is kept. The folded artificial lens is put into it. The operation usually takes only a short time and is often done as an outpatient.

Some time after the operation, the **lens capsule** left behind can become cloudy. This is called a **secondary cataract**. You then see worse again. A secondary cataract can usually be treated simply: with a **laser**, a small opening is made in the middle of the clouded capsule. Afterwards the vision is clear again.

gewusst: Cataract surgery is one of the most common operations in the world.
Even in ancient times, people tried to treat cataract by pushing the cloudy lens backwards into the eye with a needle.

teile.einleitung: In a heart attack, part of the heart muscle suddenly stops getting blood. Without oxygen, this tissue dies. A heart attack is an emergency in which quick help is very important.
wichtigste: The medical term for a heart attack is myocardial infarction.
The cause is usually a blocked coronary artery.
Typical signs are severe pain or pressure in the chest.
Women more often have nausea, shortness of breath and back pain.
If you suspect one, you call 144 straight away in Switzerland.
A stent is a small mesh tube that keeps a vessel open.
Diabetes, smoking and high blood pressure raise the risk.

abschnitte.text: The heart muscle is supplied with blood through the **coronary arteries**. Over the years, deposits can build up on the vessel walls. If such a spot tears open, a blood clot forms and blocks the vessel. Then part of the heart muscle no longer gets any oxygen. This is called a **heart attack** or, in technical language, a **myocardial infarction**.

Typical signs are **severe pain or pressure in the chest**. The pain can spread into the arms, neck, jaw or back. Many of those affected feel afraid, break out in a cold sweat and look pale. In **women**, nausea, shortness of breath and back pain are more common, which is often not recognised at once as a heart attack. A warning sign can be **angina pectoris**, a sudden tight feeling in the chest.

If you suspect a heart attack, you call the emergency number **144** at once. Every minute counts, because the longer the vessel stays blocked, the more heart muscle dies. The person should not exert themselves and should **sit quietly with the upper body raised**. You loosen tight clothes. If the person becomes unconscious and does not breathe normally, you start resuscitation.

In hospital, doctors often carry out a **cardiac catheter examination**. A thin tube is pushed along a blood vessel up to the heart. With **contrast medium**, the narrowed coronary arteries become visible in the X-ray image. The blocked vessel is widened with a small balloon. After that, a **stent**, a fine mesh tube, keeps the vessel open. Sometimes a **bypass operation** is needed, in which a piece of vessel goes around the narrow spot.

Several things raise the risk of a heart attack: **smoking**, high blood pressure, high blood fats, being overweight, little exercise and **diabetes**, an illness with permanently raised blood sugar. Anyone who exercises a lot, eats a balanced diet and does not smoke lowers their risk clearly. Age and family also play a part.

gewusst: The term angina pectoris comes from Latin and literally means “tightness of the chest”.
The first stents were put into people in the 1980s.

teile.einleitung: The cerebrum is the largest part of our brain. Here thinking, language, learning and remembering arise, and from here we control our conscious movements.
wichtigste: In humans, the cerebrum is the largest part of the brain.
It consists of a left and a right half.
On the outside lies the strongly folded cerebral cortex.
The cortex is grey because the cell bodies of the nerve cells lie there.
Each half has four lobes: frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital.
The motor cortex controls voluntary movements.

abschnitte.titel: The largest part of the brain
abschnitte.text: The **cerebrum** makes up by far the largest part of the human brain. It covers the other parts of the brain, such as the cerebellum and the brain stem, almost completely. It consists of two **halves**, the hemispheres. A thick strand of nerve fibres, the **corpus callosum**, connects the two halves. The left half mainly controls the right side of the body, and the right half the left.

On the outside of the cerebrum lies the **cerebral cortex**, also called the cortex. It is only a few millimetres thick. It is folded into many **ridges** and **grooves**. Because of this folding, a very large area with many nerve cells fits into the limited space of the skull. You can imagine it like a large cloth that you scrunch up so that it fits into a small box.

The cortex looks grey. In this **grey matter** lie mainly the cell bodies of the nerve cells. Beneath it lies the **white matter**. It consists mainly of nerve fibres wrapped in pale, fat-rich **myelin sheaths**. These fibres connect different parts of the brain with each other and pass signals on quickly.

Each half has four large **lobes**. The **frontal lobe** lies behind the forehead and is important for planning and acting. In front of the central groove lies the **motor cortex**, which sends commands for conscious movements to the muscles. Behind it, in the **parietal lobe**, lies the body-sense cortex for touch, pressure and temperature. In the **temporal lobe** at the side at the level of the ears lies the hearing cortex, and in the **occipital lobe**, seeing is mainly processed.

The higher abilities are mainly assigned to the cerebrum: **conscious perception**, thinking, language, learning and memory. Many jobs are done by several areas together. When you read a poem aloud, for example, seeing, language and movement of the mouth work at the same time. The brain can change through practice, which is why you get better with training.

gewusst: If you spread out the cerebral cortex, it would be much larger than the surface of the brain as we see it.
Seeing is processed right at the back of the head, even though the eyes are at the front.

teile.einleitung: Your body is made of countless cells. Cells of the same kind with the same job join together into a **tissue**. Tissues then make up organs such as the heart, skin or stomach.
wichtigste: A tissue is a group of cells of the same kind with the same job.
In humans, four basic tissues are distinguished: epithelial, connective and supporting, muscle and nerve tissue.
Epithelial tissue covers the surface of the body and lines cavities.
Bone and cartilage belong to the connective and supporting tissue.
Nerve tissue carries electrical signals.
The science of tissues is called histology.

abschnitte.text: A **tissue** is a group of **cells of the same kind** that together carry out a particular job. Between the cells there is often a material, the **intercellular substance**. Several tissues together form an **organ**. The stomach, for example, consists of mucous membrane, muscle tissue, connective tissue and nerves. In humans and animals, four **basic tissues** are distinguished.

**Epithelial tissue** covers the surface of the body, for example as the top layer of skin. It also lines cavities such as the mouth, gut or blood vessels. **Connective and supporting tissue** connects and supports the body. This includes **bone**, **cartilage**, tendons and fatty tissue. **Cartilage tissue** is firm and yet flexible. It shapes the outer ear and covers the joint surfaces so that the bones glide smoothly on each other.

**Muscle tissue** can contract and provides movement. There are skeletal muscles, smooth muscles and **heart muscle tissue**. Heart muscle tissue works without our control and beats for a whole life without a break. **Nerve tissue** consists of nerve cells and glial cells. It carries **electrical signals** through the body, for example from the eye to the brain or from the brain to the muscles.

The science of tissues is called **histology**. The word comes from the Greek “histos” for tissue. For this, experts cut wafer-thin slices of tissue and stain them. Under the **microscope** you can then see the individual cells. In hospitals, pathologists examine tissue samples in order to recognise diseases.

Plants have tissues too. The **protective tissue** protects the plant from the outside. In the **conducting tissue** there are two important parts: the **xylem** carries water and minerals from the roots upwards as far as the leaves. The **phloem** carries sugar that is made in the leaves to the other parts of the plant. In the wood of a tree, a large part consists of xylem.

gewusst: Cartilage has no blood vessels, which is why it heals only very slowly after an injury.
The annual rings of a tree arise because the xylem grows differently in spring and in summer.

teile.einleitung: The brain and the red blood cells constantly need glucose. When we do not eat for a longer time, the liver therefore makes new sugar itself. This metabolic pathway is called **gluconeogenesis**, which roughly means “new formation of sugar”.
wichtigste: In gluconeogenesis, mainly the liver makes glucose from lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids.
To a large extent it is the reverse of glycolysis, but it bypasses three steps.
Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate into oxaloacetate in the mitochondrion, with biotin as a coenzyme.
PEP carboxykinase turns oxaloacetate into phosphoenolpyruvate using up GTP.
Glucose-6-phosphatase releases free glucose in the last step.
Glucagon stimulates gluconeogenesis in the liver especially strongly.

abschnitte.text: **Gluconeogenesis** takes place mainly in the **liver**, and to a lesser extent in the kidney. The starting substances are **lactate** from the muscles and red blood cells, **glycerol** from the breakdown of fat and **glucogenic amino acids** from proteins. From these, new glucose is made and released into the blood. This is especially important in long fasting, when the glycogen stores are empty.

In many steps, gluconeogenesis is the **reverse of glycolysis**. Three steps of glycolysis, however, cannot simply be reversed, because they release too much energy. The cell needs enzymes of its own for them. These **bypass reactions** are the key of the metabolic pathway. They use up energy in the form of ATP and GTP.

First, **pyruvate carboxylase** in the **mitochondrion** converts pyruvate into **oxaloacetate**. As a coenzyme it needs the vitamin **biotin**. Then **PEP carboxykinase** turns oxaloacetate into **phosphoenolpyruvate**, **using up GTP**. Later, **fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase** bypasses the reaction of phosphofructokinase-1. In the last step, **glucose-6-phosphatase** splits off the phosphate group, and **free glucose** is formed.

Muscles also store glucose as glycogen. But they **cannot release free glucose into the blood**, because they lack **glucose-6-phosphatase**. Their sugar stays for their own work. In return they deliver lactate to the liver, which makes glucose from it again. This cycle is called the **Cori cycle**. Gluconeogenesis is controlled by hormones: **glucagon** and cortisol promote it, and insulin inhibits it.

Humans cannot make **net glucose** from **fatty acids with an even number of carbons**. When these fatty acids are broken down, **acetyl-CoA** is formed. The step from pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, however, cannot be reversed. So acetyl-CoA **cannot be turned back into pyruvate**. Only the **glycerol** from fat can be made into sugar. Plants and some bacteria, by contrast, have a detour, the glyoxylate cycle.

gewusst: The Cori cycle is named after the married couple Carl and Gerty Cori, who received the Nobel Prize in 1947.
The brain of an adult uses around 100 grams of glucose or more every day.

teile.einleitung: The **gluteal muscles** lie in the bottom and are among the strongest muscles of your body. Without them you could not stand up well, climb stairs or walk upright.
wichtigste: The large gluteal muscle lies in the bottom.
It is one of the largest muscles of the body.
There is a large, a middle and a small gluteal muscle.
The large gluteal muscle pulls the leg backwards.
It helps with getting up from a chair and works especially hard when climbing stairs.
It is very important for humans walking upright.

abschnitte.text: The **buttocks**, also called the bottom, consist mainly of muscles and fat. When you sit on a chair, you sit on your buttocks. Under the skin lie three muscles on top of each other: the **large**, the **middle** and the **small gluteal muscle**. They connect the pelvis with the thigh bone. The large gluteal muscle lies on the outside and gives the bottom its shape.

The **large gluteal muscle** is one of the largest muscles in the human body. Its Latin name is **musculus gluteus maximus**, which means “largest gluteal muscle”. It is thick and very strong. Its main job is to pull the leg **backwards** at the hip joint. It also helps to straighten the pelvis and the upper body.

The gluteal muscle is always working. When **getting up from a chair**, it straightens the hip and lifts you up. When **climbing stairs**, walking uphill, jumping and running, it works especially hard. When strolling on flat ground, it is needed less. The middle and small gluteal muscles make sure that the pelvis does not tip to the side when you stand on one leg.

Humans walk on two legs. For that they need a **strong gluteal muscle** that holds the body upright over the legs. In great apes such as chimpanzees, this muscle is much smaller, because they mostly move on four limbs. Researchers therefore see a link between the large gluteal muscle and **walking upright** in humans.

Someone who sits a lot uses the gluteal muscle little. Then it can become weaker. Exercise such as hiking, cycling, climbing stairs or squats keeps it strong. A strong gluteal muscle takes strain off the back and knees. That is why exercises for the buttocks are part of training in many sports.

gewusst: The technical term “gluteus” comes from the Greek word for buttock.
Some injections are given into the gluteal muscle, because there is a lot of muscle tissue there that takes up the medicine.

teile.einleitung: Your heart beats day and night, without a break. With every heartbeat it pumps blood through your whole body. This happens all by itself, and you do not have to think about it.
wichtigste: With every heartbeat the heart muscle contracts.
The heart beats by itself, even at night.
An adult’s heart beats about 100,000 times a day.
In a long life, a heart beats several billion times.
The blood brings oxygen and nutrients to all parts of the body.
An ECG records the heart’s electrical currents as a zigzag line.
In Switzerland, 144 is the emergency number for the ambulance service.

abschnitte.text: The heart is a strong **muscle**, about as big as your fist. With every heartbeat the **heart muscle contracts** and pushes the blood into the vessels. Then it relaxes and fills with blood again. The blood brings **oxygen and nutrients** to all parts of the body, from the toes to the brain.

You do not have to command your heart to beat. It **beats by itself**. In the heart there is a small pacemaker of its own, the **sinus node**. It keeps sending out fine electrical signals. Even at night the heart takes **no break** but just keeps on beating.

An adult’s heart beats about **100,000 times in a day**. In a long life this adds up to **several billion** heartbeats. When you run, the heart beats fast. **When you sleep** it beats more slowly, because the body then needs less oxygen.

Doctors can measure the electrical signals of the heart. To do this they stick small electrodes on the skin. A device records the **heart’s currents** as a **zigzag line**. This examination is called an **ECG**. It does not hurt and shows whether the heart is beating in the right rhythm.

What helps the heart most is **plenty of exercise**: cycling, swimming, running or playing outdoors. That makes the heart muscle strong. Healthy food and enough sleep are good for it too. If a person’s heart stops beating, in Switzerland you call the emergency number **144** straight away.

gewusst: Every day a heart pumps several thousand litres of blood through the body.
Small animals such as mice have a much faster heartbeat than big animals such as elephants.

teile.einleitung: How well do the kidneys work? The most important measure for this is the **glomerular filtration rate**, **GFR** for short. It states how much fluid all the glomeruli together filter out of the blood per minute.
wichtigste: In a healthy young adult, the GFR is around 120 ml per minute.
Inulin is regarded as the ideal marker for measuring the GFR exactly.
The estimated GFR is usually related to 1.73 square metres of body surface.
The filtration fraction is the share of the plasma that is filtered, normally about 20 per cent.
The macula densa measures the salt content and adjusts the filtration.
Thanks to autoregulation, the GFR stays roughly constant when blood pressure varies.

abschnitte.text: In the **glomeruli** of the kidneys, fluid is constantly filtered out of the blood, the **primary urine**. The **glomerular filtration rate** says how much of it is produced per minute. In a healthy young adult it is **around 120 ml per minute**. Calculated over a day, that comes to about 170 to 180 litres. With age, the GFR slowly falls.

Ideal is a substance that is filtered freely but afterwards is neither taken back nor additionally released. Such a substance is **inulin**, a sugar from plants. It is regarded as the **ideal marker** but is laborious to measure. In everyday practice, the blood value **creatinine** is mostly used, a breakdown product from the muscles. From it the **estimated GFR** is calculated. It is usually related to **1.73 square metres of body surface**, so that large and small people can be compared.

Filtration depends on pressures. The **capillary pressure** presses fluid out. Working against it are the pressure in Bowman's capsule and the **colloid osmotic pressure** of the blood proteins. Example: 50 mmHg minus 15 mmHg minus 25 mmHg gives an **effective filtration pressure** of 10 mmHg. The **filtration fraction** states what part of the plasma is filtered: with a GFR of 120 ml/min and a plasma flow of 600 ml/min, that is 120 divided by 600, so **20 per cent**.

Blood pressure varies during the day. Even so, the GFR stays roughly constant thanks to **autoregulation**. Part of this works through the vessel wall: when the pressure rises, the supplying vessel narrows. If the **supplying vessel** of a glomerulus narrows, less blood arrives and the filtration rate **falls**. In addition, the **macula densa**, a group of cells in the distal tubule, measures the **salt content** of the urine and gives feedback to the glomerulus.

The GFR shows doctors how hard the kidneys are working. If it is clearly lowered over a longer time, this is called **chronic kidney disease**. Depending on the value, it is divided into stages. The dose of some medicines also depends on the GFR, because the kidneys excrete these substances.

gewusst: The whole blood plasma of a person is filtered by the kidneys about sixty times every day.
Creatinine also depends on muscle mass, so very muscular people often have somewhat higher values.

teile.einleitung: The brain, too, produces waste substances. Unlike the rest of the body, however, it has no ordinary lymph vessels. Researchers have discovered a cleaning system of its own: the **glymphatic system**.
wichtigste: The glymphatic system was first described in 2012 by the team around Maiken Nedergaard.
The name is put together from “glia” and “lymphatic”.
Its main job is to flush waste substances out of the brain.
In this, cerebrospinal fluid, the brain water, flows through the brain tissue.
With their extensions, astrocytes form the walls of the channels along the blood vessels.
According to studies in mice, the system works hardest during sleep.

abschnitte.text: In the rest of the body, the **lymphatic system** carries away surplus fluid and waste substances. In the brain, such vessels are largely missing. How it cleans itself was unclear for a long time. In **2012**, the Danish researcher **Maiken Nedergaard** and her team described the **glymphatic system** for the first time. The studies were done mainly on mice.

The name joins two words: **glia** and **lymphatic**. “Glia” stands for the **glial cells**, the helper cells in the brain. They play an important role in this system. “Lymphatic” recalls the lymphatic system, because the glymphatic system has a similar job: it flushes **waste substances** out of the brain.

The brain floats in a clear fluid, the **cerebrospinal fluid** or brain water. In the glymphatic system, this fluid flows along the **blood vessels** into the brain tissue. The walls of these channels are formed by the extensions of the **astrocytes**, which are star-shaped glial cells. On their end feet sit water channels called **aquaporin-4**. They are important for the flow. The fluid picks up waste substances and flows away again along the veins.

Studies in mice showed: the glymphatic system works hardest **during sleep**. In sleep, the space between the brain cells widens, and the fluid can flow through more easily. Researchers therefore suspect that sleep also serves to clean the brain. Whether it works in exactly the same way in humans is still being studied.

Among the waste substances that are removed through the glymphatic system is **beta-amyloid**. This protein substance is deposited in the brain in **Alzheimer's disease**. Researchers therefore ask whether disturbed removal plays a part in such diseases. Many questions are still open, and the field of research is still young.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight but uses around 20 per cent of the energy and produces a correspondingly large amount of waste.
Until a few years ago, the glymphatic system was in no biology book.

teile.einleitung: After a meal, the body often has more sugar in the blood than it needs just then. It builds the surplus up into **glycogen**, the sugar store in the liver and muscles. This building up is called **glycogenesis**.
wichtigste: Glycogenesis is the building up of glycogen from glucose.
Humans store the largest amounts of glycogen in the liver and skeletal muscle.
The direct building block is activated glucose, UDP-glucose.
Glycogen synthase links the glucose units through α-1,4-glycosidic bonds.
The branching enzyme forms the α-1,6-glycosidic branches.
The starter molecule is the protein glycogenin.
Insulin promotes glycogenesis, and phosphorylation inhibits glycogen synthase.

abschnitte.text: **Glycogenesis** takes place mainly in the **liver** and in **skeletal muscle**. There, humans store the largest amounts of glycogen. The liver uses its store to keep blood sugar stable between meals. The muscles need their glycogen as a fast source of energy for their own work. The opposite route, the breakdown of glycogen, is called **glycogenolysis**.

First, glucose receives a phosphate group in the cell. In the **liver cell**, this is preferably done by **glucokinase**, also called **hexokinase IV**. It only works properly at high glucose concentrations, that is, after eating. This produces glucose-6-phosphate. **Phosphoglucomutase** converts it into **glucose-1-phosphate**. From this, with the help of UTP, the activated form **UDP-glucose** is made. It is the direct building block for glycogen synthesis.

Right at the start is a protein called **glycogenin**. It serves as the **starter molecule** and attaches the first glucose units to itself. After that, **glycogen synthase** takes over. It lengthens the chain by linking glucose units through **α-1,4-glycosidic bonds**. The **branching enzyme** cuts off pieces and attaches them again at the side through **α-1,6-glycosidic bonds**. This produces a strongly branched molecule.

Glycogenesis is regulated by hormones. **Insulin** promotes it most strongly in the liver and muscle. It activates glycogen synthase by having phosphate groups removed. **Phosphorylation**, that is, attaching a phosphate group, in contrast **inhibits** glycogen synthase. Hormones such as **glucagon** and adrenaline trigger such phosphorylations. This way, when energy is needed, glycogen is not built up and broken down at the same time.

The many **branches** have an advantage. Each branch has an end at which enzymes can work. The more ends there are, the faster the cell can attach or split off glucose. In addition, the branches make the glycogen dissolve better. This way the body has a store that holds a lot of sugar and is still quickly available.

gewusst: In some rare inherited diseases, the glycogen storage diseases, an enzyme for building up or breaking down glycogen is missing.
UDP-glucose is also important in plants, where it helps to build cellulose.

teile.einleitung: Hypoxia means a lack of oxygen in the body’s tissue. Without enough oxygen, cells cannot work properly. The body has astonishing ways of adapting to a lack of oxygen, though.
wichtigste: Hypoxia is a lack of oxygen in the tissue, hypoxaemia too little oxygen in the blood.
If haemoglobin is missing, for example after blood loss, it is called anaemic hypoxia.
In histotoxic hypoxia, for example from cyanide, cells cannot use oxygen.
A pulse oximeter measures oxygen saturation at the finger.
With a lack of oxygen, the kidney makes more erythropoietin.
The factor HIF controls the adaptation of the cells.
Lung vessels in poorly ventilated areas narrow.

abschnitte.text: Every cell needs **oxygen** to get energy from nutrients. Oxygen enters the blood through the lungs. There it is carried by the red blood pigment **haemoglobin** in the red blood cells. If there is too little oxygen in the arterial blood, it is called **hypoxaemia**. If oxygen is missing in the tissue, it is called **hypoxia**. This can happen, for example, at great height, where the air is thinner.

Hypoxia can have different causes. In **anaemic hypoxia**, the oxygen pressure is normal, but **haemoglobin** is missing as a carrier, for example after heavy blood loss. In **histotoxic hypoxia**, there is enough oxygen, but the cells cannot use it. This happens in **cyanide poisoning**: the poison blocks an important enzyme of cell respiration, cytochrome c oxidase.

With severe lack of oxygen, skin and lips can turn bluish. This is called **cyanosis**. It usually becomes visible when there is more than about **5 g/dl** of oxygen-poor haemoglobin in the capillary blood. With very little haemoglobin, it can therefore be absent. Without taking blood, **oxygen saturation** is measured with a **pulse oximeter**. This small device is clipped on to the finger and shines red and infrared light through it.

With a lack of oxygen, the **kidney** makes more **erythropoietin**, EPO for short. This hormone stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells. The adaptation is controlled by the **hypoxia-inducible factor**, **HIF** for short. It switches on genes for blood formation, growth of vessels and metabolism. Research into it won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in **2019**. In the lungs, the vessels of poorly ventilated areas also narrow. This **Euler-Liljestrand mechanism** redirects the blood to well-ventilated air sacs.

gewusst: On the summit of Mount Everest, a breath contains only about a third as much oxygen as at sea level.
The pulse oximeter was developed in Japan in the 1970s and is now found in every hospital.

teile.einleitung: Haemoglobin is a protein in the red blood cells that binds oxygen and carries it around the body. It gives the blood its red colour. Without haemoglobin, your muscles and your brain could not work.
wichtigste: Haemoglobin is the protein in the red blood cells that binds and carries oxygen.
It contains iron, to which the oxygen attaches.
Haemoglobin colours the blood red.
In the lung it takes up oxygen and releases it again in the body.
Part of the carbon dioxide is also brought back to the lung with haemoglobin.
Too little haemoglobin is called anaemia.
To make haemoglobin, the body needs enough iron from food.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the Greek word haima for blood. Haemoglobin is a large **protein** made up of four chains. Each chain carries a haem group with an **iron** atom in the middle. An oxygen particle can attach to each iron atom. So one haemoglobin molecule can carry four oxygen molecules at the same time.

In the **lung** there is a lot of oxygen, so the haemoglobin loads up almost completely there. The heart then pumps the blood to all parts of the body. In the muscles and organs there is less oxygen, so the haemoglobin releases it there. At the same time, it takes along part of the **carbon dioxide** that is made in the cells. Back in the lung, the carbon dioxide is breathed out.

Haemoglobin with oxygen is bright red; without oxygen it is dark red. That is why blood from the arteries is brighter than blood from the veins. Veins look bluish through the skin, but the blood in them is red all the same. A **red blood cell** contains about 270 million haemoglobin molecules. Red blood cells live about 120 days and are then broken down in the spleen and liver.

For haemoglobin, the body needs **iron**. It is found, for example, in meat, pulses, wholegrain foods and green vegetables. Someone with too little iron makes too little haemoglobin, which is called **anaemia**. Those affected are often tired, pale and quickly out of breath. That is why the haemoglobin value is measured beforehand when giving blood.

At great height, for example on the Jungfraujoch at over 3,400 metres, the air is thinner. After a few weeks, the body makes more red blood cells and with them more haemoglobin. That is why some athletes train at altitude, for example in St Moritz. **Carbon monoxide** also binds strongly to haemoglobin and pushes out the oxygen. That is why this gas from exhaust fumes or fire is so dangerous.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that is an important building block of the body.
A blood cell that carries oxygen with haemoglobin.
A lack of blood, when there is too little haemoglobin in the blood.
A poisonous, invisible gas that pushes oxygen off haemoglobin.

gewusst: The body makes around two million new red blood cells every second.
Squid and octopuses have blue blood, because their blood pigment contains copper instead of iron.
The building block haem in haemoglobin is built similarly to the green leaf pigment chlorophyll.

teile.einleitung: Hand washing is one of the simplest ways of protecting yourself and others from illness. With water and soap, dirt and germs are rinsed off the hands. It takes only about 20 seconds.
wichtigste: First you wet the hands, then you soap them.
After that you rinse and dry the hands.
The thumb is forgotten especially often.
Before eating, you absolutely wash your hands.
You also wash them after playing outside and after stroking animals.
Singing “Happy Birthday” twice takes about 20 seconds.
Global Handwashing Day is on 15 October.

abschnitte.text: With our hands, we touch many things all day: door handles, toys, animals and other people. In doing so, **germs** that you cannot see get onto the hands. Some of them can make you ill. If we then touch our face or eat, they get into the mouth. **Hand washing** with **water and soap** removes most germs and the dirt.

First you **wet** the hands. Then you **soap** them well, inside, outside and between the fingers. The **thumb** is forgotten especially often, because it sticks out a little. So you take hold of it with the other hand and wash it separately. After that you **rinse** the soap off and **dry** the hands with a clean cloth. So that you wash long enough, you can sing a short song such as “Happy Birthday” twice. That takes about **20 seconds**.

You absolutely wash your hands **before eating**, so that the germs do not get into the mouth with the food. It is also important after the **toilet**, after blowing your nose and after **playing outside**. Outside, the hands come into contact with soil and many germs. After stroking **pets**, you wash your hands as well, because there are germs in the fur and on the muzzle. If there is no water when you are out and about, a **hand disinfectant** helps, but with visible dirt, washing is better.

Back in **1847**, the doctor **Ignaz Semmelweis** recognised that clean hands protect the sick. He had the doctors in his hospital in Vienna clean their hands thoroughly, and after that far fewer patients fell ill. Today we know how important hand washing is all over the world. That is why every year on **15 October** there is **Global Handwashing Day**. It reminds us that clean hands can prevent many illnesses.

gewusst: Wet hands pass on germs more easily than dry ones. That is why drying is important.
Soap dissolves grease, and many germs cling to this grease. That is why water with soap works much better than water alone.

teile.einleitung: The heart is a strong muscle that pumps blood through the whole body without a break. It lies in the chest, a little to the left of the middle of the ribcage, and is about as big as your fist. In a long life it beats several billion times.
wichtigste: The heart pumps blood through the body.
It is made up mainly of muscle.
The heart lies in the chest, a little to the left of the middle of the ribcage.
It has four hollow spaces, two atria and two ventricles.
The heart valves stop blood from flowing back.
The left ventricle pumps the blood into the main artery and so into the whole body.
At rest, an adult’s heart beats about 60 to 80 times a minute.
You can feel your pulse easily at your wrist.

abschnitte.text: The heart lies in the ribcage between the two lungs, behind the breastbone and shifted a little to the left. It is about as big as the fist of its owner. In an adult it weighs about 300 grams. The ribs protect it like a cage. It is wrapped in the **pericardium**, a firm covering.

The heart is divided by a wall into a left and a right half. Each half has an **atrium** and a **ventricle**, so there are four hollow spaces altogether. Between the atrium and the ventricle, and at the exit of the ventricles, lie the **heart valves**. They work like valves that open in only one direction. The typical heart sound is made when the valves close.

The right half of the heart pumps blood low in oxygen into the lungs. There it takes up fresh oxygen, and this is the **pulmonary circulation**. The blood flows back into the left half of the heart. The left ventricle pumps it with great force into the **main artery**, the aorta, and from there into the whole body. That is why the wall of the left ventricle is especially thick.

At rest, an adult’s heart beats about 60 to 80 times a minute, and faster in children. At 70 beats a minute, that is 4200 beats in an hour. When you run fast, your muscles need more oxygen, and the heartbeat gets faster. Each beat sends a wave through the arteries, the **pulse**. You can feel it easily at your wrist on the thumb side, or at your neck.

The heart has its own pacemaker, the **sinus node** in the right atrium. It sends out electrical impulses at regular intervals, which make the heart muscle contract. The brain can only speed the rhythm up or slow it down. Doctors measure these currents with an **ECG**. If there are disturbances, an artificial pacemaker can help, and in cardiac arrest a defibrillator.

begriffe.erklaerung: The upper chamber of one half of the heart, which the blood flows into first.
The lower chamber of one half of the heart, which pumps the blood out.
A valve in the heart that stops blood from flowing back.
A pressure wave in the blood vessels that you feel with every heartbeat.
The main artery, the largest artery in the body.

gewusst: At rest, the heart pumps about five litres of blood a minute through the body.
The heart of a blue whale weighs around 180 kilograms.
The first heart transplant was carried out by Christiaan Barnard in South Africa in 1967, and in Switzerland the first succeeded in Zurich in 1969.

teile.einleitung: A hair whorl is a spot on the head where the hairs grow in a spiral around a centre point. Almost everyone has one, mostly at the top of the back of the head.
wichtigste: At the hair whorl, the hairs grow in a circle around a centre point.
Most people have it at the top of the back of the head.
In the majority, it turns clockwise.
Two whorls on the head are called a double crown.
The direction of growth is set by the slanting hair follicles.
In a horse's passport, the hair whorls are drawn in.

abschnitte.text: A **hair whorl** is a spot where the hairs grow in a **spiral**. The **hair follicles**, in which the hairs sit, stand so slanted in the skin there that the hairs grow in a circle around a centre point. From above, it looks like a small whirlpool. In the middle, you can sometimes see a little scalp.

Most people have their hair whorl at the **top of the back of the head**. From there, the hairs spread out in all directions. Studies show that in the majority, the whorl turns **clockwise**. In a minority, it runs anticlockwise. Some people have two whorls next to each other, which is called a **double crown**.

The direction in which the hairs grow is fixed by the slanting follicles. That is why the hairs at a whorl can hardly be combed lastingly in another direction. Often they stick out there. With a double crown, styling is even harder. A clever haircut can help to make the whorl less visible. The hair whorl stays in the same place for life.

Animals with fur also have hair whorls. On a **horse**, they are traditionally used for identification. In the **horse's passport**, besides the white markings, the position of the hair whorls is also drawn in. They are different in every horse and do not change. This way, a horse can be recognised reliably.

gewusst: For its papers, a horse's hair whorl is almost as important as a passport photo is for us.
Cattle and dogs also have hair whorls in their coats.

teile.einleitung: Hypotension means low blood pressure. Many people with low blood pressure feel perfectly healthy. Sometimes, though, you feel dizzy, especially when getting up quickly.
wichtigste: In adults, hypotension usually means values below about 100/60 mmHg.
Many people with low blood pressure have no complaints.
A drop in blood pressure on standing up is called orthostatic hypotension.
The Schellong test checks the circulation lying and standing.
A short loss of consciousness is called a syncope.
Drinking enough and getting up slowly help many people.
After heavy blood loss, hypovolaemic shock is a risk.

abschnitte.text: The heart pumps blood through the vessels. The blood presses against the vessel walls, and this is the **blood pressure**. It is measured in **mmHg**, millimetres of mercury, with two numbers: the first applies when the heart pumps, the second when it relaxes. In adults, **hypotension** usually means values below about **100/60 mmHg**. Many people with such values, however, have no complaints at all.

When you stand up quickly, blood sinks into the legs. Normally the body reacts at once: pressure sensors in the vessels, the **baroreceptors**, notice the drop. Then the **pulse** rises and the vessels narrow, so that the blood pressure is held. If the circulation reacts too slowly, your vision goes black or you feel dizzy. This is called **orthostatic hypotension**. With the **Schellong test**, blood pressure and pulse are measured first lying down and then several times standing.

If the blood pressure drops very sharply for a short time, the brain gets too little blood. Then you can lose consciousness for a moment. This is called a **syncope**, in everyday language a faint. Lying down, you usually recover quickly, because the blood flows more easily to the head again. That is why you lay a fainted person down and raise their legs a little, if they are not injured.

For many people with low blood pressure, simple things help: **drinking enough** and **getting up slowly**. Fluid increases the amount of blood, and getting up slowly gives the circulation time. Exercise and alternating hot and cold showers can also train the circulation. **Compression stockings** press on the leg veins from outside so that the blood does not pool in the legs. A strong drop in blood pressure after heavy **blood loss** is dangerous, however: in **hypovolaemic shock**, the organs no longer get enough supply, and you need 144 at once.

gewusst: Lying down, the blood pressure in the head and feet is almost the same, but standing it is much higher in the feet.
Standing for a long time in the heat, for example at a concert, can lead to fainting in people with low blood pressure.

teile.einleitung: Hair comes in many colours: black, brown, blond and red. The colour comes from a natural pigment in the hair. In old age, hair often turns grey or white.
wichtigste: Hair colour comes from a pigment in the hair.
A lot of dark pigment makes dark hair, and little pigment makes light hair.
Black and dark brown are the most common hair colours in the world.
Red is the rarest natural hair colour.
The sun can make light hair even lighter.
In old age, hair turns grey and later white.

abschnitte.text: In hair there is a natural **pigment**, **melanin**. It is made in the hair root. There is a dark, brown-black kind and a lighter, reddish-yellow kind. A lot of dark pigment makes **dark hair**, and little of it makes **light hair**. How much pigment is made, and which kind, depends on the genes.

Most people in the world have **black** or **dark brown** hair. Dark brown hair is also called **brunette**, a word that comes from French. Light yellow hair is called **blond**. Many small children are blond, and their hair becomes darker later. **Red** is the rarest natural hair colour. Only a few people have red hair naturally.

**Sunlight** bleaches the pigment in the hair. That is why light hair often becomes even lighter in summer. With **hair dye**, you can colour the hair artificially in another colour, for example at the hairdresser's. The newly growing hairs, however, have their own colour again. That is why after a few weeks you see the natural colour at the roots.

With age, the hair root makes less and less **pigment**. The hair then turns **grey** and later **white**. A single hair is either coloured or colourless. The grey impression comes about because coloured and white hairs are mixed. When this begins varies greatly and often runs in the family.

gewusst: Grey hairs hardly exist as such: usually you see a mixture of coloured and white hairs.
Red hair is much more common in Scotland and Ireland than in most other countries.

teile.einleitung: Many men and some women too lose hair on the head in the course of their lives. If the scalp becomes completely bare in one area, this is called **baldness**. Usually it is down to the genes and is not an illness.
wichtigste: Whether a man goes bald depends mainly on his genes.
Often bare areas appear first at the temples, called receding temples.
By the age of 50, about half of men have visible hereditary hair loss.
A ring of hair often remains at the back and sides, because the hair roots there are less sensitive.
In women, the hair usually becomes thinner at the parting on the top of the head.
A bald head needs sun protection in summer, because the hair is missing.

abschnitte.text: The most common cause of baldness is **hereditary hair loss**. Whether and when someone gets it depends mainly on their **genes**. In the people affected, certain hair roots react sensitively to a **chemical messenger** made by the body. Over time the hairs become thinner and shorter until in the end they no longer grow back visibly. About half of men have visible hereditary hair loss by the age of 50.

In men, baldness often begins at the **temples**. The bare spots are called “**Geheimratsecken**” in German, which means privy councillor corners. Many older officials with the title “privy councillor” used to have such corners, hence the name. Often a spot at the top of the back of the head also goes bare. It reminds people of the **tonsure**, a hairstyle in which monks once shaved a round spot on the head.

Even with a large bald patch, a **ring of hair** often remains at the back and sides of the head. The **hair roots** there are **hereditarily less sensitive** and carry on growing. In women, hereditary hair loss usually looks different: the hair becomes thinner mainly at the **parting** on the top of the head, and a completely bare spot rarely forms.

Hair protects the scalp from the sun. With a bald head, this protection is missing. The skin is therefore especially at risk of **sunburn** in summer. In the long run, too much sun can also promote skin cancer. That is why a hat, a cap or sun cream is important, especially in the mountains, where UV radiation is stronger.

Many people wear their bald head with confidence, and some even shave their head completely. Anyone who wants to do something about it can get medical advice. There are medicines that slow hair loss. In a **hair transplant**, usually **your own hair roots from the back of the head** are moved to the bare areas. Because these roots are not sensitive, the hairs keep growing there.

gewusst: A person normally loses about 50 to 100 hairs every day, which mostly grow back.
Some monkeys, for example some macaques, also get a kind of bald head in old age.

teile.einleitung: In each kidney there are around a million tiny filters. Their core is the **glomerulus**, a small tangle of blood vessels. Here the first urine is filtered out of the blood.
wichtigste: The glomerulus is a tangle of fine blood capillaries in the kidney.
Glomerulus and Bowman's capsule together form the renal corpuscle.
Blood flows in through the vas afferens and out through the vas efferens.
The vas efferens is an arteriole, not a vein.
The filter consists of capillary endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocytes.
Filtration is driven mainly by the blood pressure in the capillaries.

abschnitte.text: The word **glomerulus** comes from Latin and means “little ball of yarn”. It is a bundle of fine **capillaries**, the smallest blood vessels. It is surrounded by a cup-shaped casing, **Bowman's capsule**. Together they form the **renal corpuscle**. Here the work of the kidney begins: cleaning the blood and forming urine.

Blood reaches the glomerulus through a small vessel, the **vas afferens**. After filtering, it leaves through the **vas efferens**. The special feature: this vessel leading away is also an **arteriole**, not a vein. So two arterioles lie one after the other here. Because the width of both vessels can be changed, the body can control the pressure in the glomerulus precisely.

The **glomerular filter** consists of three layers. On the inside lies the **capillary endothelium** with many small pores. Next comes the **glomerular basement membrane**. On the outside, the **podocytes** wrap around the capillaries with finger-like **foot processes**. Between the processes, narrow slits remain free. Water, salts and sugar get through, but blood cells and large proteins do not. **Albumin** hardly gets through because of its size and its **negative charge**.

What drives the filtering? Mainly the **blood pressure in the capillaries**. It presses fluid out of the blood into Bowman's capsule. This fluid is called **primary urine**. Between the capillaries lie the **mesangial cells**. They support the tangle of vessels, can contract and clear away deposited substances.

An inflammation of the glomeruli is called **glomerulonephritis**. In it, the filter can become leaky. Then protein or even blood gets into the urine. Doctors therefore check the urine with test strips. High blood pressure and diabetes can also damage the glomeruli in the long run. If both kidneys no longer work enough, a blood wash, **dialysis**, is needed.

gewusst: Bowman's capsule is named after the English doctor William Bowman, who described it in the 19th century.
The body takes almost all the water back from the primary urine, and only about 1 per cent is passed as urine.

teile.einleitung: A skin rash is a change in the skin, for example with red spots, blisters or wheals. It can be caused by viruses, bacteria, allergies or plants. Often its appearance gives away what cause is behind it.
wichtigste: A rash over the whole body is called, in technical terms, an exanthem.
In measles, the rash typically begins behind the ears.
Hand, foot and mouth disease causes blisters on the hands, feet and in the mouth.
Shingles arises from the chickenpox virus that has stayed in the body.
Scarlet fever is caused by bacteria and often shows a strawberry tongue.
Hives cause itchy wheals, often because of an allergy.
Nickel often causes a contact rash.

abschnitte.text: In a skin rash, the skin changes visibly. Red spots, small bumps, **blisters** or raised **wheals** can form. A rash that spreads over the whole body is called an **exanthem** in technical language. It often occurs in infectious diseases. You should not confuse it with a **haematoma**, which is a bruise.

In **measles**, the patchy rash usually begins behind the ears and on the face and then spreads. A vaccination protects against measles. **Hand, foot and mouth disease** mainly affects children under ten and causes blisters on the palms, soles of the feet and in the mouth. The virus of **chickenpox** stays in nerve cells after the illness. If it becomes active again decades later, the painful **shingles** results.

Not every rash comes from viruses. **Scarlet fever** is caused by **streptococci**, that is, by bacteria. Typical are a sore throat, fever, a fine rash and a red, bumpy **strawberry tongue**. Because bacteria are the cause, the doctor can prescribe antibiotics.

If you grab **stinging nettles**, fine **stinging hairs** break off and inject irritants into the skin. Itchy, burning wheals form. **Hives**, technical term **urticaria**, looks very similar. It often arises from an allergy, for example to foods or medicines. The metal **nickel** in belt buckles or jeans buttons is one of the most common triggers of a **contact allergy**, in which an itchy eczema forms.

gewusst: The German word for hives, “Nesselsucht”, comes from the stinging nettle (“Nessel”), because the wheals look exactly the same.
Someone who had chickenpox as a child usually carries the virus in them for life without noticing.

teile.einleitung: The cerebrum is made up of two halves, a left one and a right one. They look almost the same, but they take on partly different jobs. A thick bundle of fibres joins them so that they work together.
wichtigste: A deep longitudinal fissure divides the cerebrum into two halves.
The corpus callosum joins the two halves of the brain.
Each half of the brain controls mainly the opposite side of the body.
In most right-handed people, the language centres are on the left.
Broca’s area is important for forming language, Wernicke’s area for understanding it.
The different jobs of the halves are called lateralisation.
Roger Sperry received the Nobel Prize in 1981 for experiments with a severed corpus callosum.

abschnitte.text: From above you see a deep groove running down the middle of the cerebrum. It is called the **longitudinal fissure** and divides it into a **left** and a **right hemisphere**. Deep down, the two halves are joined by the **corpus callosum**. It is made up of many millions of nerve fibres. In this way the two halves can constantly exchange information.

Each half of the brain controls mainly the **opposite side of the body**. So the left half of the brain moves the right hand, and the right half moves the left hand. That is why, after a **stroke** in the left half of the brain, the **right side of the body** is often paralysed. Feelings from the skin also arrive in the opposite half each time.

In most **right-handed people**, the language centres are in the **left hemisphere**. **Broca’s area** is important mainly for **forming language**, that is, for speaking. **Wernicke’s area** is important mainly for **understanding language**. If one of them is damaged, **aphasia** can result, a language disorder. The areas are named after doctors of the 19th century.

The fact that the two halves of the brain take on partly different jobs is called **lateralisation**. The right half, for example, is often more involved when we recognise faces or find our way around in space. But the idea that some people are more “left-brained” and others more “right-brained” is a myth. For almost everything, both halves work closely together.

In the past, in some people with severe epilepsy the corpus callosum was cut. The researcher **Roger Sperry** studied how these people perceive and think. He showed that each half has abilities of its own. For this he received the **Nobel Prize** in Medicine in **1981**, together with two other researchers.

gewusst: In most left-handed people, too, the language centres are in the left half of the brain.
The corpus callosum is the largest fibre connection in the human brain.

teile.einleitung: Your eye is not hollow inside. Most of it is filled with a clear, jelly-like mass, the **vitreous body**. It keeps the eye in shape and lets light through to the retina.
wichtigste: The vitreous body fills most of the eyeball.
It consists largely of water.
A healthy vitreous body is transparent and jelly-like.
It lies between the lens and the retina.
It gives the eye its round shape.
In old age it partly turns liquid and shrinks.

abschnitte.text: Light enters the eye through the cornea, the pupil and the **lens**. Behind it lies the **vitreous body**. It fills the whole space as far as the **retina** on the back wall of the eye. That makes it the largest part of the eyeball. On the retina, the image forms that travels along the optic nerve to the brain.

The vitreous body consists for the most part of **water**, around 98 per cent. In addition there are fine fibres of **collagen** and a substance called **hyaluronic acid**, which binds a lot of water. This produces a mass that is like jelly. A healthy vitreous body is **transparent** and **jelly-like**. It has no blood vessels, so that nothing disturbs the light on its way to the retina.

The vitreous body gives the eye its **round shape** and makes it stable, rather as air keeps a ball firm. It presses the retina gently against the wall of the eye. It also lets light pass almost without hindrance. Only this way can a sharp image form on the retina.

Some people see small **dots** or **threads** floating against a bright background, such as the sky. These are called **mouches volantes**, which is French for “flying flies”. They are tiny clumps in the vitreous body that cast shadows on the retina. They are usually harmless. In **old age**, the vitreous body often partly turns liquid and shrinks. Then more such shadows can appear. If you suddenly see very many or flashes of light, you should go quickly to the eye doctor.

In some eye diseases, for example a **detached retina**, the vitreous body is removed in an operation. This operation is called **vitrectomy**. Afterwards the eye is often filled with **gas** or **silicone oil**. This presses the retina into place. Gas is replaced over time by the body's own fluid, and silicone oil is usually taken out again later.

gewusst: The vitreous body makes up about two thirds of the eyeball, but has a volume of only about 4 millilitres.
The name comes from the fact that the mass is as clear as glass.

teile.einleitung: Haemodialysis is a blood wash for people whose kidneys no longer work. A machine takes over part of the kidneys' work. It cleans the blood of waste substances and removes surplus water.
wichtigste: Haemodialysis removes toxins mainly by diffusion through a membrane.
Surplus water is removed by ultrafiltration.
Usually three treatments a week are needed, each lasting about four to five hours.
On the arm, an arteriovenous fistula is often made.
Heparin stops the blood from clotting in the machine.
Blood and dialysis fluid flow in opposite directions.
In peritoneal dialysis, the peritoneum serves as the membrane.

abschnitte.text: The **kidneys** filter the blood every day. They remove waste substances such as **urea** and surplus water, which leave the body in the urine. If the kidneys no longer work, these substances collect in the body, and that is life-threatening. Then **haemodialysis** helps, a kind of artificial kidney. It is usually carried out **three times a week**, each time for about four to five hours. In between, those affected have to be careful with drinking and with foods rich in potassium.

In the **dialyser**, the filter, blood and **dialysis fluid** are separated by a **semi-permeable membrane**. Small substances such as urea move by **diffusion** from the place of high concentration to the place of low concentration, that is, from the blood into the fluid. Blood and dialysis fluid flow in **opposite directions**. In this **counter-current**, the difference is kept up along the whole length, and more is removed. Water is removed by **ultrafiltration**: a difference in pressure presses it out of the blood.

For dialysis, a lot of blood has to flow through the machine. For this, an **arteriovenous fistula** is often made on the arm, also called a **Cimino shunt**. In an operation, an artery is joined to a vein. This makes the vein strong and easy to puncture. So that the blood does not **clot** outside the body in the tubes and the filter, **heparin** is usually given. How well a treatment works is calculated with the value **Kt/V**, which measures how much urea was removed.

There is another method: **peritoneal dialysis**. In it, your own **peritoneum** serves as the membrane. A dialysis solution is filled into the abdominal cavity through a thin tube and changed after a few hours. This treatment can be done **at home**. Many people on dialysis are waiting for a **kidney transplant**. In Switzerland, the foundation **Swisstransplant** coordinates the distribution of donated organs.

gewusst: The first working artificial kidney was built by the Dutch doctor Willem Kolff in the 1940s.
With their kidneys, a healthy person filters around 180 litres of blood fluid every day.

teile.einleitung: The haematocrit says what percentage of the blood volume is made up of blood cells. It is an important value in the blood count. With it, you can recognise, for example, a lack of fluid or anaemia.
wichtigste: The haematocrit is determined almost entirely by the red blood cells.
In healthy men it is about 40 to 50 per cent, in women a little lower.
Traditionally, it is determined by spinning blood in a small tube.
With a lack of fluid, the haematocrit rises.
Right after a heavy bleed, it is often hardly changed.
Rule of thumb: haematocrit is about three times haemoglobin in g/dl.
In 1997, the UCI introduced a limit of 50 per cent.

abschnitte.text: Blood consists of a yellowish fluid, the **plasma**, and of **blood cells**. The **haematocrit** says what share of the blood volume the cells make up. Almost all of this is **red blood cells**, the erythrocytes: they make up far more than 99 per cent of the cell volume. White blood cells and platelets hardly count. In healthy men, the haematocrit is about **40 to 50 per cent**, in women a little lower.

Traditionally, you fill blood into a thin tube and **centrifuge** it, that is, you spin it very fast. The heavy cells settle at the bottom, and the plasma stays on top. The ratio of the column of cells to the total height gives the haematocrit. Today, automatic machines in the laboratory usually measure it. As a **rule of thumb**: the haematocrit in per cent is about **three times** the haemoglobin value in g/dl. At 14 g/dl haemoglobin, that is about 42 per cent.

With a severe **lack of fluid**, for example in diarrhoea or great heat, plasma water is lost. The cells stay behind, and the haematocrit **rises**. After a sudden heavy **bleed**, it is often still hardly changed, because cells and plasma are lost in the same proportion. Only when tissue fluid flows in or infusions are given is the blood thinned, and the value falls. A low haematocrit can point to **anaemia**.

A high haematocrit means more oxygen transport, but also thicker blood. In the 1990s, some professional cyclists illegally injected the hormone **EPO** to make more red blood cells. That is why the cycling federation **UCI** introduced a limit of **50 per cent** in 1997. Anyone above it was not allowed to start, to protect their health. The value is abnormally raised in **polycythaemia vera**: in this disease of the bone marrow, far too many red blood cells are made without control.

gewusst: The word haematocrit is put together from Greek words for “blood” and “separation”.
Someone who lives in the mountains for a few weeks often has a slightly higher haematocrit than in the lowlands.

teile.einleitung: The heart muscle is the muscle that the heart is mostly made of. It works tirelessly, day and night, without you having to control it consciously. It is one of the muscles in the whole body with the greatest stamina.
wichtigste: The heart muscle forms the main part of the heart wall.
It works tirelessly without you controlling it consciously.
In this it differs from skeletal muscle, which you move at will.
The heart muscle has its own pacemaker, the sinus node.
It is supplied with blood and oxygen through the coronary arteries.
The wall of the left ventricle is the thickest, because it pumps the blood into the whole body.
Endurance sport can strengthen the heart muscle.

abschnitte.text: Humans have three kinds of muscle tissue. **Skeletal muscle** moves your arms and legs, and you control it consciously. **Smooth muscle** works unconsciously in the intestines, stomach and blood vessels. The **heart muscle** is a separate, third kind. Under the microscope it looks striped like skeletal muscle, but works unconsciously like smooth muscle.

The cells of the heart muscle are branched and tightly linked to one another by special connections. As a result, an electrical impulse spreads across the whole heart in a flash. In this way many cells contract almost at the same time and pump together. Heart muscle cells contain a great many **mitochondria**, the power stations of the cell. That is why they do not tire like other muscles.

The heart muscle does not need a command from the brain to beat. The **sinus node** in the right atrium sets the rhythm. Through the **conduction system**, the signal is passed on to the ventricles. Nerves and hormones such as adrenaline can only make the heartbeat faster or slower. Even a heart outside the body can go on beating for a while if it is supplied with a nutrient solution.

Although the heart is constantly pumping blood, the heart muscle is not fed directly from the inside. It has its own vessels, the **coronary arteries**, which lie around the heart like a wreath. If they become blocked, part of the heart muscle no longer gets any oxygen. Then a **heart attack** happens, and muscle tissue dies. Dead heart muscle cells can hardly renew themselves and are replaced by scar tissue.

Regular exercise such as cycling, swimming or cross-country skiing strengthens the heart muscle. A trained heart pumps more blood with each beat. That is why the resting pulse of endurance athletes is often low, sometimes below 50 beats a minute. Experts then speak of an **athlete’s heart**. Smoking and lack of exercise, on the other hand, harm the heart muscle.

begriffe.erklaerung: Muscles that you move consciously.
The natural pacemaker of the heart in the right atrium.
Small power stations in the cells that make energy.
The vessels that supply the heart muscle with blood.

gewusst: The heart muscle starts to beat in the first weeks of pregnancy.
In a long life, the heart muscle never takes a single real break.
The heart muscle cells of an adult hardly divide any more.

teile.einleitung: In every cell there are small areas with special jobs, the **organelles**. One of them is the **Golgi apparatus**. It works like a post office: it changes proteins, sorts them and sends them to their destination.
wichtigste: The Golgi apparatus changes, sorts and packs proteins.
It was described in 1898 by the Italian doctor Camillo Golgi.
A single stack of flattened membrane cisternae is called a dictyosome.
The cis side takes in vesicles from the endoplasmic reticulum.
Secretory proteins are released from the cell by exocytosis.
Lysosomes arise by vesicles pinching off at the Golgi apparatus.

abschnitte.text: The Italian doctor **Camillo Golgi** described the organelle in **1898**. He had developed a new staining method for nerve cells. With it, he saw a fine net in the cells under the microscope. Later it was named after him, the **Golgi apparatus**. For a long time, some researchers doubted whether it really exists. Only with the electron microscope could it be seen exactly.

The Golgi apparatus consists of flat sacs wrapped in membrane, the **cisternae**. They lie on top of each other like a stack of pancakes. A single such stack is called a **dictyosome**. The Golgi apparatus has two sides. The **cis side** faces the **endoplasmic reticulum** and takes in small bubbles, the **vesicles**, from there. On the opposite **trans side**, finished vesicles pinch off again.

The main job of the Golgi apparatus is to **change, sort and pack proteins**. Many proteins carry short **sugar chains**. In the Golgi apparatus, these sugar chains are **rebuilt**. After that, the proteins get a kind of address. This way the cell knows whether a protein belongs in the cell membrane, in a lysosome or outside. Then it is packed into a suitable vesicle.

Proteins that the cell is meant to release are called **secretory proteins**. Their vesicles travel to the cell membrane and merge with it. This way the contents get outside. This process is called **exocytosis**. Other vesicles become **lysosomes**. These contain digestive enzymes and break down old cell parts or substances that have been taken in. In **gland cells**, which release many substances, the Golgi apparatus is especially well developed, for example in the pancreas.

Plant cells also have a Golgi apparatus, often with many separate dictyosomes. There it makes, among other things, building blocks for the **cell wall**. When a plant cell divides, **Golgi vesicles** build the **cell plate** after the nucleus has divided. From it the new wall between the two daughter cells arises.

gewusst: In 1906, Camillo Golgi received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with the Spaniard Santiago Ramón y Cajal.
The abbreviation cis means “on this side” in Latin, and trans means “on the other side”.

teile.einleitung: The hypothalamus is a small but very important part of the brain. It controls body temperature, hunger, thirst and the daily rhythm. It also links the nervous system with the hormone system.
wichtigste: The hypothalamus belongs to the diencephalon and lies under the thalamus.
It regulates body temperature to a set point of around 37 °C.
Leptin from fatty tissue dampens the feeling of hunger in the hypothalamus.
Osmoreceptors trigger thirst when the blood is too concentrated.
The suprachiasmatic nucleus is the inner clock.
It makes ADH and oxytocin, which are released in the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland.
In stress, it starts the chain of hormones that ends in cortisol.

abschnitte.text: The **hypothalamus** lies deep inside the brain, below the **thalamus**. Both belong to the **diencephalon**, the technical word for which is diencephalon. The hypothalamus is only about as big as an almond. Beneath it hangs the **pituitary gland** on a stalk. Together they control many processes in the body without our having to think about them.

The centre of **temperature control** lies in the hypothalamus. It compares the measured body temperature with a **set point** of around 37 °C. If it is too warm, it triggers **sweating**, and if it is too cold, we begin to **shiver**. **Thirst** is also triggered here: **osmoreceptors** measure whether the blood is too concentrated. Then more **ADH** is released so that the kidney saves water. For **hunger**, the hormone **leptin** from fatty tissue helps: the more fat is stored, the more leptin, and this dampens hunger.

A small nucleus in the hypothalamus is called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**. It lies above the crossing of the optic nerves and gets information about light directly from the **retina**. So it knows whether it is day or night. It is regarded as the central **inner clock** and sets the body’s **daily rhythm**, for example when we get tired. Experts speak of the circadian rhythm, from the Latin for “about a day”.

In the hypothalamus there are special nerve cells that make **hormones** themselves. That is why it counts as the **link** between the nervous system and the hormone system. The hormones **ADH** (vasopressin) and **oxytocin** are made here and travel along long nerve fibres to the **posterior lobe of the pituitary gland**. There they are released into the blood. Other control hormones reach the anterior lobe through a vessel system of their own, the **hypophyseal portal system**. In **stress**, the hypothalamus starts a chain through the pituitary gland to the adrenal cortex, which makes **cortisol**. This chain is called the **HPA axis**.

gewusst: A fever arises because the hypothalamus sets its set point for temperature higher. That is why you shiver at first despite the heat.
Jet lag after a long flight arises because the inner clock in the hypothalamus is still ticking to the old time.

teile.einleitung: The heart does not beat at exactly the same rhythm all the time like clockwork. The gaps between heartbeats vary a little. This variation is called heart rate variability, or HRV for short.
wichtigste: HRV describes the variation in the gaps between heartbeats.
The gaps are usually measured between the R waves in the ECG.
A high HRV at rest, compared with your own normal value, usually shows good recovery.
The parasympathetic nervous system acts on the heart mainly through the vagus nerve.
A well-known measure of HRV is called RMSSD.
Alcohol the evening before usually lowers HRV during the night.

abschnitte.text: Someone with a pulse of 60 beats a minute does not have exactly one beat every second. Sometimes the gap lasts a little longer, sometimes a little shorter. These fine differences are called **heart rate variability**. A certain amount of variation is healthy. It shows that the heart can adapt quickly to new conditions.

The heart is influenced by the **autonomic nervous system**, which works without our will. The **sympathetic nervous system** makes the heart faster, for example during stress or sport. The **parasympathetic nervous system** slows it down and brings calm. It acts mainly through a cranial nerve, the **vagus nerve**. The more strongly the parasympathetic system acts, the greater the HRV usually is.

HRV is also linked with breathing. When you **breathe in**, the heart rate rises slightly, and when you breathe out it falls again. This is called **respiratory sinus arrhythmia**. Despite the difficult name, this is completely normal and is often easy to see in young people.

For HRV, the gaps between heartbeats are measured very precisely. In an **ECG**, doctors usually take the tall peaks, the **R waves**. A common measure is called **RMSSD**. It is worked out from the differences between successive gaps. Today chest straps and some sports watches also measure HRV.

Athletes use HRV to plan their training. It is best to measure **in the morning at rest after waking up**, always under the same conditions. If HRV is high compared with your own normal value, the body has usually recovered well. If it is low, it can point to tiredness, stress or an illness starting. **Alcohol** the evening before also usually lowers HRV during the night.

gewusst: What matters is the comparison with your own normal value, because HRV is very different from person to person.
On average, HRV decreases with age.

teile.einleitung: Hay fever is an allergy to pollen, the fine dust from flowers of plants. Many people in Switzerland know it. It is annoying, but not infectious.
wichtigste: Hay fever is not infectious.
In an allergy, the body’s defences react too strongly.
Many people have hay fever in spring and summer.
In Switzerland, birch pollen often triggers hay fever.
Hazel flowers as early as winter and can cause symptoms early.
MeteoSwiss publishes pollen forecasts.
Washing your hair in the evening rinses pollen away.

abschnitte.text: Hay fever is an **allergy**. Here the body’s **defences** take something harmless for dangerous, in this case **pollen**. They react too strongly. The nose runs or is blocked, and you have to sneeze often. The **eyes itch and water**. Hay fever is **not infectious**, so you cannot catch it from other people.

Pollen is carried through the air by the wind. As early as winter, the **hazel**, a shrub, blooms. It can set off hay fever very early in the year. In spring, trees such as the **birch** follow. Their pollen is a common trigger in Switzerland. In early summer the **grasses** join in. That is why many people have symptoms mainly in **spring and summer**.

In Switzerland, **MeteoSwiss**, the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, publishes pollen forecasts. A network of measuring stations measures how much pollen is in the air. This way people with hay fever know on which days they should take special care. After rain, the air often has less pollen for a while.

Pollen stays caught in hair and clothes. So it helps to **wash your hair** in the evening and not to take your clothes off in the bedroom. It is best to air rooms at times when there is little pollen. Sunglasses protect the eyes. Against the symptoms there are **medicines** from the chemist’s, such as nasal sprays and tablets.

Anyone who suffers badly can have a doctor test which pollen triggers the allergy. Sometimes **desensitisation** helps. Here you are given small amounts of the trigger over a longer time so that the body’s defences get used to it. Untreated hay fever can spread to the airways in some people and lead to asthma.

gewusst: The name hay fever is actually misleading: it is not caused by hay but by pollen.
A single catkin of the hazel can release millions of pollen grains.

teile.einleitung: Even when we lie completely still, our body needs energy. This energy at complete rest is called the basal metabolic rate. It depends on weight, age, muscles and health.
