wichtigste: The basal metabolic rate is the body's energy need at complete rest.
It is needed for breathing, heartbeat, body warmth and the work of the organs.
A rule of thumb says: 1 kcal per kilogram of body weight per hour.
For movement and work, the activity metabolic rate is added.
The basal and activity metabolic rates together make up the total energy expenditure.
The brain needs around 20 per cent of the energy at rest.
Muscles, age and fever influence the basal metabolic rate.

abschnitte.text: The **basal metabolic rate** is the energy that the body needs when it is completely at rest. The heart beats, the lungs breathe, the liver and kidneys work, and the body keeps its warmth at about 37 degrees. For all this it uses energy from food. Energy is often measured in **kilocalories** (kcal) or kilojoules.

A rough **rule of thumb** says: at rest, the body needs about 1 kcal per kilogram of body weight per hour. A person of 60 kg therefore needs 60 times 24 hours times 1 kcal, which is **1,440 kcal** a day. This is only an estimate. The real basal metabolic rate is a little different in every person.

Someone who moves, works or does sport needs additional energy. This is called the **activity metabolic rate**. In physically active people it is much higher than in people who sit a lot. The basal and activity rates together make up the **total energy expenditure**, that is, the whole energy need of a day. If you eat about as much as you use, your weight stays the same.

**Muscle tissue** is metabolically active. It uses energy even when sitting or lying, while fatty tissue uses only a little. That is why people with a lot of muscle mass have a higher basal metabolic rate. With increasing age, adults usually lose muscle mass, and the **metabolism** becomes slower. That is why the basal metabolic rate mostly falls in old age.

The **brain** makes up only about 2 per cent of body weight. Even so, at rest it uses around **20 per cent** of the energy, because the nerve cells work constantly, even in sleep. In **fever**, metabolic processes run faster. That is why the energy need temporarily rises clearly. The thyroid gland also influences how fast the metabolism works.

gewusst: Even in deep sleep, your body constantly uses energy.
In proportion to its weight, the brain is one of the biggest energy users of the body.

teile.einleitung: In a cardiac arrest, the heart no longer pumps blood through the body. Without help, the person dies within a few minutes. Quick action by helpers can save lives.
wichtigste: In a cardiac arrest the person is unconscious and not breathing normally.
Gasping is not normal breathing but a sign of cardiac arrest.
The check of the breathing lasts at most 10 seconds.
In Switzerland you call the emergency number 144 straight away.
Several helpers take turns at giving chest compressions about every 2 minutes.
In adults, coronary heart disease is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death.
ROSC means that a circulation of the person’s own returns.

abschnitte.text: In a **cardiac arrest**, no more blood flows. The brain and organs no longer get oxygen. After just a few seconds the person becomes **unconscious**. In adults, the most common cause of sudden cardiac death is **coronary heart disease**, that is, narrowed coronary arteries. Often there is then a dangerous heart rhythm disorder such as **ventricular fibrillation**.

You speak to the person loudly and check whether they react. Then you check the breathing: tilt the head back, look, listen and feel. This takes **10 seconds** at most. **Gasping** looks like single, rare breaths for air. It is not normal breathing but a sign of cardiac arrest. Then resuscitation must be started at once.

First you call the **emergency number 144** and, if possible, have someone fetch a **defibrillator**. Then **chest compressions** begin. Good chest compressions reach about a quarter to a third of the normal pumping power of the heart. That is enough to supply the brain for a time. Because pressing is very tiring, several helpers take turns about **every 2 minutes**. With children, according to the European ERC guidelines, you begin with **5 rescue breaths**.

The ambulance service carries on the resuscitation with equipment and medicines. As standard it gives **adrenaline**, a hormone that narrows the blood vessels and stimulates the heart. If the heart beats again by itself, this is called **ROSC**. That is the English abbreviation for the return of spontaneous circulation.

After successful resuscitation the person goes to the **intensive care unit**. There they are closely monitored and treated. In the first days, **fever** is deliberately avoided, because a high body temperature can do extra harm to the damaged brain. The doctors also look for the cause of the arrest.

gewusst: Every minute without resuscitation lowers the chance of survival clearly, which is why help from ordinary people counts for so much.
Many public defibrillators tell you exactly what to do in a spoken voice.

teile.einleitung: Hygiene covers everything we do to stay healthy and to stop diseases from spreading. This includes washing your hands, brushing your teeth, showering, clean clothes and a clean home. Many of these habits are simple, but they protect you and others very effectively.
wichtigste: Hygiene means measures that protect health through cleanliness.
You always wash your hands after the toilet and before eating.
With water and soap, hands get properly clean.
If you have to sneeze and have no tissue, you sneeze into the crook of your arm.
Everyone uses their own toothbrush so that no germs are passed on.
You brush your teeth at least twice a day.
Clean drinking water and good waste water disposal are important parts of hygiene.

abschnitte.text: **Personal hygiene** includes washing your hands, showering or bathing and washing your hair. It is best to brush your teeth in the morning and the evening with toothpaste that contains fluoride. Everyone has their own **toothbrush**, towel and hairbrush so that no germs are passed on. Fingernails should be short and clean. In puberty, regular washing becomes more important because you sweat more.

When you cough and sneeze, tiny droplets with germs fly through the air. So you hold a tissue in front of your mouth and nose and throw it away afterwards. If there is no tissue, you sneeze or cough into the **crook of your arm**. That way the germs do not land on the hands with which you touch door handles and other people. This rule has been especially well known since the coronavirus pandemic.

Cleanliness is important when eating, too. You wash your hands before cooking and before eating. Raw meat and vegetables should be cut on different boards so that germs such as **salmonella** do not spread. Perishable food belongs in the fridge. You wash fruit and vegetables before eating them.

Hygiene concerns not only individual people but whole towns and cities. In the past, diseases such as **cholera** spread through dirty water. In the 19th century, cities such as Zurich built sewers and pipes for clean drinking water. Today in Switzerland, hundreds of **sewage treatment plants** clean the waste water. Worldwide, however, many people still have no access to clean water and toilets.

For a long time nobody knew that tiny germs cause diseases. The doctor **Ignaz Semmelweis** showed around 1847 that washing hands saves lives. Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch later proved that bacteria cause diseases. Thanks to better hygiene, life expectancy has risen sharply over the last 150 years.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny living things such as bacteria or viruses that can make you ill.
The inside of the elbow, which you sneeze into when there is no tissue.
A plant that cleans dirty waste water.
Bacteria that can cause diarrhoea through spoiled food.

gewusst: You should replace a toothbrush about every three months.
The word hygiene goes back to Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health, whose bowl with a snake still decorates chemists’ shops today.
A sneeze can throw droplets several metres.

teile.einleitung: The body cannot simply leave sugar lying around loose. It stores it as **glycogen**, a kind of pantry for energy. The largest stores lie in the liver and in the muscles.
wichtigste: Glycogen is a storage form of sugar.
It is built from many glucose building blocks.
In humans, most glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles.
Insulin makes sure it is stored after eating, and glucagon makes sure it is broken down in the liver.
A muscle uses its glycogen only for its own work.
Glycogen is also called animal starch, because it resembles the starch of plants.

abschnitte.text: **Glycogen** is built from many **glucose** building blocks. These hang together in long chains that branch again and again. This produces a molecule that looks a little like a tree with many branches. A single glycogen molecule can contain tens of thousands of glucose units. Because of the many ends, the body can attach or cut off sugar very quickly.

abschnitte.titel: Stores in the liver and muscles
abschnitte.text: In humans, the largest glycogen stores lie in the **liver** and in the **muscles**. The liver is the pantry for the whole body: when needed, it releases sugar into the blood. The muscles, by contrast, use their glycogen only **for their own work**. They cannot pass the sugar on to other organs. Because we have a lot of muscle mass, there is in total even more glycogen in the muscles than in the liver.

After eating, blood sugar rises. Then the pancreas releases **insulin**. It makes sure that sugar is stored as glycogen. If blood sugar is too low, **glucagon** comes into play. It makes the **liver** break down its glycogen and release glucose into the blood. In exertion or fright, adrenaline also helps with the breakdown.

Plants store sugar in a similar way, but as **starch**. Potatoes, rice and grain are full of starch. Because glycogen resembles starch, it is also called **animal starch**. The difference: glycogen is even more branched. Fungi, by the way, also store glycogen and not starch.

In a long run or a bike tour, the muscles need a lot of sugar. When the glycogen stores are empty, you suddenly feel weak and tired. That is why **endurance athletes** like to eat **pasta**, rice or bread before a competition. These carbohydrates fill up the **glycogen stores**. On the evening before a big race, there is therefore often a “pasta party”.

gewusst: Every gram of glycogen is stored together with about three grams of water.
The glycogen stores of the liver last only about a day without food.

teile.einleitung: People have very different skin colours, from very light to very dark. The main difference is made by a pigment called melanin. Skin colour can also change briefly, for example when we blush or get a fright.
wichtigste: The pigment melanin colours the skin brown.
How much melanin the skin makes is inherited.
Dark skin protects better against the sun's rays.
In the sun, the skin makes more pigment and turns brown.
In sunburn, light skin turns red.
Over midday, the sun is strongest.
When embarrassed we blush; when frightened we go pale.

abschnitte.text: In the skin there are special cells, the **melanocytes**. They make the pigment **melanin**. The more melanin the skin contains, the darker it is. How much pigment someone makes is **inherited**. From this come many different skin tones. Melanin, by the way, also colours the hair and the eyes.

Melanin holds back part of the sun's **UV rays**. That is why dark skin gets **sunburn** less often. Light skin turns red in too much sun, is hot and hurts, because it is inflamed. If you are in the sun for several days, the skin makes more pigment to protect itself. This is how a **suntan** comes about. Over midday, the sun is at its highest, and then its radiation is strongest. That is why you look for shade then.

abschnitte.titel: Why there are many skin colours
abschnitte.text: Experts explain the variety of skin colours by the **sun**. In regions with very strong sun, dark skin protects better. In regions with little sun, light skin is an advantage, because the body makes **vitamin D** with sunlight. Skin colour says nothing about how clever, kind or capable a person is. All people belong to the same species.

Skin colour can also change for a short time. When you are ashamed, more **blood** flows into the cheeks, and the face goes red. This is called **blushing**. In a fright or in illness, on the other hand, less blood flows through the skin. Then you look **pale** or white. Cold can also make the skin pale or even a little bluish.

gewusst: Almost all people have about the same number of pigment cells; they just make different amounts of melanin.
Freckles are small spots where the skin makes more pigment.

teile.einleitung: With a hairbrush, you put your hair in order. It untangles knots, smooths the hair and helps with styling. There are many different brushes and also combs.
wichtigste: With a hairbrush, you arrange and untangle the hair.
A hairbrush has many bristles made of plastic or animal hair.
A comb has teeth instead of bristles.
Long hair is brushed upwards starting from the ends.
You should clean the brush now and then.
A round brush is used together with the hairdryer.

abschnitte.text: A **hairbrush** has many small rods, the **bristles**. They can be made of plastic or of animal hair. With the brush you untangle the hair, and afterwards it lies smooth and tidy. A **comb** has a row of **teeth** instead of bristles. With it you can arrange the hair or make a parting.

Long hair that is not brushed for a long time gets tangled. This is how **knots** form. It is best to begin at the bottom with the **ends** and work slowly upwards. This way the hairs break less, and it hurts less. Someone who starts at the top pushes the knots downwards and makes them even tighter.

There are brushes for different purposes. A **round brush** is round like a roller. You wind the hair around it and blow-dry it, which gives it bounce. Flat brushes are good for untangling. Animals with fur are also brushed, for example **dogs** and **horses**. This removes loose hair and dirt.

Fallen hairs, dust and grease stay caught in the brush. That is why you should **clean** it now and then. First you pick the hairs out, then you wash the brush with warm water and a little shampoo. A clean brush looks after the hair better. It is best not to share your brush with others, so that, for example, lice are not passed on.

gewusst: In the past, many hairbrushes were made from the bristles of wild boars.
When brushing, the grease of the scalp is spread into the hair, which is why it often shines afterwards.

teile.einleitung: With the **sense of taste**, we check what we eat and drink. It helps us to enjoy tasty things and to spot what is spoiled or poisonous. Many animals taste too, some even with their feet.
wichtigste: Today we know five basic tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
All areas of the tongue can sense all tastes.
Hot is not a taste but a feeling of pain and heat.
We can only taste substances that are dissolved in saliva.
Cold makes the tongue less sensitive, which is why ice-cold ice cream tastes less sweet.
Butterflies taste with their feet, and cats cannot taste anything sweet.

abschnitte.text: The tongue distinguishes five **basic tastes**: **sweet**, **sour**, **salty**, **bitter** and **umami**. Umami is the savoury taste that you know, for example, from meat broth or mature cheese. Sweet often shows us food rich in energy. Bitter can warn of poisons, and sour of unripe or spoiled food. The **taste buds** on the tongue recognise the taste.

In the past, many school books showed a **tongue map**: sweet at the front, sour and salty at the sides, bitter at the back. That is not right. All areas of the tongue that have taste buds can sense all five tastes. There are at most small differences in sensitivity. Try it out: even the tip of the tongue notices when something is sour.

**Hot**, as with chilli, is not a basic taste. The substance capsaicin stimulates nerves that otherwise report pain and heat. That is why hot food feels hot. For us to taste anything at all, **saliva** is needed: only when the tasting substances dissolve in it do they reach the sensory cells. Very cold ice cream tastes less sweet than melted, because cold makes the tongue less sensitive.

Much of what we call “taste” actually comes from the **nose**. When we chew, scent substances rise from behind into the nose. Together with taste, this creates the **aroma**. Someone who has a cold notices this: food then tastes bland. The look, the temperature and the texture of food also influence how well we like something.

Animals taste in astonishing ways. **Butterflies** have taste sensory cells on their feet. When they land on a flower, they notice at once whether there is something sweet there. The **catfish** has taste cells almost all over its skin and so can find food in cloudy water. **Cats**, by contrast, cannot taste sweet things, because they lack a matching taste receptor. As meat eaters they do not need it.

gewusst: A catfish is, so to speak, a swimming tongue: it tastes with its whole body.
Children often find bitter tastes stronger than adults do, which is why many dislike bitter vegetables.
Without the nose, it is hard to tell apart apple and raw onion when eating.

teile.einleitung: If you look at your tongue in the mirror, you see many small raised bumps. These are the **papillae**. In many of them sit the taste buds with which we taste sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami.
wichtigste: On the tongue there are four kinds of papillae: filiform, fungiform, foliate and circumvallate.
Filiform papillae are the most common but have no taste buds and are used for touch.
Fungiform papillae can be seen as small red dots at the tip and edge of the tongue.
The large circumvallate papillae stand at the back of the tongue in a V-shaped row.
The foliate papillae lie as folds on the back side edge of the tongue.
In the taste buds sit the sensory cells that recognise tasting substances.

abschnitte.text: The surface of the tongue is not smooth but covered with **papillae**. Experts distinguish four kinds: **filiform papillae**, **fungiform papillae**, **foliate papillae** and **circumvallate papillae**. They differ in shape, size and position. Only three of the four kinds carry taste buds. Together they make sure that we can taste food and feel it well in the mouth.

The **filiform papillae**, whose name means thread-like, are the most common papillae. They are fine and pointed and give the tongue its rough surface. They have no taste buds. Instead they feel touch, which is how you notice, for example, whether a food is soft, gritty or crunchy. In cats these papillae are especially hard, which is why a cat's tongue feels like sandpaper.

**Fungiform papillae**, which means mushroom-shaped, are wider at the top than at the bottom, like a little mushroom. Because they have a good blood supply, they appear as small red dots, especially at the tip and edge of the tongue. The **foliate papillae** form several folds on the back side edge that lie next to each other like leaves. The **circumvallate papillae** are the largest. A human has only about 7 to 12 of them, and they stand at the back of the tongue in a V shape and carry especially many taste buds.

In the papillae sit tiny **taste buds**. Each contains several dozen **sensory cells**. At the top the bud has a small opening, the **taste pore**. There the sensory cells reach with fine extensions into the saliva. Only substances that are dissolved in saliva can reach the sensory cells. The cells report their information to the brain along nerves.

Different sensory cells recognise different tastes. Salty is triggered mainly by **sodium ions**, which are in table salt. The savoury taste **umami** was described at the start of the 20th century by the Japanese chemist **Kikunae Ikeda**. He studied the seaweed broth dashi and found in it the substance that triggers this taste. Umami is also known from meat broth, mature cheese or tomatoes.

gewusst: Taste sensory cells live only about one to two weeks and are then constantly replaced by new ones.
The name umami comes from Japanese and means roughly “delicious” or “tasty”.

teile.einleitung: Hair and scalp get greasy and dirty, so you wash them regularly. With shampoo, water and a few tricks, it is easy and does not sting your eyes.
wichtigste: You wash hair with shampoo.
You massage the shampoo into the scalp.
When washing, you close your eyes, because shampoo stings.
After that, you rinse the shampoo out well.
A conditioner makes long hair easier to comb.
Lice have nothing to do with dirty hair.
You never use a hairdryer next to a full bathtub.

abschnitte.text: **Shampoo** is a liquid soap for hair and scalp. Grease, sweat and dandruff collect on the scalp. That is why you massage the shampoo in well there with your **fingertips**. Foam forms and loosens the dirt. How often you have to wash your hair is different for every person.

If shampoo gets into your eyes, it **stings** unpleasantly. That is why you close your eyes when washing your hair or tilt your head back. After that, you rinse the shampoo out thoroughly until there is no more foam. **Shampoo leftovers** can irritate the scalp and make it itch.

A **conditioner** makes the hair soft and smooth. This way, long hair gets less tangled. Wet hair is best untangled with a **comb** with wide teeth. You comb carefully upwards, starting from the ends. Wet hair is more delicate than dry hair and breaks more easily.

Many think that only children with unwashed hair get **lice**. That is not true. Lice climb from head to head when heads are close together, whether the hair is clean or not. It has nothing to do with dirt. There are special products from the chemist's against lice.

After washing, you dry your hair with a towel or with the **hairdryer**. You never use a hairdryer next to a full bathtub or a washbasin full of water, though. If it falls into the water, **electric current** can flow through the water. That is life-threatening. That is why electrical devices do not belong near water.

gewusst: Lice can neither jump nor fly; they only climb from hair to hair.
Wet hair stretches and is more delicate than dry hair.

teile.einleitung: The hair root is the part of the hair that sits invisibly in the skin. Only here are there living cells that divide and make the hair grow.
wichtigste: The hair root sits in the hair follicle under the skin.
Its thickened lower end is called the hair bulb.
The dermal papilla supplies the root with blood and nutrients.
In the hair matrix, the cells divide very quickly.
Pigment cells in the root give the hair its colour.
The visible part of the hair is called the hair shaft.
If the follicle stays unharmed, a new hair grows.

abschnitte.text: A hair has two parts: the **hair root** in the skin and the **hair shaft**, which sticks out visibly. The root sits hidden in the **hair follicle**. Its lower end is thickened like a bulb and is called the **hair bulb**. From below, the **dermal papilla** reaches into the bulb. It contains fine blood vessels and brings oxygen and nutrients.

abschnitte.titel: This is where the hair grows
abschnitte.text: Around the dermal papilla lies the **hair matrix**. Its cells are among the fastest-dividing cells of the body. They push the hair upwards. Only in the hair root are there **living cells**. As soon as the cells are pushed upwards, they harden into horn and die. That is why having your hair cut does not hurt.

In the hair bulb sit **pigment cells**, the **melanocytes**. They make colouring matter and pass it on to the newly forming hair cells. This is how the hair gets its colour. If these cells make less colouring matter in old age, the hair grows back grey or white.

Cells with a **cell nucleus** hang on the hair root. In the cell nucleus is the genetic information, the **DNA**. That is why the police can obtain DNA more easily from a pulled-out hair with its root than from a cut hair. In the hardened hair shaft, hardly any of it is left.

If you pull out a hair, the hair follicle usually stays unharmed. As long as the **follicle** is preserved, it makes a **new hair**. Only when the follicle is destroyed does nothing grow there any more. That is why plucked eyebrows usually grow back.

gewusst: The cells in the hair matrix divide as fast as hardly any other cells in the body.
A hair with its root can tell a laboratory which person it came from.

teile.einleitung: Heatstroke is a dangerous emergency. In it, the whole body gets too hot because it can no longer cool itself down. With a few simple rules, you can protect yourself from it well.
wichtigste: In heatstroke the whole body gets too hot.
Heatstroke is an emergency.
Body temperature can rise above 40 degrees.
Children and animals must never be left alone in a parked car.
Drinking plenty of water helps on hot days.
Small children and old people are especially at risk.
If someone is confused or collapses, get help at once.

abschnitte.text: Normally the body cools itself down by sweating. In great heat and with a lot of effort, this may no longer be enough. Then the **body temperature** keeps on rising, to **over 40 degrees**. This is called **heatstroke**. The brain and other organs can be damaged by it. Heatstroke is therefore an **emergency**.

Someone with heatstroke often has **hot, red skin**. Many have a headache and feel dizzy and sick. Typically, someone is suddenly **confused**, talks oddly or even **collapses**. Then you have to act quickly.

If a friend suddenly becomes confused or collapses in the heat, you get **adults and help at once**. In Switzerland the emergency number is **144**. Until help comes, you bring the person into the **shade** and cool them with **wet cloths**. You can fan air over them. If they are awake, they may drink small sips of water.

A **parked car** gets very hot very quickly in the sun, much hotter than the air outside. Even a gap in the window hardly helps. That is why you must never leave **children and animals** alone in a car in summer, not even for a moment. Small children and dogs can become dangerously overheated there after only a short time.

On hot days it helps to **drink plenty of water**, even if you are not yet thirsty. It is better to do strenuous sport in the morning or in the evening and not **at midday and in the afternoon**, when it is hottest. A hat and light-coloured, light clothes protect you. **Small children and old people** are especially at risk, because their bodies cope less well with heat.

gewusst: In a parked car, it can get over 50 degrees inside on a summer day.
In summer, the Federal Office of Public Health gives tips on how to protect yourself during heatwaves.

teile.einleitung: Every hair sits in a small tube in the skin, the hair follicle. Here the hair is made and anchored. The follicle has a muscle, nerves and even stem cells.
wichtigste: The hair follicle is the casing around the root of a hair.
It wraps around the hair root like a small tube.
The arrector pili muscle makes the hair stand up, which causes goosebumps.
Stem cells in the follicle make it possible for new hairs to grow.
Around every follicle lie nerve endings, which is why you feel fine touches.
An inflammation of the follicle is called folliculitis.

abschnitte.text: The **hair follicle** is a tube-shaped pocket of the skin. It wraps around the hair root like a small tube. In the follicle, the hair is made and firmly anchored. A **sebaceous gland** also opens into it. Its fat keeps hair and skin supple.

On the hair follicle attaches a tiny muscle, the **arrector pili muscle**. When you are cold or get a fright, it contracts. Then the hair stands up, and small bumps form on the skin around the hairs: **goosebumps**. In animals with thick fur, the raised fur holds more warm air.

In the upper part of the hair follicle lie **stem cells**. These are cells that can divide again and again. When a hair falls out, they build up a new hair root. That is why a new hair usually grows after the loss. The hairs on the body are different: fine, short and light **vellus hairs** cover large parts of the skin, for example the cheeks of children. Head hairs and eyebrows are thick, coloured **terminal hairs**.

Around every hair follicle lies a fine net of **nerve endings**. If the hair moves, this is measured at the root and reported to the brain. That is why you feel even a very light touch of a single hair. Cats are especially good at feeling with their **whiskers**, also called vibrissae. Their follicles are densely supplied with nerves, so the cat feels air movements and obstacles in the dark.

Sometimes hair follicles become inflamed, usually through **bacteria**. This is called **folliculitis**. Small red bumps or tiny spots of pus form around a hair. Often it heals by itself. You should not squeeze the spots, so that the inflammation does not spread.

gewusst: Goosebumps are a leftover from the time when the ancestors of humans had much more hair.
With their whiskers, cats can feel whether they will fit through a narrow opening.

teile.einleitung: Homeostasis is the body’s effort to keep up an inner balance. Whether it is hot or cold outside, whether you eat or go hungry, your body keeps values such as temperature and blood sugar as constant as possible. To do this, nerves, hormones and organs work together like a well-practised team.
wichtigste: Homeostasis is the body’s effort to keep up an inner balance.
Important values such as body temperature, blood sugar and water content are kept constant.
Body temperature is usually around 37 degrees Celsius.
The body constantly measures values and corrects deviations.
Negative feedback often helps with this, working against a change.
The nervous system and the hormone system control homeostasis.
If the balance is upset for a long time, you can become ill.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek and means roughly “the same state”. It was coined in 1926 by the American physiologist **Walter Cannon**. As early as the 19th century, the Frenchman Claude Bernard had spoken of the **internal environment**, which has to stay stable. The cells of the body can only work well under very particular conditions. Homeostasis makes sure that these conditions are kept up.

Homeostasis works in a similar way to heating with a **thermostat**. A sensor measures the actual value and compares it with the **set point**. If it is too cold, the heating switches on, and if it is too warm, it switches off. In the body, sensory cells measure the values, and the brain or glands react to them. Because the reaction works against the deviation, it is called **negative feedback**.

Body temperature is controlled in the **hypothalamus**, a small part of the diencephalon. If you are too hot, you sweat, and the blood vessels in the skin widen. If you are too cold, you shiver, because muscle movement produces heat. At the same time the skin vessels narrow. In this way the temperature inside stays at about 37 degrees, whether you are skiing in winter or swimming in the lake in summer.

After eating, the sugar in the blood rises. The pancreas then releases the hormone **insulin**, which lowers the blood sugar. If the sugar falls too far, for example during sport, it makes the hormone glucagon, which releases sugar from stores. In this way blood sugar stays within a narrow range. In diabetes, this regulation no longer works properly.

The water and salt balance is regulated too. If you have not drunk enough, you get thirsty, and the **kidneys** pass less water. That is why the urine is then darker. In the same way, the acidity of the blood, the oxygen content and the blood pressure are constantly adjusted. By the way, a fever is not a fault in the regulation: when there is an infection, the set point is deliberately set higher.

begriffe.erklaerung: The value that the body wants to reach and hold.
Regulation in which a deviation triggers an opposite reaction.
The part of the brain that controls temperature, thirst and hunger.
A hormone that lowers blood sugar.

gewusst: Even a deviation of a few degrees in body temperature can be life-threatening.
Animals and plants, too, keep their inner balance through homeostasis.
Even whole ecosystems can partly regulate themselves.

teile.einleitung: Hand hygiene means keeping the hands clean, above all by washing them thoroughly with water and soap. Our hands touch door handles, phones and money every day and pick up many germs. Hand washing is one of the simplest and most effective ways of preventing illness.
wichtigste: Hand washing removes germs and protects against illness.
Before eating you wash your hands, so that no germs get into the mouth.
You wash your hands after the toilet, after blowing your nose and after playing outside.
Thorough washing with soap takes about 20 to 30 seconds.
Soap dissolves grease and dirt and rinses germs away.
After that you dry your hands well.
In hospitals, hand disinfection is one of the most important rules.

abschnitte.text: Many microorganisms live on the hands. Most are harmless, but some are **disease-causing germs**, for example cold viruses, flu viruses or bacteria that cause diarrhoea. We touch our faces many times an hour without noticing. This is how germs get into the body through mouth, nose and eyes. Hand washing breaks this route.

First wet the hands with water and take **soap**. Then rub the soap in everywhere: palms, backs of the hands, between the fingers, thumbs, fingertips and nails. This takes about 20 to 30 seconds, as long as humming a short birthday song twice. After that, rinse well. Finally, dry the hands with a clean cloth or a paper towel.

You always wash your hands after the toilet and before eating. It is also important before cooking and after blowing your nose, coughing or sneezing. After contact with animals, after playing outside and after coming home from the bus or train, washing makes sense. When someone in the family is ill, you should take special care. These habits protect you and others.

In hospitals and care homes, a **disinfectant** is also used, which usually contains alcohol. It kills many germs in a short time. In everyday life, water and soap are generally enough. Disinfectant is handy when there is no water nearby. If there is visible dirt, you still have to wash your hands first.

The Hungarian doctor **Ignaz Semmelweis** worked around 1847 in a maternity clinic in Vienna. He noticed that many mothers died of childbed fever, because doctors came to the birth straight from the dissecting room. He introduced hand washing with chlorinated lime, and the deaths fell sharply. At the time, many colleagues did not believe him. Today he is regarded as a saviour of mothers, and every year on 5 May the WHO marks World Hand Hygiene Day.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny living things such as bacteria or viruses that can make you ill.
All the measures that protect health through cleanliness.
Killing disease-causing germs, for example with alcohol.
A germ that can cause an illness.

gewusst: Cold water cleans the hands with soap almost as well as warm water.
Especially many germs collect under long fingernails.
Many people forget the thumbs and the fingertips when washing.

teile.einleitung: The major histocompatibility complex, MHC for short, is a group of genes and proteins on our cells. They show the immune system what is going on inside a cell. In humans it is called the HLA system and plays a big part in transplants.
wichtigste: In humans, the MHC is also called the HLA system, for human leukocyte antigens.
The HLA genes lie on chromosome 6.
MHC class I molecules are carried by almost all body cells that have a nucleus.
The HLA genes are extraordinarily varied.
Before a blood stem cell transplant, a donor as well matched as possible is sought.
Jean Dausset received the Nobel Prize in 1980, Rolf Zinkernagel in 1996.

abschnitte.text: On the surface of our cells sit **MHC molecules**. They hold small fragments of proteins out to the outside, like a shop window. **T cells** of the immune system check these fragments. If they see something foreign, for example from a virus, they attack. In humans, the molecules are called **human leukocyte antigens**, **HLA** for short, because they were first found on white blood cells.

**MHC class I molecules** are carried by almost all body cells that have a nucleus. They show pieces of proteins that are made in the cell itself. This way, the immune system can recognise infections almost everywhere. **MHC class II molecules** sit mainly on immune cells that take up germs. The HLA genes lie close together on the short arm of **chromosome 6** and are usually inherited as a block.

The HLA genes are among the most varied genes of humans, with thousands of known variants. Before a **blood stem cell transplant**, therefore, **HLA typing** is done. The better the features match, the smaller the risk that the new cells attack the body or are rejected. Siblings often match better than strangers. In Switzerland, **Blood Donation SRK Switzerland** keeps the register of blood stem cell donors.

The Frenchman **Jean Dausset** discovered the first human leukocyte antigen in the 1950s. He received the Nobel Prize in 1980 together with Baruj Benacerraf and George Snell. The Swiss **Rolf Zinkernagel** showed with **Peter Doherty** that T cells recognise infected cells only if these carry the matching MHC molecules of their own. This principle is called **MHC restriction**. For this, both received the Nobel Prize in 1996.

gewusst: The feature HLA-B27 is carried by many people with the back disease ankylosing spondylitis, but most carriers stay healthy.
Because there are so many HLA variants, two unrelated people almost never have exactly the same features.

teile.einleitung: A **stench** is an unpleasant smell. It is not only annoying but often an important warning. Some animals and plants even use stench on purpose.
wichtigste: A stench is an unpleasant smell.
The stench of spoiled food warns us that we could become ill.
Rotten eggs smell of sulphur.
A smelly substance is added to natural gas so that a leak is noticed.
If it smells of gas: open the windows and go outside.
Skunks and stink bugs defend themselves with a foul smell.

abschnitte.text: Smells come from tiny **scent substances** in the air. The nose picks them up and the brain judges them. If a smell is unpleasant, we speak of a **stench**. Often we react at once: we wrinkle our nose, turn away or hold our breath. This dislike is partly inborn and partly learned.

Stench protects us. Spoiled food smells bad because bacteria or moulds are growing in it. The smell warns us that we **could become ill**. **Rotten eggs** smell of **sulphur**: as they decay, the gas hydrogen sulphide is formed. We also smell smoke very quickly, which can be vital in a fire.

abschnitte.titel: Care with the smell of gas
abschnitte.text: **Natural gas**, which some houses use for cooking or heating, naturally has almost no smell. That is why a **smelly substance** is specially added to it. This way you notice a leak at once. If it smells of gas in the flat, the rule is: **open the windows and go outside**. Do not switch on a light, do not press a doorbell and do not make a fire, because a spark can ignite the gas. Outside you call the fire brigade on the number 118.

Some animals defend themselves with stench. The **skunk** sprays a smelly liquid from glands at its rear end when in danger. The smell is so strong that attackers mostly run away. The **stink bug** gives off a foul smell when disturbed. In Switzerland, too, there are various bugs that can smell like this.

The **titan arum** from Sumatra has one of the largest flower clusters in the world. When it blooms, it stinks of rotting meat. This attracts beetles and flies, which pollinate it. The bloom lasts only a few days. In botanical gardens, including in Switzerland, many people come to see and smell the rare event.

gewusst: The titan arum blooms only every few years, so each bloom is a small sensation.
After a while the nose gets used to a smell and hardly notices it any more.

teile.einleitung: Almost everyone has had a sore throat, often together with a cold. The throat is then inflamed and scratchy. Usually it goes away by itself after a few days.
wichtigste: With a sore throat, the inside of the throat is inflamed.
It hurts especially when swallowing.
Often the tonsils are red and swollen.
Warm tea with honey and throat sweets do you good.
Some people gargle with salt water.
The voice can become hoarse.
With a bad sore throat, the doctor looks into the throat.

abschnitte.text: With a **sore throat**, the inside of the throat is **inflamed**. Usually this comes from viruses, for example in a cold. The throat scratches, burns and feels dry. When **swallowing**, the food rubs against the inflamed spot. That is why it hurts especially then.

At the back of the throat lie the **tonsils**. They help to fend off germs. In an inflammation, they often become red and thick. The **vocal cords** can also be irritated. Then the voice sounds **hoarse**, and sometimes you can hardly speak. It helps to rest the voice.

**Warm tea with honey** soothes the throat. Spicy or hard foods, on the other hand, irritate it. **Throat sweets** get the saliva going. This keeps the throat moist and eases the scratching. Some people gargle with **salt water**: you take some of it into your mouth, gargle and spit it out again. Many also find a **throat wrap** pleasant, a cloth that you put around the neck.

Usually a sore throat goes away by itself after a few days. If it is very bad, a high fever comes with it or you can hardly swallow, you go to the **doctor**. The doctor looks into the throat with a **lamp**. This way, he or she sees how badly the throat is inflamed and whether treatment is needed.

gewusst: The tonsils belong to the body's defences and catch germs.
A spoonful of honey in tea is an old home remedy for a scratchy throat.

teile.einleitung: The skin type describes how sensitively the skin reacts to sun. The best-known classification comes from the American skin doctor Thomas B. Fitzpatrick. Someone who knows their skin type can protect themselves better from sunburn.
wichtigste: Thomas B. Fitzpatrick developed the classification in common use today in 1975.
The Fitzpatrick scale distinguishes 6 skin types.
The classification is by the skin's reaction to sun.
Skin type I always gets sunburn and practically never tans.
The self-protection time is the time without protection until sunburn begins.
Self-protection time times sun protection factor gives the theoretical protection time.
In Switzerland, skin types II and III are especially common.

abschnitte.text: The American dermatologist **Thomas B. Fitzpatrick** classified skin in 1975 by its **reaction to sun**. What matters is how easily it gets sunburn and how well it tans. Originally the scale served to dose light therapies correctly. Today it is mainly used for **sun protection**. The scale has **six skin types**.

abschnitte.titel: From type I to type VI
abschnitte.text: **Type I** has very light skin, often freckles and reddish hair. This skin always gets sunburn and practically never tans. **Type II** and **type III** have light to medium-light skin that first burns and then tans. **Type IV** and **type V** are clearly darker and rarely burn. **Type VI** has deep dark skin. In Switzerland, among people of Central European origin, types II and III are especially common.

The **self-protection time** says how long unprotected skin can stay in the sun before it goes red. It depends on the skin type and on the **UV index**. In type I it is shortest. With sun cream, the time can be lengthened. You work it out: self-protection time times **sun protection factor**. Someone with 10 minutes of self-protection time who applies SPF 30 correctly theoretically reaches 300 minutes. Experts recommend using up only about two thirds of that.

Dark skin is better protected against UV rays, but not completely. People with **skin type VI** can also get **skin cancer**, though less often. In dark skin, it is also often noticed late, for example on the **soles of the feet** or palms. That is why it is worth everyone checking their skin and avoiding strong sun.

gewusst: Reapplying cream does not lengthen the protection time; it only keeps up the protection that is already there.
Children's skin has a shorter self-protection time than the skin of adults of the same skin type.

teile.einleitung: Hair cells are the sensory cells of hearing in the inner ear. They turn vibrations into electrical signals for the auditory nerve. If they are destroyed, they do not grow back in humans.
wichtigste: Hair cells sit in the organ of Corti in the cochlea.
There is one row of inner and three rows of outer hair cells.
The inner hair cells pass on most of the hearing information.
The outer hair cells actively amplify quiet sounds.
Their fine projections are called stereocilia.
Destroyed hair cells do not grow back in humans.
Otoacoustic emissions are used to test the outer hair cells.

abschnitte.text: In the inner ear lies the **cochlea**. In it sits the **organ of Corti**, the actual hearing organ. There, there is one row of **inner** and three rows of **outer hair cells**. Together there are clearly more than ten thousand cells per ear. Around 95 per cent of the nerve fibres that carry signals to the brain are connected to the inner hair cells. They are the actual sensory cells of hearing.

On the top side of the hair cells sit fine projections, the **stereocilia**. They are arranged like steps and are coupled by fine tip links. They reach into a fluid rich in potassium, the **endolymph**. When sound vibrates, the stereocilia are bent and **ion channels** open. Then **potassium ions** flow into the cell, and it sends a signal.

The **outer hair cells** can change their length quickly. They shorten and lengthen, controlled electrically. A motor protein called **prestin** in their cell membrane makes this possible. This movement is called **electromotility**. In this way, the outer hair cells amplify quiet sounds and help to tell pitches apart precisely.

Healthy outer hair cells themselves send out weak sound signals in response to a test stimulus. These are called **otoacoustic emissions**. A small microphone in the ear canal can measure them. That is why this measurement is used in the **hearing screening** of newborns. It is painless and takes only a short time.

Very loud noises can destroy hair cells. In **mammals**, and therefore in humans, destroyed hair cells of the cochlea are not replaced. That is why **noise-induced hearing loss** usually stays for good. **Birds**, on the other hand, can form their hair cells anew. This is being researched intensively. Ear protection at concerts or near loud machines protects the hair cells.

gewusst: A healthy ear itself sends out quiet sounds that can be measured with a microphone.
Birds can replace destroyed hair cells, but humans cannot.

teile.einleitung: Altitude sickness can happen if you climb too quickly to great heights. There the air is thinner, and the body gets less oxygen. In the Swiss Alps it mainly affects mountaineers.
wichtigste: Acute altitude sickness usually occurs from about 2500 m.
The most important sign is headache.
In high-altitude pulmonary oedema, fluid collects in the lungs.
In high-altitude cerebral oedema, the brain swells and you become unsteady and confused.
The most important measure in severe altitude sickness is to descend at once.
To prevent it, acetazolamide is often used, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor.
Above 3000 m, the sleeping altitude should rise by no more than 300 to 500 m a day.

abschnitte.text: The higher you climb, the lower the **air pressure**. With every breath, less **oxygen** therefore reaches the lungs. The body can get used to it, but it needs time to do so. If you climb too quickly, **acute altitude sickness** appears. It usually occurs above about **2500 m**. In Switzerland, many mountain huts and peaks are that high, for example the **Dufourspitze** at 4634 m is the highest peak in Switzerland.

The most important sign is **headache**. In addition there is often nausea, loss of appetite, tiredness, dizziness and poor sleep. To grade the symptoms there is the **Lake Louise Score**. It is named after a place in Canada where it was developed. Doctors and mountain guides can use it to estimate how severe the altitude sickness is.

Rarely, altitude sickness becomes life-threatening. In **high-altitude pulmonary oedema**, fluid leaks into the air sacs of the lungs because the pressure in the lung vessels rises. Typical signs are **breathlessness at rest** and coughing. In **high-altitude cerebral oedema**, the brain swells. Warning signs are **unsteadiness when walking**, confusion and disturbances of consciousness. Then the most important measure is to **descend at once**. Even a few hundred metres lower, the oxygen supply improves quickly, while medicines or pressure bags only bridge the time until then.

The best protection is a **slow ascent**. Above 3000 m, the **sleeping altitude** should rise by no more than **300 to 500 m** a day. This gives the body time to adapt. Some mountaineers take the medicine **acetazolamide** to prevent it. It belongs to the **carbonic anhydrase inhibitors**: it blocks an enzyme in the kidney so that more bicarbonate is passed out. The slightly acidic blood stimulates breathing and speeds up adaptation.

gewusst: Many tourists take the railway up to the Jungfraujoch at 3454 m. If you rush around there, you notice the thin air at once.
On the summit of Mount Everest, the air pressure is only about a third as high as at sea level.

teile.einleitung: The cornea of the eye is the clear, curved front of the eyeball. It works like a clear window through which light falls into the eye. At the same time it plays a big part in letting us see sharply.
wichtigste: The cornea lies right at the front like a watch glass over the iris and pupil.
It bends the light in the eye the most, about two thirds of the total focusing power.
It has no blood vessels, so that it stays transparent.
It gets its nutrients from the tear fluid and the aqueous humour.
In the middle it is only about 0.5 millimetres thick.
At the edge it passes into the white sclera.
It is very sensitive: when it is touched, the eye closes as a reflex.

abschnitte.text: When you look someone in the eyes, you see the coloured **iris** and the black **pupil**. Above them lies, almost invisible, the **cornea**. It is transparent and curved forwards, rather like the glass of a watch. In the middle it is only about 0.5 millimetres thick, and a little thicker at the edge. There it passes into the **sclera**, the firm “white” of the eye that wraps around the whole eyeball.

For us to see sharply, the light has to fall exactly on the **retina** at the back of the eye. For this it is bent, that is, its direction is changed. The cornea provides about two thirds of this **focusing power**. The rest is done by the **lens**, which can change its shape and so helps with focusing. If the cornea is curved unevenly, this is called **astigmatism**. Then points look like short lines.

Most parts of the body are supplied through blood vessels. The cornea has none, because otherwise it would not be perfectly clear. It therefore gets oxygen and nutrients from the **tear film** on the outside and from the **aqueous humour**, a clear fluid inside the eye. In return it has a great many **nerve endings**. If something touches the cornea, this at once triggers the **blink reflex**, and the eye closes for protection.

For short-sightedness or long-sightedness, the cornea can be treated with a **laser**, for example with the **LASIK** method. The laser removes fine layers and so changes its curve. Then the image falls sharply on the retina again. If a cornea is badly clouded, it can be replaced with the cornea of a dead donor. Such **corneal transplants** have existed for many decades. Because there are no blood vessels, the new cornea is only rarely rejected.

gewusst: The cornea is one of the tissues with the most nerve endings in the whole body. That is why even a tiny speck of dust in the eye hurts so much.
Contact lenses float on the tear film directly above the cornea.

teile.einleitung: Hair can be cut, styled and tied in many ways. This is how hairstyles such as fringe, plait, bun or ponytail come about. Because hair keeps growing, you need a new haircut now and then.
wichtigste: Head hair keeps growing, so it is cut now and then.
A fringe is short hair over the forehead.
For a plait, you weave three strands together.
In a bun, the hair is twisted into a knot.
A ponytail is held together with a hair tie.
In a crew cut, short hair stands up.

abschnitte.text: Head hair keeps growing all year, about one centimetre a month. So that it does not get too long or the ends do not look damaged, you have it cut now and then. This is done at home or at the **hairdresser's**, which in Switzerland is called the “Coiffeur”. Having your hair cut does not hurt, because hair above the skin has no nerves.

A **fringe** is short-cut hair that falls straight across the forehead. It hangs like a curtain in front of the forehead. In a **crew cut**, the hair is very short and stands up. That looks a little like the spines of a hedgehog. Short hair is practical because it dries quickly and needs little care.

Long hair can be tied in many ways. For a **plait**, you weave three strands over each other in turn. For a **ponytail**, you tie the hair together at the back of the head, and it hangs down like the tail of a horse. For a **bun**, you twist the hair together and pin it in place as a knot. This way it does not get in the way during sport, for example.

A ponytail is held together with a **hair tie**. This is a stretchy band that you wind around the hair. Clips and hairgrips also hold hairstyles in place. After washing, you dry wet hair with a **hairdryer**, which blows warm air. With a brush and a hairdryer, you can also give the hair a shape.

gewusst: In Switzerland, the hairdresser is usually called a “Coiffeur”, a word from French.
A plait of three strands is one of the oldest known braiding patterns.

teile.einleitung: Hypoglycaemia, in plain words low blood sugar, means that the blood sugar is too low. Then the body, above all the brain, gets too little sugar as energy. This can become dangerous, but can often be put right quickly.
wichtigste: In low blood sugar, there is too little glucose in the blood.
The brain needs glucose as its main source of energy and quickly notices the lack.
Typical signs are shaking, sweating, paleness and ravenous hunger.
Confusion and stumbling can look like drunkenness.
For a person who is awake, glucose tablets or a sweet drink help.
You give an unconscious person nothing by mouth and call 144.
In diabetes, a skipped meal can cause low blood sugar.

abschnitte.text: Our blood carries **glucose**, a kind of sugar, to all cells. The **brain** especially needs it as its **main source of energy**. It has hardly any sugar stores of its own and depends on a constant supply. If the blood sugar falls too far, this is called **hypoglycaemia** or **low blood sugar**. Then you become unable to concentrate, confused or, in the worst case, unconscious.

When the sugar falls, the body releases **alarm hormones** such as adrenaline. You begin to **shake** and **sweat**, turn pale and get strong **ravenous hunger**. If the brain goes on lacking sugar, you become confused, speak unclearly and stumble. That is why low blood sugar can easily be mistaken for **drunkenness**. When **cycling** in traffic it is dangerous, because concentration and reactions get worse.

Low blood sugar occurs most often in people with **diabetes** who take insulin or other medicines that lower blood sugar. If they take their medicine as usual but skip a **meal**, the supply of sugar is missing. A lot of **sport** without extra carbohydrates can also lower the level too far. Many of those affected therefore measure their blood sugar regularly and always carry glucose tablets.

If the person is **awake** and can swallow, the quickest help is **glucose tablets** or a **sweet drink** such as fruit juice. This sugar gets into the blood very quickly. Cheese or nuts, on the other hand, do not help quickly, because they contain hardly any sugar. If the person is **unconscious**, you give them nothing by mouth, because they could choke. You call the ambulance on **144** and put the person in the **recovery position**.

gewusst: The brain makes up only about two per cent of body weight, but uses a large share of the sugar in the blood.
Hypoglycaemia comes from Greek: hypo means “under”, glykys means “sweet”.

teile.einleitung: Almost all living things get energy from sugar. The first step toward this is **glycolysis**. In it, one molecule of glucose is split into two smaller molecules, and the cell gains a little ATP.
wichtigste: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm of the cell.
From one molecule of glucose, two molecules of pyruvate are formed.
In most tissues, the first step is catalysed by hexokinase.
Phosphofructokinase-1 is the most important pacemaker enzyme.
In the last step, pyruvate kinase makes ATP from phosphoenolpyruvate.
Red blood cells depend entirely on glycolysis, because they lack mitochondria.

abschnitte.text: The word **glycolysis** means “splitting of sugar”. The process takes place in the **cytoplasm**, that is, in the cell fluid outside the mitochondria. It needs no oxygen. From one molecule of **glucose** with six carbon atoms, **two molecules of pyruvate** with three carbon atoms each are formed in ten steps. All in all, the cell gains **two ATP** and two NADH.

First the cell has to invest energy. In most tissues, **hexokinase** attaches a phosphate group to the glucose. Later a second phosphate is attached, which is done by **phosphofructokinase-1**. It is regarded as the most important **pacemaker enzyme**, because it sets the pace of the whole of glycolysis. After that, **aldolase** splits fructose-1,6-bisphosphate into **two triose phosphates**, that is, two sugars with three carbon atoms.

In the second half, the cell gets its investment back and more. ATP and NADH are formed. In the last step, **pyruvate kinase** makes ATP from **phosphoenolpyruvate**. If there is enough oxygen, the pyruvate travels into the mitochondria. There it is broken down further, and much more ATP is formed than in glycolysis alone.

In a fast sprint, the muscles sometimes do not get enough oxygen. Then pyruvate is converted into **lactate**. This serves mainly to regenerate **NAD+**. Without NAD+, glycolysis would stop. This way the cell can go on gaining a little energy even without oxygen. **Red blood cells** depend entirely on glycolysis, because they have **no mitochondria**.

The German researcher **Otto Warburg** observed something astonishing in the 1920s. Many **cancer cells** break glucose down increasingly to lactate, even when enough oxygen is present. This observation is called the **Warburg effect**. Because tumours therefore take up a lot of sugar, they can be made visible with certain examinations in which weakly radioactively marked sugar is used.

gewusst: Glycolysis is very old: it occurs in almost all living things, from bacteria to humans.
Yeast also uses glycolysis, and in baking bread, it produces the gas that makes the dough rise.

teile.einleitung: Your **grandparents** are the parents of your mother and your father. Many children in Switzerland spend a lot of time with “Grosi” and “Grossvati”, which are Swiss German words for grandma and grandpa. Grandparents often tell exciting stories from earlier times.
wichtigste: Grandparents are the parents of your parents.
Every person has four grandparents.
The mother of your mother or father is your grandmother, and the father is your grandfather.
In German-speaking Switzerland, many children say “Grosi” and “Grossvati”.
For your grandparents, you are a grandchild.
The parents of your grandparents are your great-grandparents, of whom every person has eight.

abschnitte.text: Every person has a mother and a father. The parents of your mother and the parents of your father are your **grandparents**. The mother of your mother is your **grandmother**, and the father of your father is your **grandfather**. Because you have two parents and each of them again has two parents, every person has **4 grandparents**: two grandmothers and two grandfathers.

In **German-speaking Switzerland**, grandparents have many loving names. For the grandmother, many children say **“Grosi”**, and some also say “Grossmami”. For the grandfather, many say **“Grossvati”** or “Grosspapi”. In French-speaking Switzerland people say “grand-maman” and “grand-papa”, and in Ticino “nonna” and “nonno”. For your grandparents, you are their **grandchild**, that is, their granddaughter or grandson.

A family can be drawn as a **family tree**. At the bottom you stand, above you your parents, then your grandparents. The parents of your grandparents are called **great-grandparents**. Every person has **8** of them, because with every generation the number doubles. One step further up, there are already 16 great-great-grandparents.

Grandparents are usually much older than their grandchildren. You can work out the difference. Example: Grosi is 68 years old and Nora is 8 years old. 68 minus 8 gives **60**. So Grosi is 60 years older than Nora. This difference always stays the same, even when both get older.

Many grandparents in Switzerland regularly look after their grandchildren, for example on a fixed day each week. They play, cook, hike or craft together. Grandparents can tell you what it was like when they were children themselves: without phones, often with fewer toys and with different games. Someone who asks their grandparents about the past learns a lot about their own family.

gewusst: People live longer today than in the past, so many children even still know their great-grandparents.
Ten generations back, every person has, in calculation, 1,024 ancestors in that one generation.

teile.einleitung: The sense of smell is the ability to perceive scents. You smell with your nose, more exactly with a small area high up in the nasal cavity. The sense of smell warns you of dangers and even helps you to taste.
wichtigste: You smell with your nose.
The smell cells lie in the olfactory lining at the top of the nasal cavity.
Humans can tell thousands of different smells apart.
Smells are passed directly to the brain and often awaken memories and feelings.
Without a sense of smell, food tastes bland.
Dogs smell much better than humans.
The sense of smell warns of smoke, gas and spoiled food.

abschnitte.text: Scent substances are tiny particles that float in the air. When you breathe in, they get into the nose as far as the **olfactory lining**. This is about as big as a postage stamp and sits right at the top of the nasal cavity. There, millions of **smell cells** with fine hairs are waiting. When you sniff a flower, more air flows upwards and you smell more strongly.

The smell cells have **receptors** that, like locks, fit only certain scent substances. Humans have around 350 different kinds of such receptors. The signals travel along the olfactory nerve to the **olfactory bulb** in the brain. From there they also run to areas for feelings and memories. That is why the scent of fresh “Zopf”, the Swiss plaited loaf, can suddenly remind you of Sundays at your grandparents'.

The tongue recognises only a few basic tastes such as sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami. The whole **aroma** of a strawberry or a chocolate, however, is recognised by the nose. When you chew, scent substances rise from the mouth to the back of the nose. When you have a cold, many things therefore taste the same. As a test, hold your nose shut and eat a piece of apple.

The sense of smell protects you from dangers. You smell smoke before you see a fire. Spoiled milk or mouldy bread smell unpleasant so that you do not eat them. Natural gas actually has no smell, so a strongly smelling substance is added to it. This way you quickly notice a leak.

A dog has many times as many smell cells as a human. That is why **sniffer dogs** are used, for example avalanche dogs in the Swiss Alps or dogs that track down drugs. Pigs, too, find truffles under the ground with their noses. Salmon find their way back to the place of their birth by the smell of their home river. Insects such as butterflies smell with their antennae.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small area at the top of the nose containing the smell cells.
A sensory cell that recognises scent substances.
The part of the brain that first processes smell signals.
The whole taste impression of a food, mainly through the nose.

gewusst: Smell cells are renewed roughly every few weeks.
Newborn babies recognise their mother already by her smell.
You get used to a smell quickly and after a while hardly notice it any more.

teile.einleitung: Ignaz Semmelweis was a doctor from Hungary who worked in Vienna in the 19th century. He recognised that clean hands save lives. At the time many did not believe him, but today he is seen as a model for hygiene in hospitals.
wichtigste: Ignaz Semmelweis came from what is now Hungary.
He worked in a hospital in Vienna.
In 1847 he introduced hand disinfection for doctors.
The hands were disinfected with a chlorinated lime solution.
The doctors brought the dangerous germs with them from the mortuary.
At that time it was not yet known that bacteria cause diseases.
Many doctors rejected his demands.

abschnitte.text: **Ignaz Semmelweis** was born in 1818 in Buda, which today belongs to **Budapest** in **Hungary**. He studied medicine and from 1846 worked as a doctor at the General Hospital in **Vienna**. There he noticed something puzzling: in one ward, far more women died of a dangerous **fever** than in another ward.

abschnitte.titel: The trail leads to the mortuary
abschnitte.text: Semmelweis looked for the difference between the wards. In the ward with many deaths, doctors and students worked who had earlier examined the dead in the **mortuary**. In 1847 a colleague died after he had cut himself with a knife during such an examination. He showed similar signs of illness. Semmelweis concluded that the doctors were bringing something dangerous from the corpses on their **hands**.

In **1847**, Semmelweis introduced a simple rule: all doctors had to wash their hands in **chlorinated lime solution** before examining patients. Chlorinated lime kills germs. After this, the number of deaths in his ward fell sharply. Semmelweis did not know, however, what exactly passed on the disease. In his time it was not yet known that **bacteria** cause diseases.

Many doctors **rejected** his demands. Some felt insulted because they themselves were seen as the cause of the disease. Others thought his explanation unscientific. Semmelweis later returned to Hungary and worked in Pest. He died in 1865 without his discovery having been generally recognised.

Only some years later did researchers such as **Louis Pasteur** and **Robert Koch** show that tiny living things cause diseases. This proved that Semmelweis was right. Today he is seen as a model for **hygiene in hospitals**, because he showed that clean hands save lives. In every hospital, including in Switzerland, hand disinfection is among the most important rules.

gewusst: The medical university in Budapest today bears the name Semmelweis.
Semmelweis is sometimes called one of the fathers of hospital hygiene.

teile.einleitung: A hearing aid is a small electrical device that makes sounds louder. It helps people who cannot hear well to understand conversations better again. You wear it on or in the ear.
wichtigste: A hearing aid picks up sounds and passes them into the ear more loudly.
A tiny microphone catches the sounds, and a small loudspeaker passes them on.
It needs power from a battery or a rechargeable battery.
Many hearing aids sit behind the ear, others in the ear canal.
You take the hearing aid out for showering.
Hearing aid acousticians fit it to the person.
In the past, people used an ear trumpet.

abschnitte.text: Some people cannot hear well, and are said to be **hard of hearing**. They find it difficult to understand conversations, especially when it is loud. This can be present from birth, be caused by illness or noise, or come on slowly in old age. A **hearing aid** helps them. It picks up sounds and passes them into the ear **more loudly**. In this way people who are hard of hearing can hear better again and join in conversations more easily.

A hearing aid is a small **electrical device**. A tiny **microphone** catches the sounds. A chip inside **amplifies** them and adjusts them to the person’s hearing. They reach the ear through a small **loudspeaker**. For all this the device needs power from a **battery** or a **rechargeable battery**. Because it is an electrical device, it does not put up with much water. So you take it out for **showering** and swimming.

Many hearing aids sit **behind the ear**, and a thin tube or wire leads the sound into the ear canal. Others are so small that they sit completely **inside the ear canal** and can hardly be seen. For a hearing aid to fit well, you need an expert. **Hearing aid acousticians** test the hearing and set the device to suit it. In Switzerland, disability insurance (**IV**) or **AVS** (old-age insurance) contribute to the costs under certain conditions.

Before there were electrical hearing aids, people used an **ear trumpet**. This is a funnel that you hold to your ear. It gathers the sound and leads it into the ear. Later came electrical devices, which at first were big and heavy. Today hearing aids are tiny and some can even connect to a mobile phone. For people who can hear almost nothing, there is also the **cochlear implant**, which is put in by an operation.

gewusst: Loud music through headphones can damage your hearing permanently. So it is worth not setting the volume too high.
Some hearing aids can be connected to a mobile phone so that phone calls come straight into the ear.

teile.einleitung: When the heart beats, it makes sounds. These are called heart sounds. With a stethoscope, doctors can hear them well and so check whether the heart is healthy.
wichtigste: In a healthy heartbeat you normally hear 2 heart sounds.
The heart sounds are made mainly when the heart valves close.
An extra sound heard when listening is called a heart murmur.
After running, the heart sounds follow one another faster.
Heart sounds are quiet, so it has to be silent when listening.
You can also hear them by laying your ear on the chest.

abschnitte.text: You can listen to the heart with a **stethoscope**. You place the round chest piece on the skin and listen through the tubes in your ears. You hear best on bare skin. Through a thick jumper you hear the heart sounds **less well**, because the fabric dampens the sound. Because heart sounds are **quiet**, the room has to be silent.

The heart sounds are made mainly when the **heart valves close**. In a healthy heartbeat you normally hear **two heart sounds**. The first sound is made when the ventricles contract and the valves to the atria shut. The second sound is made when the valves at the exit of the ventricles close. Together it sounds roughly like “lub dub”.

After a fast run, the heart beats faster. Then the **heart sounds follow one another faster**. At rest or when sleeping, the pauses between them are longer. Anyone who counts heart sounds can also work out the heart rate this way.

Sometimes you hear an extra whooshing or hissing sound when listening. This is called a **heart murmur**. It can arise when blood flows through a narrowed or leaking valve. In children, however, quiet heart murmurs are often harmless. The doctor decides whether a closer look is needed.

You can also hear heart sounds **without a stethoscope**. To do so, you lay your **ear on the chest** of another person. This is how doctors used to listen. The stethoscope was invented in France at the start of the 19th century and was at first a simple wooden tube.

gewusst: The inventor of the stethoscope was the French doctor René Laennec.
The word stethoscope comes from Greek and means roughly “looking at the chest”.

teile.einleitung: Cardiac output tells you how much blood the heart pumps in one minute. It is an important value for describing how well the heart is performing. You can work it out with a simple calculation.
wichtigste: Cardiac output is stroke volume times heart rate.
At rest, an adult’s heart pumps about 5 litres a minute.
At 5 litres a minute, that is 7200 litres a day.
In athletes, cardiac output can rise to over 25 litres a minute.
With the Fick principle, it is worked out from oxygen consumption.
The cardiac index is cardiac output per square metre of body surface.

abschnitte.text: **Cardiac output** is the amount of blood that the heart pumps into the body in one minute. It is usually given in **litres per minute**. Two things determine it: the **stroke volume**, that is, how much blood is pushed out with each heartbeat, and the **heart rate**, that is, how often the heart beats in a minute.

The formula is: **cardiac output = stroke volume times heart rate**. An example: a heart has a stroke volume of 80 millilitres and beats 60 times a minute. 80 times 60 makes 4800 millilitres, which is **4.8 litres a minute**. In a healthy adult at rest it is about **5 litres a minute**. That is roughly the whole amount of blood in the body.

When you exert yourself, the muscles need much more oxygen. So stroke volume and heart rate rise. An athlete under load has, for example, a stroke volume of 150 millilitres and a heart rate of 180. That makes 27,000 millilitres, which is **27 litres a minute**. Well-trained hearts have a larger stroke volume.

A day has 24 hours times 60 minutes, which is 1440 minutes. With a cardiac output of 5 litres a minute, the heart pumps 5 times 1440, which is **7200 litres** a day. That is so much that you could fill several bathtubs with it.

In the 19th century, the German physiologist **Adolf Fick** described a method for working out cardiac output. In the **Fick principle**, you divide the oxygen the body takes up by the difference in oxygen content between arteries and veins. Example: 250 millilitres of oxygen a minute divided by 50 millilitres per litre of blood gives **5 litres a minute**. To compare people of different sizes, the **cardiac index** is used: the cardiac output per square metre of body surface.

gewusst: In a long life the heart pumps well over 100 million litres of blood.
At rest, a large share of the blood flows through the kidneys, liver and intestines, but during sport mainly into the muscles.

teile.einleitung: The skin barrier is the outermost protective layer of our body. It keeps water in the body and harmful substances and germs out. Its most important part is the horny layer of the epidermis.
wichtigste: The horny layer, stratum corneum, is the most important barrier against loss of water.
Its structure is described with the brick-and-mortar model.
The barrier lipids consist mainly of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids.
The acid mantle has a pH of about 5.
If the protein filaggrin is missing, the risk of atopic eczema rises.
The epidermis renews itself in about four weeks.
Very frequent washing with soap can weaken the barrier.

abschnitte.text: The topmost layer of the epidermis is called the **horny layer** or **stratum corneum**. It consists of dead, flat and hardened cells. Between them lie fats, the **lipids**. Experts compare this with a wall: the cells are the **bricks**, the lipids the **mortar**. This **brick-and-mortar model** shows why the layer is so dense and lets hardly any water out.

The lipids between the horny cells consist mainly of **ceramides**, **cholesterol** and **free fatty acids**. They arrange themselves in dense layers. The protein **filaggrin** helps to build the horny layer and supplies **natural moisturising factors**. In people with changed filaggrin genes, the barrier is often disturbed. Their skin is dry, and the risk of **atopic eczema** is clearly higher.

The healthy surface of the skin is slightly acidic, roughly in the range **pH 4.5 to 5.5**. This is called the **acid mantle**. It holds back many germs and supports enzymes that build the barrier. Detergents in soaps dissolve skin fats out of the horny layer, and alkaline soaps raise the pH. Someone who washes very often therefore gets dry, irritated skin more easily. Moisturising creams can help.

New skin cells form right at the bottom, in the **basal layer** of the epidermis. They move upwards, lose their cell nucleus and harden into horn. After about **four weeks**, they flake off at the surface. This is how the barrier renews itself all the time. How well it works is measured with the **transepidermal water loss**: it shows how much water evaporates through the skin. If the barrier is damaged, this value rises.

gewusst: In most places, the horny layer is thinner than a sheet of paper and yet protects the whole body.
On the soles of the feet, the horny layer is much thicker than on the eyelids.

teile.einleitung: In heart failure, the heart is too weak to pump enough blood for the body. It is also called a weak heart. It often develops slowly and mainly affects older people.
wichtigste: In heart failure the heart does not pump enough blood for the body’s needs.
Left-sided heart failure leads to shortness of breath because of congestion in the lungs.
Right-sided heart failure often shows itself in swollen legs.
The NYHA classification divides heart failure into 4 stages.
The blood value NT-proBNP helps with the diagnosis.
Diuretics flush water out of the body.
The old heart medicine digitalis comes from the foxglove.

abschnitte.text: In **heart failure**, the heart can no longer pump enough blood through the body. The organs and muscles get too little oxygen. Those affected quickly become tired and are less able to perform. Common causes are **coronary heart disease**, an earlier heart attack or **high blood pressure** over many years.

Depending on which half of the heart is weak, different signs appear. In **left-sided heart failure**, the blood backs up into the lungs. This leads to **shortness of breath**, especially when lying down or when exerting yourself. In **right-sided heart failure**, the blood backs up into the body. Then water collects in the tissue, and the **legs swell**.

The **NYHA classification** divides heart failure into **4 stages**. In the first stage there are no symptoms in everyday life, and in the fourth there are symptoms even at rest. With ultrasound, doctors measure the **ejection fraction**, that is, the share of blood that the left ventricle pushes out with each beat. If it is **40 per cent or less**, this is called heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). The blood value **NT-proBNP** also helps with the diagnosis.

Heart failure is usually treated with several medicines. **Diuretics** flush excess water out of the body. Other medicines take the strain off the heart or lower blood pressure.
