A very old heart medicine is **digitalis**. It comes from the **foxglove**, a poisonous plant that also grows in Switzerland. Sometimes a special pacemaker helps.

People with heart failure should **weigh themselves every day**. If their weight rises quickly within a few days, this can show that water is collecting. Then the treatment must be adjusted. Also important are suitable exercise, little salt and giving up smoking.

gewusst: The healing effect of foxglove on the heart was already described by the English doctor William Withering in the 18th century.
In many countries, heart failure is one of the most common reasons for older people to stay in hospital.

teile.einleitung: The Hippocratic Oath is one of the oldest promises about a doctor’s duties. It is named after the Greek doctor Hippocrates. Many of its ideas are still important in medicine today.
wichtigste: Hippocrates came from the Greek island of Kos.
The oath was originally written in ancient Greek.
The first thing you swear by is the god Apollo.
The duty of confidentiality is already in the Hippocratic Oath.
You should treat your teacher like your own parents.
“Primum non nocere” is often linked with the oath, but it is not in it in that form.
The Declaration of Geneva is regarded today as a modern version.

abschnitte.text: The **Hippocratic Oath** was originally written in **ancient Greek**. It is named after the doctor **Hippocrates**, who came from the island of **Kos** and lived in the 5th century BC. Whether he wrote the oath himself is uncertain. It belongs to a collection of old medical writings, the Hippocratic Corpus.

The oath begins with an oath by the gods. The first one named is **Apollo**, who was also regarded as the god of healing. Next come his son Asclepius and other goddesses of health. At that time, such oaths by the gods were a very serious promise.

One part of the oath is about the relationship to the teacher. The person swearing promises to treat their **teacher like their own parents**. They are to support the teacher if he needs help. They also promise to pass on the knowledge to the teacher’s children and to other students.

The doctor promises to help the sick and not to harm them. He also promises **not to give deadly substances** to anyone, **even if asked**. A duty that is still valid today is the **duty of confidentiality**: what the doctor learns in the course of his work, he is to keep to himself. In Switzerland, medical confidentiality is today also protected by law.

The Latin phrase **“Primum non nocere”** means “first, do no harm”. It is often linked with the oath, but it is not in it in that form. Today doctors mostly no longer swear the old oath. The **Declaration of Geneva** of the World Medical Association from 1948 is regarded as the modern version. Since then it has been revised several times.

gewusst: The Hippocratic Oath is around 2400 years old.
The name Declaration of Geneva comes from the fact that the World Medical Association adopted it in Geneva in 1948.

teile.einleitung: The Human Genome Project aimed to decode the whole genetic information of humans. It began in 1990 and is regarded as one of the biggest undertakings in biology. Its results are now the basis of much research in medicine and biology.
wichtigste: The public project started in 1990, launched mainly by US authorities.
At first James Watson led the US part, and from 1993 Francis Collins.
Craig Venter competed with his company Celera Genomics.
Mainly Sanger sequencing was used.
In 2001 the first drafts appeared in “Nature” and “Science”.
The project cost around 3 billion US dollars.
In 2022 the T2T consortium achieved the first gap-free sequence.

abschnitte.text: In almost every cell of our body there is **DNA**, a long molecule that holds the genetic information. It is written like a text of just four letters, the **bases** A, T, G and C. A person’s entire DNA is called their **genome**. It consists of around three billion such base pairs. Working out the order of these letters is called **sequencing**.

The public **Human Genome Project** was started in **1990**, mainly by US authorities, and soon research centres from several countries joined in. At the start, **James Watson** led the US part, and from 1993 **Francis Collins** took over and led the project to the end. The researcher **Craig Venter** competed with his company **Celera Genomics**. He relied on a fast method called shotgun sequencing. This race speeded up the whole undertaking.

Mainly **Sanger sequencing** was used, named after the chemist **Frederick Sanger**. It is also called the chain-termination method. In the project it was heavily automated, so that machines could work day and night. In 2000 the first draft was announced publicly. In **2001** the results appeared in the journals “Nature” and “Science”. In 2003 the project was declared complete.

The public project cost around **3 billion US dollars**. Today, thanks to new methods, sequencing a genome costs only a tiny fraction of that. The sequence of 2003, however, still had gaps, for example at the **centromeres**, the constrictions of the chromosomes. Only in **2022** did the **Telomere-to-Telomere Consortium** (T2T) close these gaps with new long-read methods. For the first time there was a gap-free human genome.

gewusst: If you printed out the three billion letters of the genome, you would get many hundreds of thick books.
Frederick Sanger received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice.

teile.einleitung: The back of the hand is the outside or upper side of the hand. If you lay your hand flat on the table, you see it on top. Under its thin skin, you can see veins, tendons and knuckles well.
wichtigste: The back of the hand is the outside of the hand; the inside is called the palm.
When the hand lies flat on the table, the back of the hand points up.
The skin there is thin, so the veins shimmer bluish through it.
Under the skin run tendons that stretch the fingers.
In a fist, you see the knuckles as small hills.
In hospital, a needle for a drip is often placed on the back of the hand.
On the back of the hand, many people have fine little hairs.

abschnitte.titel: Top and bottom of the hand
abschnitte.text: The hand has two sides. The inside is called the **palm**, the outside the **back of the hand**. The palm has thick skin with fine lines and no hairs. The back of the hand has thin, soft skin that can be moved easily. That is why you can pull the skin up a little there; on the palm that is hardly possible.

On the back of the hand, you often see bluish lines. These are **veins**, that is, vessels that carry the blood back to the heart. They lie close under the thin skin. That is why doctors and nurses in hospital like to place a needle for a **drip** there. This way, fluid or a medicine can flow straight into the blood.

When you make a fist, small hills stand out on the back of the hand. These are the **knuckles**, the joints between the palm bones and the fingers. When you stretch your fingers, you see fine strands under the skin. These are **tendons**. They connect the muscles in the forearm to the fingers. When the muscles pull, the tendons move the fingers as if on strings.

The skin on the back of the hand feels warmth well. That is why many parents lay the back of the hand on a child's forehead when it seems ill. This way they quickly notice whether the forehead is hot. You can measure a fever exactly only with a **clinical thermometer**, though. On the back of the hand, many people also have fine **little hairs** growing from small hair roots.

gewusst: The tendons that you see on the back of the hand belong to muscles that sit far away in the forearm.
With the knuckles of a fist, you can remember which months have 31 days: every knuckle is a long month.

teile.einleitung: Hepatitis B is an inflammation of the liver caused by the hepatitis B virus. The infection can heal by itself or last for good. A vaccination protects very well against it.
wichtigste: The hepatitis B virus is a DNA virus of the family Hepadnaviridae.
It is passed on through blood, among other ways, for example through shared syringes.
The vaccine contains the surface antigen HBsAg.
Anti-HBs antibodies show protection after vaccination.
Anti-HBc antibodies show an infection that has been had or is still present.
The infection is chronic if HBsAg can be detected for longer than six months.
Chronic hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis of the liver and liver cancer.

abschnitte.text: The **hepatitis B virus** belongs to the family **Hepadnaviridae**. It has a partly double-stranded **DNA genome**. When it multiplies, it makes a detour through an RNA intermediate stage, which it then copies back into DNA. This is called **reverse transcription**. The virus is present in the blood in large amounts and is very infectious. Even the tiniest amounts of blood on needles, for example with shared syringes, can cause an infection.

In the blood, doctors look for parts of the virus and for **antibodies**. **HBsAg** is the surface antigen of the virus coat. If it is present, the virus is in the body. **Anti-HBs antibodies** are directed against it and show **protection from vaccination** after an injection. A value above 100 IU/l counts as reliable protection. **Anti-HBc antibodies** are directed against the core of the virus. Because the core is missing from the vaccine, they show a real infection, either past or present.

If HBsAg stays in the blood **for longer than six months**, this is called **chronic hepatitis B**. In adults this rarely happens, but in babies it happens very often. The constant inflammation can leave scars on the liver, which is called **cirrhosis of the liver**. The risk of liver cancer, the **hepatocellular carcinoma**, also rises sharply. Treatment is often with **nucleos(t)ide analogues** such as **tenofovir**. They greatly reduce the amount of virus and are usually taken for a long time.

The vaccine contains **genetically engineered HBsAg**, that is, only a piece of the virus coat. The body makes protective antibodies against it without becoming ill. In Switzerland, the **Federal Office of Public Health** recommends the vaccination for babies and for teenagers who have not yet been vaccinated. Anyone who is vaccinated against hepatitis B is also protected from hepatitis D.

gewusst: The hepatitis B vaccine was one of the first vaccines to be made by genetic engineering.
The hepatitis B vaccination also protects indirectly against liver cancer, because it prevents a chronic infection.

teile.einleitung: Hepatitis C is an inflammation of the liver caused by the hepatitis C virus. It often runs for years almost without symptoms and frequently becomes chronic. With modern medicines it can now be cured in almost everyone affected.
wichtigste: The hepatitis C virus is an RNA virus of the family Flaviviridae.
It is passed on almost only through blood, for example when syringes are shared.
Without treatment, the infection becomes chronic in a large share of cases.
There is no approved vaccination (as of 2025).
Direct-acting antiviral medicines cure over 95 per cent of those treated.
Sofosbuvir blocks the viral RNA polymerase NS5B.
In 2020 Harvey Alter, Michael Houghton and Charles Rice received the Nobel Prize.

abschnitte.text: The **hepatitis C virus** has a single-stranded **RNA genome**. It belongs to the family **Flaviviridae**, as does the yellow fever virus. The virus changes very easily when it multiplies. This great **variability** is one reason why there is still no approved vaccination (as of 2025). Protection comes mainly from avoiding contact with blood and from treating infected people.

Hepatitis C is passed on almost only through **blood**. In Switzerland today this mainly concerns the sharing of **syringes and needles** when taking drugs. In the past you could also catch it through blood transfusions, but today donated blood is tested carefully. In most infected people the virus stays in the body for good, and the infection becomes **chronic**. Often you notice almost nothing for years while the liver slowly suffers damage.

In the past, treatment was with **interferon**, which often had little effect and many side effects. Today there are **direct-acting antiviral medicines**, or **DAAs** for short. They block proteins of the virus in a targeted way. One example is **sofosbuvir**. It is built into the growing RNA and stops the **RNA polymerase NS5B**. Treatment usually lasts 8 to 12 weeks. In over 95 per cent of those treated, the virus is removed for good.

For a long time doctors knew of a mysterious inflammation of the liver that was neither hepatitis A nor B. It was called **non-A, non-B hepatitis**. **Harvey Alter**, **Michael Houghton** and **Charles Rice** worked out which virus was behind it. In 1989 the hepatitis C virus was described. This made blood tests and new medicines possible. For their work, the three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2020.

gewusst: Hepatitis C is one of the few chronic viral infections that can be cured completely with tablets.
The World Health Organization has set itself the goal of greatly reducing hepatitis C as a threat to public health by 2030.

teile.einleitung: Hunger is a feeling with which the body tells us that it needs more supplies. Food gives us energy for playing, learning and growing. In Switzerland there are even special names for small meals.
wichtigste: The body needs food mainly for energy.
The brain makes us feel hunger, and the stomach and blood send it signals.
When you are very hungry, it is hard to concentrate.
The first meal is called breakfast, in Swiss German Zmorge.
The Znüni is eaten in the morning, the Zvieri in the afternoon.
Wholemeal bread with cheese keeps you full for longer than sweets.

abschnitte.text: Our body works all the time, even in sleep. The heart beats, we breathe, and the brain thinks. For this it needs **energy**, and it gets it from food. Children also need building blocks for **growing**. When energy runs short, we feel **hungry**. When we have eaten enough, we feel **full**, and then it is best to stop eating.

You often feel hunger in your tummy, for example when your stomach rumbles. But the feeling is controlled by the **brain**. The stomach and the blood send it **signals**, for example when the stomach is empty or there is little sugar in the blood. The brain then makes us feel hungry. With an empty tummy, the brain lacks energy: you find it harder to **concentrate** and get into a bad mood more quickly.

The first meal in the morning is **breakfast**, and in Switzerland people also say **Zmorge**. In the morning, at about nine o’clock, there is the **Znüni**, for example an apple or a piece of bread. In the afternoon, at about four o’clock, you eat the **Zvieri**. The name comes from “zu vier Uhr”, which means “at four o’clock”. Then there are lunch, the Zmittag, and the evening meal, the Znacht.

abschnitte.titel: What keeps you full for a long time
abschnitte.text: Not every food lasts equally long. **Wholemeal bread** and **cheese** give the body energy for a long time, because they are digested slowly. Fruit, vegetables and nuts are also good snacks. **Sweets** fill you up only briefly: the sugar goes quickly into the blood, and afterwards the hunger soon comes back. Anyone who eats regularly and drinks enough usually does not get sudden ravenous hunger.

gewusst: Sometimes the body mixes up thirst with hunger. A glass of water can then be enough to help.
A rumbling stomach happens when the stomach moves and pushes air and fluid back and forth inside it.

teile.einleitung: The cochlea is a tiny, snail-shaped organ deep in the ear. In it, sound waves are turned into nerve signals that the brain understands as sounds, voices and music.
wichtigste: The cochlea, the snail-shaped organ of hearing (German **Hörschnecke**), lies in the inner ear.
It is well protected in the petrous bone, a very hard part of the temporal bone.
The cochlea is filled with fluid.
Hair cells turn vibrations into nerve signals.
The human cochlea has about two and a half turns.
High notes are picked up at the start, low notes at the tip.
In humans, destroyed hair cells do not grow back.

abschnitte.text: The cochlea lies in the **inner ear**, well protected in the **petrous bone**. The petrous bone is part of the temporal bone and is among the hardest bones in the body. The cochlea is coiled about two and a half times around a bony axis. That is why it looks like a small snail shell. Its technical name **cochlea** comes from Latin and also means snail.

The channels of the cochlea are filled with fluids, the **perilymph** and the **endolymph**. Sound first makes the eardrum vibrate. The ear bones, the hammer, anvil and **stirrup**, pass the vibration on. The stirrup presses on the **oval window**, an opening to the cochlea. In this way the fluid inside is set in motion.

The actual organ of hearing is called the **organ of Corti**. It lies on the **basilar membrane**, a thin skin that runs through the cochlea. On the organ of Corti sit inner and outer **hair cells** with fine hairs. When the hairs are bent by the vibration, the cells send signals along the **auditory nerve** to the brain. At the start, the basilar membrane is narrow and stiff, and high notes are detected there. Low notes act further in, at the tip of the snail.

The hair cells are very sensitive. Strong noise, for example very loud music through headphones or a bang, can damage them permanently. In humans, destroyed hair cells do not form again, and the hearing loss then stays. That is why **hearing protection** is important, for example at concerts or with loud machines.

In very severe hearing loss, a **cochlear implant** can help. A thin electrode is pushed into the cochlea. It stimulates the auditory nerve directly with electrical signals and so takes over the work of the hair cells. Part of the device is worn behind the ear and picks up the sounds. With practice, many people can understand speech with it.

gewusst: A young, healthy person hears sounds of about 20 to 20,000 vibrations per second.
In each cochlea, a person has only a few thousand inner hair cells that send the signals to the brain.

teile.einleitung: The endocrine system, or hormone system, is a network of glands that release hormones directly into the blood. It controls slow but long-lasting processes such as growth, metabolism and puberty. Together with the nervous system, it is the body’s most important control centre.
wichtigste: Glands that release their hormones directly into the blood are called endocrine glands.
The pituitary gland is connected to the hypothalamus and controls many other hormone glands.
In negative feedback, a high hormone level slows down further release.
The thyroid gland needs iodine, which is why it has been added to table salt in Switzerland since 1922.
The islets of Langerhans with the insulin-making cells lie in the pancreas.
The thymus behind the breastbone is important mainly in childhood for the maturing of T lymphocytes.
Other hormone glands are the adrenal glands, the pineal gland, the ovaries and the testes.

abschnitte.text: At the very top of the control system is the **hypothalamus**, a part of the diencephalon. It is closely connected to the **pituitary gland**. This gland is only about as big as a pea, but has great influence. The pituitary gland makes controlling hormones that stimulate other glands such as the thyroid gland, the adrenal glands and the sex glands. It also makes the growth hormone.

The endocrine system works with **control loops**. One example: the pituitary gland stimulates the thyroid gland to make hormones. If the level of thyroid hormones in the blood rises, this slows down the pituitary gland. A high hormone level therefore slows down further release, which is called **negative feedback**. In this way the amount of hormones stays in the right range.

The **thyroid gland** lies at the front of the neck below the larynx and is shaped like a butterfly. Its hormones regulate metabolism and are important for growth and brain development. For this it needs **iodine**. In Switzerland, the soil and water were poor in iodine, and many people had a goitre, an enlarged thyroid gland. Since 1922, iodine has been added to table salt, first in the canton of Appenzell Outer Rhodes, and goitre has been rare ever since.

In the **pancreas** lie the **islets of Langerhans**, which make insulin and glucagon. The adrenal glands on top of the kidneys make adrenaline and cortisol. The **thymus** lies behind the breastbone and is largest in childhood. There the T lymphocytes, part of the immune defences, learn to tell the body’s own substances from foreign ones. The ovaries and testes make the sex hormones.

The **nervous system** sends signals in a flash along nerve pathways, like a phone call. The endocrine system is slower and works more like a letter delivered through the blood. In return, its effects often last longer, for hours, days or years. Both systems work closely together, especially in the hypothalamus. Diseases of the endocrine system, such as diabetes or thyroid disorders, are treated by specialist doctors in **endocrinology**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gland that releases hormones directly into the blood.
A pea-sized gland at the base of the brain that controls many other glands.
A butterfly-shaped gland in the neck that regulates metabolism.
An enlarged thyroid gland, often because of a lack of iodine.

gewusst: The islets of Langerhans are named after the German doctor Paul Langerhans, who described them in 1869 as a student.
The Bernese surgeon Theodor Kocher received the Nobel Prize in 1909 for his research on the thyroid gland.
After puberty, the thymus is gradually replaced by fatty tissue.

teile.einleitung: Hippocrates of Kos was a Greek doctor of ancient times. He is regarded as the “father of medicine”. He and his students wanted to understand illnesses by careful observation, and no longer explain them only by magic or the will of the gods.
wichtigste: Hippocrates is regarded as the “father of medicine”.
He lived roughly in the 5th century BC on the island of Kos.
For him it was important to observe the patient carefully.
For a long time, medicine explained illnesses by an imbalance of the body fluids.
His writings are collected in the Hippocratic Corpus.
The Hippocratic Oath is named after him.
The Declaration of Geneva of 1948 is a modern version of the doctor’s oath.

abschnitte.text: **Hippocrates** came from the Greek island of **Kos** and lived roughly in the **5th century BC**. Only little is known for certain about his life. He was a well-known doctor and teacher. Many students learned from him. Even in ancient times he was seen as a great doctor, and to this day he is called the **“father of medicine”**.

For Hippocrates it was especially important to **observe the patient carefully**. He and his school paid attention to appearance, breathing, fever and the course of an illness. They looked for natural causes of illnesses. This was new, because before that illnesses were often seen as a punishment from the gods.

abschnitte.titel: The theory of the body fluids
abschnitte.text: Since Hippocrates, medicine long explained illnesses with the **body fluids**. People believed that the body contained four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. If they were in balance, the person was healthy. An **imbalance** made you ill. This **humoral theory** shaped medicine in Europe until the 19th century. Today we know it is wrong.

Hippocratic medicine often relied first on a healthy way of life. What was recommended was **moderate eating, rest and exercise**, along with fresh air and baths. The body was to be able to heal itself as far as possible. Only when that did not help did people turn to medicines or operations.

The writings of Hippocrates and his school are collected in the **Hippocratic Corpus**. It contains around 60 texts. Many of them probably do not come from him himself but from other doctors of his time. The **Hippocratic Oath**, a promise about a doctor’s duties, is named after him. A modern version is the **Declaration of Geneva**, which the World Medical Association adopted in **1948**.

gewusst: On Kos, visitors are shown an old plane tree under which Hippocrates is said to have taught, but this is a legend.
Words such as “chronic” and “acute” go back to the language of the Greek doctors.

teile.einleitung: Hair does not grow without stopping but in a cycle of growth, transition and rest. Each hair has its own rhythm, which is why all the hairs never fall out at the same time.
wichtigste: A hair goes through three phases: growth, transition and rest.
The growth phase is called the anagen phase.
For head hair it lasts about 2 to 6 years.
The short transition phase is called the catagen phase.
About 85 to 90 per cent of head hairs are growing at the same time.
Eyelashes and eyebrows have a much shorter growth phase.
A head hair grows about 1 cm a month.

abschnitte.text: Every hair goes through a **cycle** with three phases again and again. In the **anagen phase**, it grows actively. In the short **catagen phase**, it stops growing. In the **telogen phase**, it rests until it falls out and a new hair grows in its place. Each hair has its own rhythm. About **85 to 90 per cent** of head hairs are in the growth phase at the same time.

For head hairs, the **anagen phase** lasts longest, usually between **2 and 6 years**. During this time, the hair grows without a break, about one centimetre a month. That is why head hairs can become very long. **Eyelashes** and **eyebrows**, on the other hand, grow for only a few months, then fall out and are replaced. That is why they stay short.

The **catagen phase** lasts only about two to three weeks. In it, the hair detaches from its supply, the root shrinks back, and the hair moves up a little. After that comes the resting phase. The hair now sits only loosely in the skin. In the end it falls out, for example when brushing or washing.

You can do sums quite well with hair growth. If a hair grows **1 cm a month**, after 3 years, that is 36 months, it is **36 cm** long. If Lena's hair is 20 cm long and grows 1.2 cm a month, 12 cm are added in 10 months: it is then **32 cm** long. If 100,000 hairs each grow 0.3 mm a day, that makes 30,000 mm together, which is **30 metres** of hair a day.

gewusst: All the head hairs together grow in one day about as much as the length of a swimming pool.
Because each hair has its own rhythm, you do not suddenly go bald despite hair loss.

teile.einleitung: Cardiovascular diseases are diseases of the heart and blood vessels, for example heart attack, stroke and high blood pressure. In Switzerland they are the most common cause of death. Many of them can be prevented by a healthy lifestyle.
wichtigste: Cardiovascular diseases are the most common cause of death in Switzerland (as of 2022).
Arteriosclerosis is the narrowing of arteries by deposits in the vessel wall.
In a heart attack, heart muscle tissue dies because a coronary artery is blocked.
The most common cause of a stroke is the blocking of an artery in the brain.
High blood pressure means a reading of 140/90 mmHg or more when measured at the doctor’s.
Smoking is a risk factor that you can influence through your own behaviour.
Exercise, healthy eating and not smoking lower the risk clearly.

abschnitte.text: Cardiovascular diseases include all diseases of the heart and blood vessels. The most important are **coronary heart disease** with heart attack, stroke, high blood pressure and heart failure. Heart rhythm disorders and blocked vessels in the legs also belong here. They usually appear only in later life. But the foundations for them are often laid much earlier in life.

In **arteriosclerosis**, fat, calcium and inflammatory cells build up in the walls of the arteries. The vessels become narrower and stiffer, like a water pipe that gets furred up with limescale. The blood can no longer flow well. If a deposit tears open, a blood clot can form that blocks the vessel completely. Arteriosclerosis is the main cause of heart attack and stroke.

The **coronary arteries** supply the heart muscle itself with blood. If one is blocked, part of the heart muscle dies, and this is a **heart attack**. Typical signs are severe pain in the chest that can spread into the arm, shortness of breath and fear. In a **stroke**, usually an artery in the brain is blocked, more rarely a vessel bursts. Sudden paralysis of one side of the body or speech problems are warning signs, and then you must call the emergency number 144 at once.

Blood pressure is measured in millimetres of mercury, or mmHg for short. According to the WHO and European guidelines, a reading of 140/90 mmHg or more at the doctor’s is called **high blood pressure**. It does not hurt for a long time, and so it often goes unnoticed. In the long run, however, it damages the blood vessels, heart, kidneys and brain. That is why it is worth it for adults to have their blood pressure measured regularly.

Some risk factors, such as age and heredity, cannot be changed. But many others can: **smoking**, lack of exercise, being overweight, too much salt, high blood fat levels and diabetes. Anyone who does not smoke, exercises regularly and eats a balanced diet greatly lowers their risk. The Swiss Heart Foundation gives information about prevention and first aid. Children, too, can learn how to get help in an emergency and how to give chest compressions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A narrowing and hardening of the arteries caused by deposits.
The vessels that supply the heart muscle itself with blood.
A sudden disturbance of the blood supply in the brain.
Something that raises the likelihood of a disease.

gewusst: According to the WHO, cardiovascular diseases are the most common cause of death worldwide.
In women, a heart attack often shows itself with different symptoms than in men, such as nausea or back pain.
In Switzerland there are volunteer first responders who can be called by an app to a cardiac arrest near them.

teile.einleitung: Heart valves are like small valves in the heart. They make sure that the blood flows in only one direction. The human heart has four of them.
wichtigste: The human heart has four heart valves.
The mitral valve lies between the left atrium and the left ventricle.
The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and the right ventricle.
The pulmonary valve leads to the pulmonary artery, the aortic valve to the aorta.
Tendon threads stop the leaflet valves from flipping over.
A narrowed valve is called stenosis, a leaking one insufficiency.

abschnitte.text: The heart has **four heart valves**. Each opens in only one direction. When it snaps shut, the blood cannot flow back. By the way, the closing of the valves can be heard as the **heart sounds** when you listen to the heart with a stethoscope.

Between the atria and the ventricles there are two **leaflet valves**. They are called that because their thin parts look like sails. On the left is the **mitral valve**, on the right the **tricuspid valve**. Fine **tendon threads** hold the leaflets in place. They stop the valves from flipping into the atria when the ventricles contract, a little like cords holding an umbrella.

At the exit of the ventricles there are two **pocket valves**. They are made of small, half-moon-shaped pockets. The **pulmonary valve** sits between the right ventricle and the **pulmonary artery**. The **aortic valve** lies at the exit of the left ventricle, where the aorta begins. When the pockets fill with blood, they close tightly.

A heart valve can become diseased in two ways. If it no longer opens wide enough, this is called **valve stenosis**, that is, a narrowing. If it no longer closes properly and leaks, this is called **valve insufficiency**. In both cases the heart has to work harder. Doctors often recognise this from a **heart murmur** and with ultrasound.

If a valve is badly damaged, it can be replaced. There are **mechanical valves** made of metal and plastic. They last a very long time, but afterwards you have to take medicines against blood clots. **Biological valves** are made of tissue from a **pig or cow**. Some replacement valves are now put in through a thin tube along a blood vessel, without opening the chest.

gewusst: The mitral valve gets its name because it reminds people of the mitre, a bishop’s headgear.
Tricuspid means “with three points”, because this valve has three leaflets.

teile.einleitung: Henry Dunant was a businessman from Geneva who had the idea of the Red Cross. After a terrible battle in Italy, he campaigned for help for the wounded. In 1901 he was one of the first people to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
wichtigste: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva on 8 May 1828.
In 1859 he witnessed the Battle of Solferino in Italy.
In 1862 his book “A Memory of Solferino” was published.
His idea led to the founding of the Red Cross in Geneva.
In 1864 the first Geneva Convention was signed in Geneva.
In 1901 he received the first Nobel Peace Prize together with Frédéric Passy.
His birthday, 8 May, is World Red Cross Day.

abschnitte.text: **Henry Dunant** was born in **Geneva** on **8 May 1828**. His family was committed to helping poor and sick people. As a young man he became a businessman. In 1859 he travelled to northern Italy to meet the French emperor Napoleon III about a business matter. There he found himself close to a great battle.

At **Solferino** in 1859, great armies fought against each other. Afterwards thousands of wounded men were left lying without help. Dunant was shocked. In the nearby village of **Castiglione** he organised their care with women from the area. They helped all the wounded, no matter which side they had fought on. Their motto was “Tutti fratelli”, which means “all are brothers”.

In 1862 Dunant wrote the book **“A Memory of Solferino”**. In it he described the suffering of the wounded. He proposed founding **neutral relief societies** for war casualties in all countries. In 1863 a committee was formed in Geneva, which became the **International Committee of the Red Cross**. At his suggestion, twelve states signed the first **Geneva Convention** in 1864. It protects the wounded and medical staff in war.

Later Dunant went bankrupt with his businesses and left Geneva. He lived for a long time in poverty and seclusion, finally in the hospital at **Heiden** in the canton of Appenzell Outer Rhodes. A journalist made him well known again. In 1901 Dunant received the first **Nobel Peace Prize**, together with the Frenchman **Frédéric Passy**. He died in Heiden in 1910. His birthday, 8 May, is now **World Red Cross Day**.

gewusst: The emblem of the Red Cross is the Swiss flag with its colours reversed, as an honour to Switzerland.
In Heiden there is now a museum that commemorates Henry Dunant.

teile.einleitung: Haematopoiesis is the technical word for the making of blood. Every day our body makes billions of new blood cells. In adults, this happens mainly in the red bone marrow.
wichtigste: In adults, blood is made mainly in the red bone marrow.
Flat bones such as the pelvis, breastbone and vertebrae are important.
Blood stem cells give rise to a myeloid and a lymphoid line.
The lymphocytes come from the lymphoid line.
Vitamin B12 and folic acid are needed to make blood.
G-CSF promotes neutrophil granulocytes, thrombopoietin the platelets.
In the long bones, the red marrow turns into fatty marrow during childhood.

abschnitte.text: Blood cells do not live for ever. Red blood cells, for example, last only about four months. That is why the body has to keep making new ones. This is called **haematopoiesis**. In adults it happens mainly in the **red bone marrow**, especially in flat bones such as the **pelvis**, **breastbone** and **vertebrae**. In newborns, almost all the bone marrow is red. During childhood, the marrow in the shafts of the long **bones** is for the most part replaced by yellow **fatty marrow**.

All blood cells descend from **blood stem cells**. They can divide and take different paths as they do so. The **myeloid line** leads to red blood cells, platelets and many white blood cells such as the **granulocytes**. From the **lymphoid line** come the **lymphocytes**, that is, B cells, T cells and NK cells. They are important defence cells. In the laboratory, blood stem cells can often be recognised by the surface marker **CD34**.

The body controls exactly how many cells of each kind are made. For this there are messenger substances. **Erythropoietin** from the kidney stimulates the red blood cells. **Thrombopoietin**, which is made mainly in the liver, stimulates the **megakaryocytes**, from which the platelets arise. The growth factor **G-CSF** promotes the making of **neutrophil granulocytes**. In addition, the bone marrow needs **vitamin B12** and **folic acid** so that the cells can divide properly. If they are missing, an anaemia with oversized red blood cells results.

Knowledge about blood making helps many sick people. After **chemotherapy**, the bone marrow often makes too few defence cells. Then **G-CSF** can be injected so that new neutrophils are made faster. In some blood diseases, **blood stem cells** are transferred. For this, stem cells are collected and counted and enriched using the marker CD34. In Switzerland, you can register as a stem cell donor with **Blood Donation SRK Switzerland** (the Swiss Red Cross blood service).

gewusst: The bone marrow of an adult makes millions of new red blood cells every second.
Haematopoiesis comes from Greek: haima means “blood”, poiein means “to make”.

teile.einleitung: The carpus is the part of the hand that borders directly on the forearm. It consists of eight small bones lying in two rows. Together they make the wrist mobile and strong.
wichtigste: The carpus consists of eight carpal bones in two rows.
Without sesamoid bones, a hand has 27 bones: 8 carpal, 5 metacarpal and 14 finger bones.
The capitate is the largest carpal bone.
The scaphoid breaks most often, often in a fall onto the outstretched hand.
The thumb forms a saddle joint with the trapezium.
Through the carpal tunnel run a nerve and the flexor tendons of the fingers.

abschnitte.text: The carpus lies between the forearm and the palm bones. It consists of eight bones in two rows. In the first row, close to the forearm, lie the **scaphoid**, **lunate**, **triquetrum** and **pisiform**. In the second row lie the **trapezium**, **trapezoid**, **capitate** and **hamate**. Together with 5 metacarpal bones and 14 finger bones, a hand has 27 bones.

Many carpal bones are named after their shape. The **lunate** looks like a half-moon. The **pisiform** is small and round like a pea; you can feel it on the little-finger side of the heel of the hand. The **hamate** has a curved projection towards the palm. The **capitate** in the middle is the largest carpal bone and carries the metacarpal bone of the middle finger.

The metacarpal bone of the thumb sits on the **trapezium**. The joint between them is called a **saddle joint**, because the surfaces are shaped like a riding saddle. It allows the thumb to be brought opposite the other fingers. This is how we can grasp, hold a pen or do up a button.

In a fall onto the outstretched hand, the **scaphoid** on the thumb side often breaks. Because its blood supply is poor, it sometimes heals slowly. The carpal bones also form a channel, which a tight band closes into the **carpal tunnel**. In it run the **median nerve** and the flexor tendons of the fingers. If it gets too tight there, fingers can tingle or go numb.

In small children, the carpal bones are still largely made of cartilage. They harden into bone bit by bit in a known order. On an **X-ray** of the hand, doctors can therefore see how far a child has grown. This is called **bone age**. It can differ a little from the real age.

gewusst: A well-known German rhyme helps with learning the names: “A boat sailed in the moonlight, in a triangle round the pea bone; big polygon and small polygon, at the head there must be a hook.”
Both hands together have 54 bones, which is about a quarter of all the bones in the body.

teile.einleitung: The hammer is one of the three tiny ear bones in the middle ear. It is joined to the eardrum and passes on its vibrations. It gets its name from its shape.
wichtigste: The hammer is called malleus in Latin.
It is joined to the eardrum.
It consists of a head, a neck and a handle.
It is connected to the anvil by a small joint.
The tensor tympani muscle attaches to the hammer.
The hammer is the longest of the three ear bones.

abschnitte.text: In the **middle ear** lie three tiny bones: **hammer**, **anvil** and **stirrup**. All three are named after their shape. The hammer is like a small hammer. In technical language it is called the **malleus**, the Latin word for hammer. It is around 8 to 9 millimetres long and therefore the **longest** of the three ear bones. The stirrup is the shortest.

The hammer consists of three parts: the **head of the hammer**, the neck and the **handle of the hammer**. The roundish head lies at the top in the **tympanic cavity**, the air-filled space of the middle ear. The handle is firmly joined to the **eardrum**. The eardrum is thin and slightly see-through. That is why a doctor can recognise the handle on it as a light streak with an ear speculum.

When sound hits the eardrum, it vibrates. Because the hammer has grown fast to it, it moves along. Between the hammer and the **anvil** lies a tiny **joint**. Through it, the hammer passes the vibration on to the anvil, and this passes it to the stirrup. The stirrup finally leads it into the inner ear, where the sensory cells sit.

A small muscle attaches to the handle of the hammer, the **tensor tympani**. In Latin it is called musculus tensor tympani. When it pulls on the handle, the eardrum is **tightened**. This way, the ear can dampen the vibrations a little. There is also such a tiny muscle on the stirrup.

gewusst: The three ear bones are the smallest bones in the human body.
A hammer in the ear is shorter than a centimetre.

teile.einleitung: Hard skin is thick, tough skin that forms in places with a lot of pressure and rubbing. You find it mainly on the soles of the feet, on the heels and on the hands. Most of the time it is a perfectly natural protection.
wichtigste: Hard skin forms where the skin is often pressed and rubbed.
It is made up of many layers of dead skin cells.
Hard skin feels tough and rough, and you feel less there.
On the hands, hard patches are called calluses.
Tight shoes can cause a corn.
Moisturising keeps hard skin soft, and a pumice stone gently rubs it away.
Hard skin that is too thick and dry on the heel can crack painfully.

abschnitte.text: The top layer of our skin is made of cells that gradually die and become horny. If a spot is often pressed or rubbed, the skin makes more of these cells there. This produces a thick, firm layer: **hard skin**. It protects the sensitive skin underneath, like a built-in cushion. Anyone who often walks barefoot therefore usually has more hard skin on their feet.

Hard skin can also form on the hands if you often grip hard. Such hard patches are called **calluses**. They arise, for example, when rowing, climbing, doing gymnastics on the high bar or working with tools. Guitar players often get hard skin on their fingertips. Because hard skin is made of cells that are no longer alive, you feel less there.

If a shoe presses on the same spot for a long time, a **corn** can form. This is a small, hard thickening of hard skin, often on a toe. In the middle it has a hard core that presses inwards and can hurt. Well-fitting shoes help to stop it forming in the first place. If it hurts, a foot care specialist can help, called a **podiatrist** (in Switzerland a Podologin or Podologe).

Hard skin is mostly not dangerous but a natural protection. If it becomes very thick and dry, however, it is no longer flexible. Then **painful cracks** can form on the heel. A **foot cream** gives the skin moisture and oil and keeps the hard skin soft. With a **pumice stone**, a light, rough stone, you can gently rub away thick hard skin after a bath. But you should never rub it all away, because a little hard skin is useful.

gewusst: Pumice stone is made from the lava of a volcano and is so full of air holes that it often floats on water.
The skin is constantly renewing itself: every day countless tiny flakes of skin fall off without us noticing.

teile.einleitung: A hip replacement is an artificial hip joint. It replaces a badly worn or injured joint and helps many people to walk without pain again. Because it sits inside the body, it is also called an endoprosthesis.
wichtigste: A total hip replacement replaces the hip socket and the head of the thigh bone.
The most common reason is advanced osteoarthritis of the hip.
Many prosthesis stems are made of a titanium alloy.
The head and the sliding surfaces are often made of ceramic or plastic.
The prosthesis is fixed in place with bone cement or without cement.
The Englishman John Charnley developed a successful hip replacement in the 1960s.
Modern prostheses often last 20 years or longer.

abschnitte.text: A **total hip replacement** replaces both parts of the hip joint: the **hip socket** in the pelvis and the **head of the thigh bone**. The artificial head sits on a **stem** that is fixed in the thigh bone. The prefix **“endo”** in the word endoprosthesis comes from Greek and means **inside**. So the prosthesis stays in the body, unlike, for example, an artificial leg, which you can take off.

The most common reason is advanced **osteoarthritis** of the hip. Here the protective cartilage is worn away, and the bones rub against each other. This hurts when walking and often even at rest. A prosthesis is also often put in after a break of the neck of the thigh bone, which happens in older people after falls.

Many prosthesis stems are made of a **titanium alloy**. Titanium is light, stable and well tolerated by the body. The artificial femoral head and the sliding surface of the socket are often made of **ceramic** or of a very hard **plastic**. These materials slide well against each other and wear down only a little.

There are two ways to fix a prosthesis in the bone. In one, it is glued in with **bone cement**, a kind of plastic that quickly sets hard. In the other, it is pressed firmly in without cement, and over time the bone **grows** onto the rough surface. Which kind is chosen depends, for example, on age and bone quality. In many cases, modern prostheses last **20 years or longer**.

The English surgeon **John Charnley** developed a hip replacement in the 1960s that proved its worth. He is regarded as a pioneer of modern hip replacement. Today the operation is a routine procedure. Especially in the first weeks afterwards, however, the prosthesis can **dislocate**, which means the head jumps out of the socket. That is why people who have had the operation must avoid certain movements at first.

gewusst: Many people can already take a few steps again with help on the day after the operation.
Hip replacements are now made in a great many sizes so that they fit exactly.

teile.einleitung: Fats consist largely of **fatty acids**. A special group are the **saturated fatty acids**. They are found mainly in animal fats, in coconut fat and in palm oil, and they tend to make fats solid.
wichtigste: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon double bond.
Their general molecular formula is CnH2nO2.
Important examples are palmitic acid (16 carbon atoms) and stearic acid (18 carbon atoms).
Coconut fat contains an especially large amount of saturated fatty acids.
Fats with many saturated fatty acids are usually solid at room temperature.
A lot of saturated fatty acids raises the LDL cholesterol in the blood.

abschnitte.text: A **fatty acid** is a chain of carbon atoms with an acid group at the end. In a **saturated fatty acid**, all the carbon atoms are joined only by **single bonds**. There is no double bond. Every carbon atom carries as many hydrogen atoms as possible, so it is “saturated”. The general molecular formula is **CnH2nO2**. Unsaturated fatty acids, by contrast, have one or more double bonds.

**Palmitic acid** has 16 carbon atoms. It is common in palm oil and in many animal fats. **Stearic acid** has 18 carbon atoms and occurs plentifully in **beef tallow** and **cocoa butter**. **Coconut fat** has an especially high share of saturated fatty acids, mainly lauric acid. Butter, cream, cheese and sausage also contain many saturated fatty acids.

Butter is solid in the fridge, while olive oil stays liquid. This is down to the fatty acids. The chains of saturated fatty acids are **straight**. That is why they can **pack closely together**, rather like pencils in a box. Fats with many saturated fatty acids are therefore usually solid at room temperature. Double bonds put kinks in the chains, so they fit together less well and the fat stays liquid.

The body needs fat as a source of energy and as a building material. It can also make saturated fatty acids itself. If you take in a great many of them, according to current knowledge the **LDL cholesterol** in the blood in particular rises. A high LDL level is seen as a risk for heart and circulatory diseases. Nutrition research therefore recommends replacing part of the saturated fatty acids with **unsaturated fatty acids**, for example from rapeseed oil, nuts or fish.

Saturated fatty acids are not forbidden. It depends on the amount. The Swiss food pyramid recommends using some plant oil such as rapeseed oil every day and using butter or cream rather sparingly. Someone who eats a varied diet, with lots of vegetables, fruit and wholegrain products, automatically gets a good mix of fats.

gewusst: Coconut fat is from a plant, but it contains more saturated fatty acids than butter.
Palmitic acid gets its name from the palm, because it was discovered in palm oil.

teile.einleitung: The hippocampus is a small part of the brain that is very important for memory. It helps us to form new memories and to find our way around in space. Every person has two of them, one in each half of the brain.
wichtigste: The hippocampus gets its name from its shape, which is like a seahorse.
It lies in the temporal lobe of the brain.
Without a hippocampus you cannot form new memories.
Place cells in the hippocampus are active at particular places.
In deep sleep, memories are transferred to the cerebral cortex.
In the dentate gyrus, new nerve cells are formed even in adults.
The fornix is the most important output pathway of the hippocampus.

abschnitte.text: **Hippocampus** is the Latin word for **seahorse**. The name comes from its curved shape, which reminds you of a seahorse. It lies deep in the **temporal lobe**, on both sides of the brain. One part of it is called the **cornu ammonis**, or Ammon’s horn. The name recalls the ram’s horns of the Egyptian god Amun.

The hippocampus is important for forming **new memories**. It collects what we experience and learn and sorts it. This became well known through the patient **Henry Molaison**. In **1953**, because of severe epilepsy, parts of both his hippocampi were removed. Afterwards he could remember much from earlier, but could **no longer form new memories**.

The hippocampus is like a temporary store. Later, important memories are transferred to the **cerebral cortex**, where they stay for a long time. This happens especially intensively **during deep sleep**. That is why enough sleep is so important for learning, for example before an exam.

In the hippocampus there are **place cells**. They are active whenever you are at a particular place. Together they form a kind of map in your head. The researcher **John O'Keefe** discovered them. For this he received the Nobel Prize in **2014**, together with May-Britt and Edvard Moser, who found related cells in a neighbouring region.

For a long time people believed that no new nerve cells are formed in the adult brain. But many studies show that in the **dentate gyrus**, a part of the hippocampus, new nerve cells are formed even in adults. How strongly this happens in humans is still being researched. Through an arch-shaped bundle of fibres, the **fornix**, the hippocampus sends its signals to other parts of the brain.

gewusst: For decades, Henry Molaison was referred to in research only by his initials, H. M.
In London taxi drivers, who have to remember very many streets, researchers found an enlarged rear hippocampus.

teile.einleitung: In a heart transplant, a person with severe heart disease receives the healthy heart of a dead donor. It is one of the most difficult operations in medicine. Switzerland has played an important part in the history of this operation.
wichtigste: In the usual transplant, the donor heart replaces the old heart in the same place.
A donor heart can be kept outside the body for only a few hours when stored cool.
The first heart transplant in Switzerland took place in Zurich in 1969.
The medicine ciclosporin from Basel made transplants far more successful.
A transplanted heart is not connected to nerves.
A VAD can bridge the time until a donor heart is available.

abschnitte.text: A **heart transplant** is considered when a person’s own heart is so weak that other treatments no longer help. The donor heart comes from a dead person who wanted to donate their organs. In the usual **orthotopic transplant**, the old heart is removed and the donor heart is placed in the same spot. Because a heart kept cool may be outside the body for only **a few hours**, everything has to happen very fast.

The first heart transplant from person to person succeeded in 1967 in Cape Town in South Africa. As early as **1969** the first heart transplant in Switzerland followed, in **Zurich**. At that time many patients did not survive for long, because their body rejected the foreign heart. In Switzerland today, the foundation **Swisstransplant** coordinates the allocation of donor organs.

The body’s defences recognise the new heart as foreign and want to fight it. This is called **rejection**. A great step forward came with the medicine **ciclosporin**, which was developed at the company **Sandoz in Basel**. From the 1980s on, transplants became far more successful with it. Whether rejection is starting is often monitored with **small tissue samples** from the heart muscle.

In the operation, the nerves leading to the heart are cut. The new heart is therefore **not connected to nerves**. It still beats, because it has a pacemaker of its own. When you exert yourself, however, it reacts **with a delay**. The pulse rises only when hormones such as adrenaline reach the heart through the blood.

Because there are too few donor hearts, many people wait for a long time. A **ventricular assist device**, or **VAD** for short, is a small pump that takes the strain off the weak heart. It is often used for **bridging** until a donor heart is available. Researchers are also working with animal hearts. In **2022**, a **genetically modified pig’s** heart was transplanted into a living person for the first time in the USA.

gewusst: Ciclosporin is obtained from a fungus that was discovered in a soil sample from Norway.
The first Swiss heart transplant was carried out by the surgeon Åke Senning, who had also put in the first implanted pacemaker.

teile.einleitung: Herd immunity is protection that a whole community builds up together. When very many people are immune to an infectious disease, the germ can hardly spread any more. People who have no protection themselves also benefit from this.
wichtigste: Herd immunity protects people without immunity of their own, because many others are immune.
You become immune through a vaccination or by having had the disease.
The **basic reproduction number R0** says how many people a sick person infects on average if there is no protection.
The more infectious a disease is, the more immune people are needed.
With measles, about 95 per cent of people must be immune.
If the vaccination rate falls below the necessary threshold, outbreaks can happen again.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 thanks to worldwide vaccination programmes.

abschnitte.text: A disease germ needs people it can infect. If many people are **immune**, it keeps meeting someone it cannot get any further with. In this way the **chains of infection** break. People who cannot be vaccinated are then protected as well, for example babies who are still too young, or sick people with weak defences. That is why we talk about protection for the whole “herd”.

How infectious a disease is is described by the **basic reproduction number**, or **R0** for short. It tells you how many people a sick person infects on average when nobody is immune yet and there are no protective measures. A disease goes into decline when each sick person infects fewer than one other person on average. Then the number of cases gets smaller each time.

In a simplified way, the necessary threshold is worked out like this: 1 minus 1 divided by R0. With R0 = 4 this gives 1 minus 0.25, which is 0.75. Then about **75 per cent** of people must be immune. The greater R0 is, the higher the threshold. The calculation is a model: in reality, people’s age, contacts and place of residence also play a part.

**Measles** is one of the most infectious diseases of all. In a population without protection, one sick person can infect very many others. That is why very high immunity of around **95 per cent** is needed. If the vaccination rate in an area falls below that, outbreaks keep happening. In Switzerland, the Federal Office of Public Health recommends the measles vaccination for children.

A great success of vaccinations is **smallpox**. With worldwide vaccination programmes, the disease was pushed back step by step. In 1980 the **World Health Organization** (WHO) declared smallpox eradicated. So far it is the only infectious disease of humans that has been completely wiped out.

gewusst: The term herd immunity originally comes from veterinary medicine, where it was about protecting whole herds of cattle.
Smallpox is still the only infectious disease of humans that has been eradicated.

teile.einleitung: Glaucoma, in German called the “green star”, is an eye disease in which the optic nerve is slowly damaged. It often goes unnoticed for a long time, so check-ups at the eye doctor are important.
wichtigste: The medical term for the “green star” is glaucoma.
In glaucoma, the optic nerve is damaged.
The most important risk factor is raised pressure inside the eye.
Normal pressure inside the eye lies roughly between 10 and 21 mmHg.
The aqueous humour drains away through Schlemm's canal.
Acute angle closure is an emergency.
Nerve fibres that are lost cannot be regained.

abschnitte.text: In medicine, the “green star” is called **glaucoma**. It means a group of eye diseases in which the **optic nerve** is gradually damaged. The optic nerve carries the images from the eye to the brain. If its nerve fibres die, lasting **visual field loss** results: certain areas can then no longer be seen. Without treatment, this can lead to blindness.

In the eye, a clear fluid is constantly made, the **aqueous humour**. It is made in the ciliary body and drains away in the angle of the chamber through the trabecular meshwork into **Schlemm's canal**. If this drainage is disturbed, the **pressure inside the eye** rises. Normal is about 10 to 21 mmHg. A permanently higher pressure presses on the head of the optic nerve and is the most important risk factor. There are, however, also glaucomas with normal pressure.

abschnitte.titel: Often unnoticed for a long time
abschnitte.text: The most common form is **open-angle glaucoma**. It develops slowly and does not hurt. The losses begin at the outer edge of the visual field. The brain fills in gaps for a long time, so it is often noticed only late. That is why experts recommend regular **screening examinations** from middle age, in which the eye pressure is measured and the optic nerve is looked at.

Rarer is **acute angle closure**. In it, the angle of the chamber suddenly closes, and the pressure rises sharply. Typical are strong pain, a rock-hard eyeball, worse vision and nausea. This is an eye **emergency** that has to be treated at once so that the optic nerve is not permanently damaged.

Open-angle glaucoma is usually first treated with **pressure-lowering eye drops**. They reduce the making of aqueous humour or improve the drainage. If that is not enough, there are laser treatments or operations. What matters: nerve fibres that have already been lost cannot be regained. The treatment is meant to prevent further damage.

gewusst: Glaucoma is one of the most common causes of blindness in the world.
In open-angle glaucoma, many of those affected notice nothing for a long time, even though the optic nerve is already being damaged.
